title: Ash documentation review draft
text:
Ash documentation
The book begins with small calculations and follows how their data and functions connect. Work through the programs, predict their results, and use the observations to explain each step.
Begin with reader setup and Learn Ash. The library chapters develop reusable abstractions; the effects chapters develop requests, control, and scoped resources. The Cases then calculate algorithms and apply those ideas to larger problems. Follow each part in order, using its introduction for reading and practice guidance.

title: Reader setup
text:
Prepare Ash
The learning path uses the ash command-line tool. You need Git and a Rust toolchain that includes Cargo. Clone Ash with its Git URL, select the exact commit for this edition, and build it:
The executable is now target/debug/ash. Make the shorter name ash available in the current terminal:
Keep this terminal open while you work through the learning path. ASH_LIBRARIES selects the same checkout’s source libraries. The buffer lesson uses it with --root ffi="$ASH_LIBRARIES"; ordinary lessons need no root option. ASH_NATIVE_CACHE lets successive native builds reuse their dependencies. Native buffer builds currently require Linux x86-64 GNU, the matching Rust toolchain, cached Cargo dependencies, and a native linker. Their generated executables print a value without the interpreter’s : Type suffix.

title: Reader setup
text:
git clone git@github.com:dikini/ash-lang.git
cd ash-lang
git switch --detach 354c76b391fe4af665cf6a03479a9874a57cb3e3
cargo build --locked

export PATH="$PWD/target/debug:$PATH"
export ASH_LIBRARIES="$PWD/libraries"
export ASH_NATIVE_CACHE="$PWD/target/ash-doc-native"

title: Reader setup
text:
Read a diagnostic
When a lesson shows a rejected program, its transcript includes the command and the complete English message. A leading $ marks the shell prompt; do not type it. --message-format human --locale en selects that presentation explicitly. This compiler’s human renderer emits plain text without terminal color; it has no color option to set.
Ash prints canonical absolute source paths. In the displayed messages, only the checkout prefix is replaced by /path/to/ash-doc/. Your terminal will show your checkout’s actual location. The remainder of each path, source excerpt, label, and message is unchanged. Run the named checked-in example from the working directory given by its learning path to compare the message directly. A copy saved with another filename will naturally show that name instead.
Read the explanation first, then follow its source labels back to the program. The reason: line gives a secondary identifier for the kind of failure; it is not a replacement for the explanation. These source rejections write their messages on standard error, leave standard output empty, and exit with status 1.

title: Learn Ash
text:
Before you begin
These chapters form one path through Ash. Work with the programs as you read. Writing a program, predicting its result, and checking that prediction will teach you more than reading the finished code alone. The path is written for beginners; no prior programming experience is assumed.
You need a text editor, a terminal, Git, and a Rust toolchain with Cargo. Follow Prepare Ash to clone the source selected for this edition, build the command-line tool, and make ash available in your terminal. Keep that terminal open while you work through a lesson.
To compare a rejection with its displayed message, run the named checked-in example from the learning-path directory:
The first seventeen lessons use that shared directory for diagnostic commands. The two continuation chapters and the closing lesson state their own lesson-local src directory. The diagnostic commands use checked-in files even when the exploration asks you to edit your own program.ash or main.ash. Follow the shared diagnostic reading notes for the prompt, English output, and source-path convention.

title: Learn Ash
text: cd /path/to/ash-doc/content/learn

title: Learn Ash
section: How to work through a lesson
text:
How to work through a lesson
Keep your working programs in a scratch directory outside the checked-in lesson src trees. The chapters build on those working programs; each exercise names a fresh starting point. For a program with imports, keep its entry and required sibling files together in that directory.
Use the same cycle for each program:

Edit the program in your text editor.
Predict the value it will produce.
Run the program with ash.
Inspect the value and type that ash displays.
Explain why the program produced that result.

When your prediction differs from the result, pause. Work through the expressions one at a time, change the program, and run it again.

title: Learn Ash
text:
Learning with an assistant
You can work through every chapter without an assistant. If you use an LLM chat or coding agent, give it the current lesson, your program, and the output from ash. This instruction establishes its role:

Use this lesson, the repository, and the output from ash as evidence. Ask one question at a time. Help me compare my prediction with the result. Use only ideas introduced so far unless I ask to look ahead. Do not give me a finished exercise solution before helping me reason about it.

An assistant can help you examine a program or form a question. Run the program with ash to test what it does.

title: Learn Ash
text:
Contents

An Ash program — produce values with expressions and functions.
Using another source file — connect modules through imports, public declarations, and qualified names.
Using more than one input — supply chained inputs, pause at a partial call, and read function arrows.
Choosing a result — use integer equality, Boolean values, and exhaustive matching to select a result.
Naming intermediate values — make a block’s steps visible with local bindings.
Making values travel together — keep fixed collections of typed values together with tuples and tuple patterns.
Working with text — display, measure, and convert text with String values.
Defining data — name a new type and the constructors for its possible values.
Handling data forms — follow a data definition with patterns and exhaustive cases.
Patterns in depth — name exactly what a value contains with wildcards, nested patterns, and literal patterns.
Following recursive data — follow a self-reference with a recursive function and a stopping form.
The edges of the language — meet the forms Ash declines and the idioms that cover each absence.
Ordering from data — build the natural numbers and comparison from a data definition.
Functions as values — receive, construct, and return function values.
Definitions for many types — reuse functions and data definitions through type parameters.
Module channels — choose which public names cross a module boundary, and re-export them through a facade.
Opaque types — keep a type nameable across a boundary while hiding how its values are built.


Continuation chapters

Generalizing local functions — distinguish local generalization from a fixed function value.
Defining local recursion — use annotated recursive groups and distinguish guarded construction from forcing unfinished data.



Closing chapter

Where Ash goes next — meet interfaces, effects, and scoped resources in small programs, and follow them into the paths that develop them.

title: Learn Ash
text:
Continue learning
Working with effects and scoped resources begins with one new question: how can a calculation request a value that a surrounding handler supplies? It builds on the functions and signatures used in this path.

title: An Ash program
text:
Expressions calculate values
It is common to think of a program as a list of commands: do this, then do that. An Ash source file has a different shape. It contains definitions. Those definitions describe expressions, and expressions calculate values.
A runnable Ash program also needs a place to begin. Ash uses a definition named main. When you give a source file to ash, it evaluates main () and reports the resulting value and its type. Our first program keeps that calculation small enough to see as a whole.
Open a text editor, enter these two lines, and save them as program.ash:
The second line defines the calculation: its right side is the integer 42. The first line is its signature. Read Unit -> Int as “takes a Unit value and produces an Int value.” Unit, the unit type, has one value, written (); Int is the type of integer values.
Predict the value that main () produces, then run the file from your terminal:
Ash reports:
The report keeps the promise of the two lines. The right side of main is an expression, and evaluating it produces the reported value; the signature supplies the type.
Because main receives (), it needs no input before calculating its result. The entry rules require this starting definition to live in the file selected for execution.
Nothing in our first expression had to be worked out: 42 is already a value. An expression may also combine values with an operation. Suppose we still want 42, but want to obtain it by addition. Change the program to this:
The right side of main is now the expression 40 + 2. Before running the file, work out its value. The same command now reports:
Both programs produce the same value. In the first, the expression is already 42. In the second, Ash evaluates an addition to produce 42.
Expressions can contain smaller expressions. Consider what must happen when two different arithmetic operations appear together:
Multiplication groups more tightly than addition. Use that rule to predict the value before running. Ash reports 7 : Int; compare it with these steps:
The smaller multiplication produces 6; the addition then uses that value to produce 7.
Suppose we want the addition to happen first instead. Parentheses let us make that grouping part of the expression:
Only the grouping has changed. Predict its value, then run the file. Ash reports 9 : Int. The calculation now proceeds this way:
Parentheses make 1 + 2 the smaller expression that Ash evaluates first.
So far, main has held the entire calculation. Even the nested examples fit on one line. As a calculation grows, we need a way to name a useful part and use it inside another expression.

title: An Ash program
text:
main : Unit -> Int
main () = 40 + 2

ash program.ash
42 : Int


main : Unit -> Int
main () = 1 + 2 * 3

1 + 2 * 3
1 + 6
7


main : Unit -> Int
main () = (1 + 2) * 3

(1 + 2) * 3
3 * 3
9


With a learning assistant: Run both grouping programs. Show the assistant your predictions, the two programs, and the actual results from ash. Explain the difference yourself, then ask the assistant to question your explanation one step at a time.

title: An Ash program
text:
Giving a calculation a name
The next program names a calculation increment. It adds one to an integer:
increment : Int -> Int
increment number = number + 1

main : Unit -> Int
main () = increment 41
The first two lines belong together. The signature Int -> Int says that increment takes an integer and produces an integer. In the definition, number is a parameter: it stands for whichever input increment receives. The expression number + 1 describes how the result is calculated.
The last line uses the expression increment 41. This is a function call, and 41 is its argument. To understand the call, use 41 wherever the definition uses its parameter. This replacement of a parameter by its argument is called substitution. Predict the result before running:
ash program.ash
42 : Int
The substitution explains that observation:
increment 41
41 + 1
42
The argument replaces the parameter with 41, so the addition and the enclosing main both produce 42.
Once a calculation has a name, it can take part in another calculation. Add a function that doubles an integer, then use both functions in main:
increment : Int -> Int
increment number = number + 1

double : Int -> Int
double number = number * 2

main : Unit -> Int
main () = double (increment 20)
The parentheses keep increment 20 together as the argument to double. Start with that inner call and work outward to predict the result. Running the program reports 42 : Int, matching the trace:
double (increment 20)
double 21
21 * 2
42
Here the result of increment becomes the input to double. Connecting functions in this way is called function composition.

title: An Ash program
text:
Where does evaluation begin?
Our latest source file contains three definitions, yet Ash begins with main. Is main merely a name we happened to choose? We can find out by giving the same kind of calculation a different name:
answer : Unit -> Int
answer () = 42
Which definition in this file could supply the required main () call? Run the saved example from content/learn to check that entry requirement:
$ ash --message-format human --locale en what-is-an-ash-program/src/07-missing-main.ash
The entry module must define its own `main`; importing one is not enough.
  --> /path/to/ash-doc/content/learn/what-is-an-ash-program/src/07-missing-main.ash:1:1
1 | answer : Unit -> Int
  | ^ This is the entry module.
2 | answer () = 42
  | ^ This is the entry module.
reason: entry.missing-main
The first sentence names what is missing: the entry module must define its own main. The source labels cover this file’s answer definition and identify it as the entry module. Nothing in those lines is named main. The sentence also mentions imports; we will meet those in the next chapter. For this one-file program, rename both occurrences of answer to main to give Ash its starting definition.
The definition of answer describes a calculation, but Ash does not guess which definition should start the program. It looks for main and begins by evaluating main (). This is why every working program in the lesson has included that name.

title: An Ash program
text:
Exercise: square, then double
Start with a fresh copy of src/06-composition.ash in your scratch directory, saved as program.ash. Then compose a different pair of functions:

Define square : Int -> Int that multiplies its input by itself, and call it from main as double (square 3).
Work from the inner call outward and predict the result.
Run the program and compare the result with your calculation.


With a learning assistant: Show the assistant your program, prediction, and actual result from ash. Ask it to point to one expression at a time and ask what value that expression produces. Request a complete solution only after you have explained your own.

title: An Ash program
text:
The whole program
We can now answer the question in the title. At its simplest, an Ash program is one source file containing definitions, including one named main where evaluation begins. A definition gives a calculation a name. The expression on its right determines the value it produces, and function calls let one calculation use a value produced by another.
When you run the file, Ash evaluates main () and reports the resulting value and type. Every program here fits in one source file, but Ash programs need not stop there. The next question is how a definition in one file can be used from another.

title: Using another source file
text:
What remains inside a module?
The programs in the first chapter kept every definition in one source file. That kept each calculation in view as a whole. As a program grows, some definitions begin to belong together: arithmetic functions form one group, data-handling functions another, and main connects them for the result we want.
Ash lets us place such a group in its own source file. One file can then name the other and use the definitions it makes available. The files do not become separate programs. They are parts of one program, connected by an import.
Create a directory for this program. Inside it, create two files:
Begin with arithmetic.ash. It contains the calculation that will produce our answer:
Both definitions work as they did in the first chapter. double takes an integer and doubles it. answer calls double. The new word is pub, short for public. It says that another source file may use answer.
Now put this program in main.ash:
The first line connects the files. arithmetic names arithmetic.ash in the same directory; an import path leaves off the .ash extension. The name after as is the alias used in this file. We chose Arithmetic, so the call writes Arithmetic.answer.
Follow the qualified call into arithmetic.ash, then use its definition of double to predict the result. Run the entry file from calculation:
Ash follows the import, checks both files, and reports:
We can follow the same path by hand. main calls Arithmetic.answer (). answer calls double 21, and that expression produces 42:
Each Ash source file forms a module. The import gives the entry module a name for the imported module, and the qualified name Arithmetic.answer identifies one public definition in it. The alias belongs to main.ash; it is the name this file chose for that import.
Only answer carries pub. The helper double has no such marker. It is available throughout arithmetic.ash, which is why answer can call it, but it is not available through the import.
We can test that boundary by changing main.ash to call the helper directly:
Compare the requested name with the declarations carrying pub. Does this import make that call available? Run the saved version from content/learn:
The message names double as private. Its first label marks the inaccessible member in the call; the second takes us to double’s declaration in arithmetic.ash, where there is no pub. The import succeeded, but it did not make that helper public. Restore Arithmetic.answer () to use the module’s public calculation. Make public the definitions another module needs and leave supporting calculations inside their own module. The visibility rules preserve that distinction across an import.

title: Using another source file
text:
import arithmetic as Arithmetic

main : Unit -> Int
main () = Arithmetic.double 21

$ ash --message-format human --locale en using-another-source-file/src/02-private-main.ash
The declaration `double` is private to its defining module.
  --> /path/to/ash-doc/content/learn/using-another-source-file/src/02-private-main.ash:4:22
4 | main () = Arithmetic.double 21
  |                      ^ This name is not accessible here.
  --> /path/to/ash-doc/content/learn/using-another-source-file/src/arithmetic.ash:1:1
1 | double : Int -> Int
  | ^ The inaccessible declaration is here.
reason: resolve.unavailable-export


With a learning assistant: If an imported name is rejected, show the assistant both source files and the complete diagnostic. Ask it to connect the message and labels to the import, alias, declaration, and call before it suggests a change.

title: Using another source file
text:
Exercise: move square
Make a new two-file program in a fresh scratch directory, with arithmetic.ash and main.ash beside each other. This time the module offers a public square, and main asks for Arithmetic.square 6:

Define square : Int -> Int in arithmetic.ash, multiplying its input by itself, and mark it public.
Import the file in main.ash as Arithmetic, predict the value and type of the call, and run ash main.ash.
Remove pub from square, run the program once more, and explain the change in terms of the two modules.

title: Using another source file
text:
One program, two files
The entry file passed to ash is the program; an import only extends it. The alias belongs to the importing file, pub marks what crosses the module boundary, and definitions without it remain available only inside their own module.
Our functions still take one input each. What do the arrows and calls mean when a function needs more than one?

title: Using more than one input
text:
Supplying two inputs
Our functions have received one value at a time. double received one number; Arithmetic.answer received (). Many calculations need more information. To add two numbers, for example, a function must receive both of them.
Ash does not require a new kind of call for this. We can use a technique called currying. A function receives the first input and leaves a function ready to receive the second. Supplying both inputs in one line is the same process written without a pause. We can see the two steps by starting with a complete call and then stopping halfway through it.
Here is a function that adds two integers:
The definition names two parameters, left and right. In the call add 20 22, the inputs line up with those parameters from left to right. Predict the value, then save and run the program. Ash reports:
The substitution accounts for that result:
The signature tells the same story as the definition. Function arrows group from the right — the arrow is right-associative — so we read
as
The first Int is the first input. After that input arrives, what remains has the type Int -> Int: a function waiting for the second input. When the second Int arrives, the calculation produces the final Int.
crumbs: 5  Using more than one input

title: Using more than one input
text:
add : Int -> Int -> Int
add left right = left + right

main : Unit -> Int
main () = add 20 22

42 : Int

add 20 22
20 + 22
42

Int -> Int -> Int

Int -> (Int -> Int)
crumbs: 5  Using more than one input

title: Using more than one input
text:
Pausing after the first input
To make that middle step visible, remove 22 from the call. Since main now produces a function, its result type must change as well:
add : Int -> Int -> Int
add left right = left + right

main : Unit -> Int -> Int
main () = add 20
Before running, count the inputs still needed. add has received 20 for left; what remains to receive right, and what type does it have? Run the program to compare that prediction:
<function> : Int -> Int
No second integer has arrived, so the result is a function of type Int -> Int. The tool displays the function as <function>; that display does not show its body. Such a call is called a partial call, or partial application: it supplies some, but not all, of a function’s inputs. The result is still useful. It remembers the input already supplied and can receive the rest later.
Three margin figures show the same progression visually: the signature against its boxes, types layered over values in the complete call, and the partial call followed from add 20 through add_20 to 42.









Figure 5.1: Curried function.









Figure 5.2: Function application.









Figure 5.3: Partial application.




We can name the waiting function and use it in the next line:
add : Int -> Int -> Int
add left right = left + right

main : Unit -> Int
main () = {
    let add_20 = add 20
    add_20 22
}
The braces collect these lines into one block; its last line gives the block’s value. The binding let add_20 = add 20 gives the waiting function the name add_20. It remembers 20 and has type Int -> Int. The next line supplies 22 as its remaining input. Predict the result, then run the program and compare Ash’s 42 : Int with these steps:
add_20 22
add 20 22
20 + 22
42
crumbs: 5  Using more than one input

title: Using more than one input
text:
Exercise: multiply three numbers
Start from a fresh copy of src/01-two-inputs.ash in your scratch directory, and build a three-input multiplication with this signature:
multiply_three : Int -> Int -> Int -> Int
Then try three calls in main, one at a time: supply every input and predict the integer; supply only two and predict the waiting function’s type; give that function its final input and check the result. Use the arrows in the signature to account for every input and every result.
crumbs: 5  Using more than one input

title: Using more than one input
text:
From inputs to decisions
Several inputs change nothing about how a call reads: each value arrives from the left, each arrow says what remains, and a complete call reaches the final result. A partial call simply stops earlier, leaving a function that is still waiting.
Every calculation so far has followed one fixed route. What happens when the program must examine a value and choose the route?
crumbs: 5  Using more than one input

title: Choosing a result
text:
Asking a question
Every calculation in the preceding lessons followed one route. Once a call began, we could trace it from expression to expression without asking which step should come next. A useful program must sometimes let a value decide.
Ash makes that decision in two parts. First, an expression produces either true or false. Then a match provides one expression for each possibility.
Integer equality asks whether two integer expressions produce the same value. The result has type Bool:
Work through the addition before the equality, and predict the Boolean result. Running the program answers the equality:
The addition supplies the left input to equality:
Bool has exactly two values, true and false. Change the right side of the equality to 41 and predict the result before running the program again. The answer to the question changes, but the type remains Bool.
A Boolean value can tell us which result to use. It does not choose by itself; we must say what each of its two possible values means.

title: Choosing a result
text:
main : Unit -> Bool
main () = 20 + 22 == 42

true : Bool

20 + 22 == 42
42 == 42
true

title: Choosing a result
text:
Describing both choices
The following function receives a condition and two possible integer results:
choose : Bool -> Int -> Int -> Int
choose condition when_true when_false = match condition {
    true => when_true
    false => when_false
}

main : Unit -> Int
main () = choose true 42 0
Read the match from its first line. It examines condition. Each line inside the braces is an arm. The part before => names a possible form of the value; the expression after => gives the result for that form.
Use the supplied condition to choose an arm, then predict the value that arm returns. Run your working program; it reports 42 : Int. Trace why:
choose true 42 0
match true { ... }
42
If the call began choose false 42 0, the second arm would apply and the result would be 0. Both arms produce an Int, which agrees with the final Int in the signature of choose.
choose receives its inputs as evaluated values. The match selects one arm body after receiving the condition; it does not delay evaluation of the function’s arguments. Evaluating arguments before the body runs is called strict evaluation. The application and matching rules distinguish those steps.

title: Choosing a result
text:
Calculating the condition
A condition need not be written directly as true or false. Any expression that produces a Bool can guide the same match:
choose : Bool -> Int -> Int -> Int
choose condition when_true when_false = match condition {
    true => when_true
    false => when_false
}

main : Unit -> Int
main () = choose (20 + 22 == 42) 42 0
The parentheses keep the equality together as the first input to choose. Predict the condition first, then the selected result. Running the program reports 42 : Int, matching the trace:
choose (20 + 22 == 42) 42 0
choose true 42 0
42
The question and the choice are separate expressions. This separation lets the same choose function work with any calculation that produces a Bool.

title: Choosing a result
text:
Accounting for every value
Since Bool has two possible values, a match on Bool needs two arms. Consider a function that accounts only for true:
choose : Bool -> Int -> Int
choose condition number = match condition {
    true => number
}

main : Unit -> Int
main () = choose false 42
Compare the possible Bool values with the patterns in the match. Which input has no result expression? Run this version from content/learn:
$ ash --message-format human --locale en choosing-a-result/src/04-missing-choice.ash
These cases do not cover every possible input; for example, `false` is not covered.
  --> /path/to/ash-doc/content/learn/choosing-a-result/src/04-missing-choice.ash:2:27
2 | choose condition number = match condition {
  |                           ^ These cases do not cover every possible input; for example, `false` is not covered.
3 |     true => number
  | ^ These cases do not cover every possible input; for example, `false` is not covered.
4 | }
  | ^ These cases do not cover every possible input; for example, `false` is not covered.
reason: coverage.non-exhaustive
The message supplies false as an input the cases miss and labels the incomplete match. Add an arm such as false => 0 to give that input a result. An exhaustive match covers every possible form of the value it examines. Ash checks this before running the program, so execution cannot arrive at a choice with no corresponding expression.

With a learning assistant: Show the assistant the incomplete match and the complete diagnostic. Ask how the named missing value connects to the labelled match. Then explain why that value is possible and what arm would complete the match before asking for feedback.

title: Choosing a result
text:
Exercise: keep or double
Start from a fresh copy of src/02-choose.ash in your scratch directory.
Build a gate for one integer. When the gate is true, the number passes through unchanged; when it is false, the number doubles:
keep_or_double : Bool -> Int -> Int
Call the function once with each Boolean value, predicting both results before you run them. Then replace the direct Boolean in the call with an integer equality, and check that both arms still produce an Int, as the signature promises.

title: Choosing a result
text:
A complete decision
A choice now has two parts: one expression answers the question, and the match spends that answer, giving each possible value of Bool its own arm. Ash checks the coverage before running, so no call can reach a value the match leaves unanswered.
Each arm so far has held a short expression. When one route needs several steps, repeating a growing expression becomes hard to read; the next lesson gives the steps names.

title: Naming intermediate values
text:
Naming one result
A short expression often tells its own story. We can read double (increment 20) from the inside out and keep the intermediate value in mind. As more steps join the calculation, that silent value becomes easier to lose. A name can record what a step produced and give the next step something clear to use.
Ash uses a block when an expression needs such local names. The multiple-inputs lesson already used one to group a program’s lines. The block still produces one value, just as the smaller expressions in earlier lessons did. The difference is that it lets us describe the route to that value in several ordered steps.
Begin by naming the result of an addition:
The braces surround a block. Its first line is a let binding:
Ash evaluates the expression on the right and associates the resulting value with the name on the left. That name is available in the rest of the block; we say it is in scope there.
The last line is different. It is the expression whose value becomes the value of the whole block. Predict the value bound to answer and the value returned by the final expression, then run the program. Ash reports 42 : Int. Trace how that result follows:
The addition binds 42 to answer; the final expression uses that value. A binding names the intermediate result, while the final expression determines what the block returns.

title: Naming intermediate values
text:
main : Unit -> Int
main () = {
    let answer = 40 + 2
    answer
}

let answer = 40 + 2


let answer = 40 + 2   -- answer stands for 42
answer                -- the block produces 42

title: Naming intermediate values
text:
Letting one step use another
A block becomes more useful when a later binding uses a value named earlier:
main : Unit -> Int
main () = {
    let incremented = 20 + 1
    let doubled = incremented * 2
    doubled
}
Read the bindings from top to bottom. Predict each named value and the final result before running. Ash reports 42 : Int; the later initializer uses the value produced by the earlier one:
incremented = 20 + 1 = 21
doubled     = 21 * 2 = 42
The first binding produces 21, the next produces 42, and the final expression returns doubled. The binding rules explain how each initializer runs before its new names become available to the remainder.
These names belong to the block. They help explain this calculation without adding definitions that the rest of the source file can call. A useful local name describes the value’s part in the calculation: incremented says more than x, even though both names could refer to the same integer.

title: Naming intermediate values
text:
Names appear in order
The order of the bindings matters. A later binding can use an earlier name, but an earlier binding cannot reach forward to a name that has not appeared:
main : Unit -> Int
main () = {
    let answer = later + 2
    let later = 40
    answer
}
At the initializer later + 2, which names have already been introduced? Run this version from content/learn to check your account:
$ ash --message-format human --locale en naming-intermediate-values/src/03-forward-reference.ash
No term named `later` is in scope.
  --> /path/to/ash-doc/content/learn/naming-intermediate-values/src/03-forward-reference.ash:3:18
3 |     let answer = later + 2
  |                  ^ This name could not be resolved here.
reason: resolve.unknown-name
The message says later is not in scope and labels the use in answer’s initializer. Only names bound before a use are in scope there; later’s binding comes after it.
Move let later = 40 above the binding for answer, then run the program again. The revised order mirrors the dependency: first obtain later, then use it to obtain answer.

title: Naming intermediate values
text:
Exercise: expose the hidden steps
Rewrite this nested expression as a block:
main : Unit -> Int
main () = double (increment 20)
Start from the first lesson’s composition program: make a fresh scratch copy of its src/06-composition.ash. Keep the existing increment and double definitions. In the block:

name the result of increment 20;
name the result of doubling that value; and
use the second name as the block’s final expression.

Predict the value after each binding, then run the program. The rewritten calculation should still produce 42 : Int.

title: Naming intermediate values
text:
A calculation with visible steps
A block is an expression that introduces local names before producing its final value; read its bindings top to bottom and the source order is the calculation’s order. The last expression decides what leaves the block.
One name stands for one value. When two values belong to the same step, they need to travel together — the next lesson introduces a value that keeps such parts side by side.

title: Making values travel together
text:
Making a pair
A let binding gives one value a local name. That value may be the result of a long calculation, but it is still passed and returned as a unit. Sometimes two values describe one piece of information: a number and whether it is ready, or the two numbers at the ends of an interval. We want to keep the parts together without losing their individual types.
A tuple is one value made from a fixed number of other values. Its type is a product type, because the parts are present together rather than chosen between. Its commas are important. They show where one part ends and the next begins, both in the value and in its type.
The smallest tuple with several parts is a pair:
The expression puts two values into one pair. Predict its part order and the corresponding type order, then run the program:
The integer appears first and the Boolean second, giving type (Int, Bool). The pair is not an integer followed by a separate Boolean result. It is one result with two parts. If we exchanged the parts, the type would also change to (Bool, Int).
Parentheses alone already grouped arithmetic and function arguments in earlier lessons. The comma is what makes this expression a tuple. Thus (42) is still the integer 42, while (42, true) is a pair.

title: Making values travel together
text:
main : Unit -> (Int, Bool)
main () = (42, true)

(42, true) : (Int, Bool)

title: Making values travel together
text:
Receiving one pair
A function can receive a tuple as one input. Its parameter pattern names the parts:
sum_pair : (Int, Int) -> Int
sum_pair (left, right) = left + right

main : Unit -> Int
main () = sum_pair (20, 22)
The signature has one arrow. sum_pair receives one (Int, Int) value and produces an Int. The pattern (left, right) has the same shape as that input. Predict what each name binds and what their addition produces. Running confirms 42 : Int; the pattern assigns the parts in order:
sum_pair (20, 22)
20 + 22
42
This differs from the earlier function add : Int -> Int -> Int, defined in the multiple-inputs lesson. add receives one integer and then another; sum_pair receives one pair. Both can perform the same addition, but their inputs have different shapes and their signatures say so. Compare the complete calls with what remains after the first input:








Figure 8.1: sum_pair : (Int, Int) -> Int — one pair input, one integer result.









Figure 8.2: add : Int -> Int -> Int — separate integer inputs, one integer result.






Comparison
add
sum_pair




Type
Int -> Int -> Int
(Int, Int) -> Int


Full call
add 20 22
sum_pair (20, 22)


First supplied value
20 : Int
(20, 22) : (Int, Int)


Result after one input
Function of type Int -> Int
42 : Int



The curried add can pause after receiving 20; its second integer arrives in a later call. The one input to sum_pair contains both integers, so that call produces their sum. This follows from these two signatures.
sum_pair(20, 22) is the same call as sum_pair (20, 22). The space before ( is optional. The comma inside the parentheses makes (20, 22) one pair argument containing two parts.

title: Making values travel together
section: Naming the parts inside a block
text:
Naming the parts inside a block
Tuple patterns also work in the let bindings from the preceding lesson:
main : Unit -> Int
main () = {
    let pair = (20, 22)
    let (left, right) = pair
    left + right
}
The first binding gives the whole pair one name. The second binding takes that value apart by matching its shape. Afterward, the rest of the block can use left and right separately.
Predict the two part bindings and the final sum before running. The program reports 42 : Int. Trace how the whole pair supplies the separate names:
pair  = (20, 22)
left  = 20
right = 22
left + right = 42
Constructing a tuple brings values together. A tuple pattern gives its parts names. Neither operation changes the parts themselves.

title: Making values travel together
section: Shape is part of the type
text:
Shape is part of the type
A tuple always has a fixed number of parts. A triple is therefore not a pair, even when every part has the same type:
sum_pair : (Int, Int) -> Int
sum_pair (left, right) = left + right

main : Unit -> Int
main () = sum_pair (20, 21, 22)
Count the parts in the supplied value and in sum_pair’s input type. Does the one tuple argument have the required shape? Run from content/learn:
$ ash --message-format human --locale en values-travel-together/src/04-triple-is-not-a-pair.ash
This function argument must have type `(Int, Int)`, but has type `(Int, Int, Int)`.
  --> /path/to/ash-doc/content/learn/values-travel-together/src/04-triple-is-not-a-pair.ash:5:20
5 | main () = sum_pair (20, 21, 22)
  |                    ^ This has type `(Int, Int, Int)`.
  --> /path/to/ash-doc/content/learn/values-travel-together/src/04-triple-is-not-a-pair.ash:1:12
1 | sum_pair : (Int, Int) -> Int
  |            ^ This function requires an argument of type `(Int, Int)`.
  --> /path/to/ash-doc/content/learn/values-travel-together/src/04-triple-is-not-a-pair.ash:5:11
5 | main () = sum_pair (20, 21, 22)
  |           ^ This is the containing function application.
reason: type.argument
The first label identifies the triple, and the signature label identifies the pair required by sum_pair. There is no missing second call and no extra curried input. The one input has the wrong tuple shape. Supplying (20, 22) restores the two-part input and produces 42 : Int.

title: Making values travel together
text:
Exercise: keep two results
Start from a fresh copy of src/02-pair-input.ash in your scratch directory.
Give one pair of integers to a function that answers with two results at once:
sum_and_product : (Int, Int) -> (Int, Int)
Its result pair should hold the input’s sum and product. In main, use a local tuple pattern to name those two results and add them.
With (6, 7) as the input, predict the pair the function produces and the integer main reports, accounting for the type of each intermediate value before you run the program.

title: Making values travel together
text:
One value, several parts
A tuple is one value with a fixed set of parts, and its type records their number, order, and types. A pattern of the same shape gives those parts names, in a definition or a local binding alike.
Tuples suit combinations chosen at the point of use. A program also needs data whose names say what a value means and which forms it may take; the next lesson defines such data.

title: Working with text
text:
A first piece of text
Every result so far was an integer, a Boolean, or a tuple built from them. A program that greets its user, signs a message, or answers with a word works with text. Text is a value in Ash too. It has its own type, String, and ash displays it beside its type, as it displayed 42 : Int.
A string literal is text written between double quotes:
Predict what ash will display for this program, then run it:
The display puts the value in quotes and its type after the colon. The quotes mark where the text begins and ends; the string is the text between them, held as one value.

title: Working with text
text:
main : Unit -> String
main () = "Hello, Ash!"

"Hello, Ash!" : String

title: Working with text
section: A line break inside the quotes
text:
A line break inside the quotes
Some characters cannot be typed directly between the quotes. The escape \n stands for the line break, so one string can hold two lines:
main : Unit -> String
main () = "line one\nline two"
Predict the displayed value before running it:
"line one\nline two" : String
The value does not split across two output lines. The display repeats the escape spelling \n, keeping the result readable as one string. Ash admits six escapes: \" and \\ write a quote and a backslash, \n and \r write line breaks, \t writes a tab, and \0 writes a NUL. The lexical structure chapter lists them.

title: Working with text
text:
Measuring text
How much text does a string hold? The @builtin.string module supplies the operations defined for strings. It belongs to the @builtin root, which names modules that ship with the compiler, so this import needs no file of our own:
import @builtin.string as Text

main : Unit -> Int
main () = Text.byte_length "a\nb"
The alias Text gives the operations short qualified names. Text.byte_length reports how many bytes the string’s text occupies. Count them here: a letter, one line break written as an escape, another letter. Predict the integer before running:
3 : Int
The escape \n counts once, as one character of the text.

title: Working with text
text:
Text as bytes
A string is text. A program that stores text or sends it along works with its bytes, and Text.to_utf8 converts a string into those bytes:
import @builtin.string as Text

main : Unit -> Bytes
main () = Text.to_utf8 "a\nb"
Predict the result’s type and how many numbers its display will hold, then run it:
[97, 10, 98] : Bytes
The result’s type is Bytes, displayed as a list of numbers, one per byte. Three numbers appear, the same three that byte_length reported, so measuring a string and converting it describe its text consistently. The number in the middle is where the line break landed.

title: Working with text
text:
Equality still belongs to integers
The choosing-a-result lesson asked whether two integers are equal with ==. The same question about two strings comes naturally. Predict whether ash accepts this program, then run it from content/learn to compare with the complete message:
main : Unit -> Bool
main () = "a" == "a"
ash refuses the program before running it:
$ ash --message-format human --locale en working-with-text/src/05-string-equality.ash
This operator requires an `Int` operand, but this operand has type `String`.
  --> /path/to/ash-doc/content/learn/working-with-text/src/05-string-equality.ash:2:11
2 | main () = "a" == "a"
  |           ^ This has type `String`.
  --> /path/to/ash-doc/content/learn/working-with-text/src/05-string-equality.ash:2:15
2 | main () = "a" == "a"
  |               ^ This operator requires `Int` operands.
reason: type.operator-operand
The first label points at the left operand and reports its type, String. The second label points at the operator itself and repeats its requirement: operands of type Int. The operator rules fix those operand types, and they cover addition too: in this edition + and == combine and compare integers only, so no operator joins two strings into one. The string module does supply a comparison by name — Text.equal takes the two strings as one pair — but at this surface text is measured and converted, not combined.

title: Working with text
text:
Exercise: a two-line greeting
Start from a fresh copy of src/03-byte-length.ash in your scratch directory.
A name tag holds two lines — Hello, on the first and Ada on the second — built from one string literal. Adapt the program so that main displays that string, then predict and check two more things: how many bytes Text.byte_length reports for the greeting, and which number in the Text.to_utf8 display holds the line break.

title: Working with text
text:
Text among the values
Text behaves like the values you already know: it displays beside its type, and escapes write the characters the keyboard cannot. The @builtin.string module measures text and converts it to bytes. What this edition does not offer is an operator that combines strings; + and == remain with integers.
A string suits text written at the point of use. A program also needs data whose names say what a value means and which forms it may take; the next lesson defines such data.

title: Defining data
text:
Naming the possible forms
An integer says how many; a Boolean says yes or no; a tuple keeps a fixed set of parts together. These types are useful, but their names do not always say what the values mean in a particular program. The integer 42 might be a score, a count, or a value found by a search. A program becomes easier to understand when its data can carry those distinctions.
An Ash data definition introduces a new type and lists the forms that values of that type may take. The form names belong to the program’s subject. They let the data say more than its underlying integers and Booleans could say alone.
Suppose a signal can tell a calculation either to continue or to stop:
Read the definition as a description: a Signal is either Go or Stop. Signal is the new type. Go and Stop are its constructors, the two ways to construct a value of that type.
The vertical bar means “or.” It separates one possible form from the next. The indentation keeps the alternatives together as one definition.
A type defined by listing its constructors is called an algebraic data type (ADT).1 The separated alternatives give the sum, and the fields of one constructor give the product; both parts appear as the definitions in this lesson grow.
The expression Go is already a complete value. Predict which constructor and type name Ash will report, then run:
Change main to produce Stop. Ash then reports Stop : Signal. The two values differ, but both belong to the type named by the definition.

title: Defining data
text:
type Signal =
    Go
    | Stop

main : Unit -> Signal
main () = Go



1 Some literature abbreviates abstract data type as ADT instead. In this path, ADT always means algebraic data type.
Go : Signal

title: Defining data
section: A form that carries a value
text:
A form that carries a value
A constructor may also keep fields inside the value it constructs. A search, for example, may either find an integer or find nothing:
type Result =
    Found(Int)
    | Missing

main : Unit -> Result
main () = Found(42)
The data definition gives us two cases to consider:

Found(number) represents a result that contains an integer;
Missing represents a result with no integer to carry.

Found is a constructor that needs one Int. The expression Found(42) supplies that field and produces a Result. Missing needs no fields and is a Result by itself.
Predict how the report will distinguish a found integer from an integer alone, then run. Ash preserves the form and field:
Found(42) : Result
The type describes what every Result may look like. A particular value uses one constructor from that definition.

title: Defining data
section: A new name makes a new type
text:
A new name makes a new type
Two data definitions remain distinct even when their constructors have the same field types:
type Score = Score(Int)
type Count = Count(Int)

keep_score : Score -> Score
keep_score score = score

main : Unit -> Score
main () = keep_score (Count(42))
Both constructors carry one integer. Follow the supplied constructor back to its type declaration, then compare that identity with the input required by keep_score. Does the shared field shape establish the required type? Run this version from content/learn:
$ ash --message-format human --locale en defining-data/src/03-distinct-types.ash
This function argument must have type `Score`, but has type `Count`.
  --> /path/to/ash-doc/content/learn/defining-data/src/03-distinct-types.ash:8:22
8 | main () = keep_score (Count(42))
  |                      ^ This has type `Count`.
  --> /path/to/ash-doc/content/learn/defining-data/src/03-distinct-types.ash:4:14
4 | keep_score : Score -> Score
  |              ^ This function requires an argument of type `Score`.
  --> /path/to/ash-doc/content/learn/defining-data/src/03-distinct-types.ash:8:11
8 | main () = keep_score (Count(42))
  |           ^ This is the containing function application.
reason: type.argument
The message names both nominal types. The argument label points into Count(42), while the signature label identifies Score as the required input. Replace Count(42) with Score(42) and the call produces Score(42) : Score. The constructor tells Ash which data definition created the value; changing only its contained integer could not repair this mismatch.

title: Defining data
text:
Exercise: describe a reading
Start from a fresh copy of src/02-result-with-value.ash in your scratch directory.
Define a type named Reading for a sensor that may or may not have a value:

Exact(Int) carries a measured integer;
Unavailable carries no fields.

Write main : Unit -> Reading and construct an Exact reading, predicting its value and type before running. Then change only the result expression to an unavailable reading and predict that observation too.
Finish by explaining, in one sentence per constructor, what information that form represents. A data definition should describe the values of the program, not merely demonstrate syntax.

title: Defining data
text:
Data shaped for the program
A data definition creates a type by naming every way to construct its values — some constructors are complete on their own, others carry fields, and the type name keeps even same-shaped values distinct.
We can now build every form of Result. A useful function must also be able to handle them; the next lesson connects these definitions to the matches and patterns we already know.

title: Handling data forms
text:
Matching the data definition
The preceding lesson gave Result two possible forms. We can construct Found(42) or Missing, and their shared type tells us that either value may arrive wherever a Result is expected. A function that receives one must be prepared for both.
The data definition guides the function. For each constructor in the definition, we write a pattern with the same shape and an expression that says what that form means for the calculation.
Suppose we want the integer carried by a found result, and zero when there is no integer:
Place the data definition beside the match:
Each constructor has a corresponding arm. The pattern Found(value) does two jobs: it recognizes the Found form and gives its integer field the local name value. The Missing form has no field to name.
Predict which arm handles Found(42), what value binds, and what the function returns. Run it, then change the call to value_or_zero Missing and predict that result before running again.
The observations are 42 : Int and 0 : Int. The Found pattern binds its field to value; the Missing arm supplies its own integer because there is no field. Both paths agree with the signature’s result type.

title: Handling data forms
text:
type Result =
    Found(Int)
    | Missing

value_or_zero : Result -> Int
value_or_zero result = match result {
    Found(value) => value
    Missing => 0
}

main : Unit -> Int
main () = value_or_zero (Found(42))

Found(Int)    Found(value) => value
Missing       Missing      => 0

title: Handling data forms
section: Letting the equations follow the forms
text:
Letting the equations follow the forms
When a function begins by matching one of its inputs, Ash can place the patterns directly in separate equations:
type Result =
    Found(Int)
    | Missing

value_or_zero : Result -> Int
value_or_zero Found(value) = value
value_or_zero Missing = 0

main : Unit -> Int
main () = value_or_zero (Found(42))
The signature still belongs to the whole function. The two equations describe what that function does for the two forms of Result. Before running, locate the equation selected by each input and compare with the explicit match. The first call reports 42 : Int; the two calculations are:
value_or_zero Found(42)
42
and
value_or_zero Missing
0
This definition and the explicit match answer the same question. Use the shape that keeps the explanation close to the data. Separate equations are useful when the entire definition follows the input’s forms.

title: Handling data forms
section: Following every branch of the definition
text:
Following every branch of the definition
The data definition is also a checklist. If an equation handles Found but no equation handles Missing, the function is incomplete:
type Result =
    Found(Int)
    | Missing

value_or_zero : Result -> Int
value_or_zero Found(value) = value

main : Unit -> Int
main () = value_or_zero Missing
Compare every form allowed by Result with the equations. Which form has no result, and would changing only main’s input fulfill the function’s contract? Run this version from content/learn:
$ ash --message-format human --locale en handling-data-forms/src/03-missing-constructor.ash
These cases do not cover every possible input; for example, `Missing` is not covered.
  --> /path/to/ash-doc/content/learn/handling-data-forms/src/03-missing-constructor.ash:5:1
5 | value_or_zero : Result -> Int
  | ^ These cases do not cover every possible input; for example, `Missing` is not covered.
6 | value_or_zero Found(value) = value
  | ^ These cases do not cover every possible input; for example, `Missing` is not covered.
reason: coverage.non-exhaustive
The message names Missing and labels the incomplete value_or_zero definition. Restoring value_or_zero Missing = 0 gives that form its own result. The problem exists whether or not main happens to construct Missing. The signature accepts any Result, and the data definition says that Missing is one. The equations must keep that promise.
When a constructor carries several fields, its pattern must have the same number and order of parts. The pattern then supplies a local name for each part the expression needs.

title: Handling data forms
text:
Exercise: respond to a signal
Start from a fresh copy of src/02-equations.ash in your scratch directory, and return to the earlier definition:
type Signal =
    Go
    | Stop
Give Signal a function again: signal_value : Signal -> Int, with one equation per constructor — Go produces 1, Stop produces 0. Call it with each value and predict both results.
Then rewrite the equations as one explicit match, keeping the signature and both observations unchanged. Explain how each line of the data definition leads to one equation and one match arm.

title: Handling data forms
text:
Functions that follow data
Handling a data type means one pattern per permitted form: the constructor identifies the form, the pattern names its fields, and Ash checks the coverage before running. The data so far has contained only existing values, but a definition may also refer to the type it defines, letting one value lead to another of the same shape. The next lesson follows that self-reference with a recursive function.

title: Patterns in depth
text:
Naming the field a calculation needs
The preceding lesson matched each constructor of a data type with its own equation, and every pattern named every field its constructor carries. Real functions are rarely that thorough. A report of the points earned from a marked answer has no use for the points possible, and a function that keeps the first integer of a pair never inspects the second. This lesson extends the pattern vocabulary for such functions: ignore a field without naming it, follow a value two layers deep, build a pattern from the small values themselves, and state a type beside a pattern.
A marked answer carries two integers, the points earned and the points possible; a blank answer carries nothing:
The Marked equation names its first field earned and writes _ for the second. Predict the result for the marked answer shown, then run the program; Ash reports 42 : Int.
Now change the call to earned_points (Marked(42, 60)) and predict again. The second field changed, and the result did not; Ash again reports 42 : Int. The _ pattern is called the wildcard: it matches whatever value occupies its field and binds no name for it, so one equation serves every possible second field. The Blank equation names no field because its constructor carries none.

title: Patterns in depth
text:
type Answer =
    Marked(Int, Int)
    | Blank

earned_points : Answer -> Int
earned_points Marked(earned, _) = earned
earned_points Blank = 0

main : Unit -> Int
main () = earned_points (Marked(42, 50))

title: Patterns in depth
section: Ignoring a field is not ignoring a case
text:
Ignoring a field is not ignoring a case
The wildcard answers a question about fields. It does not answer the other question the function must answer: which constructors have equations. Remove the Blank equation:
type Answer =
    Marked(Int, Int)
    | Blank

earned_points : Answer -> Int
earned_points Marked(earned, _) = earned

main : Unit -> Int
main () = earned_points (Marked(42, 50))
Every field of Marked is named, so the remaining equation looks complete. Compare its patterns with the data definition; which constructor has no result? Run this version from content/learn:
$ ash --message-format human --locale en patterns-in-depth/src/02-missing-case.ash
These cases do not cover every possible input; for example, `Blank` is not covered.
  --> /path/to/ash-doc/content/learn/patterns-in-depth/src/02-missing-case.ash:5:1
5 | earned_points : Answer -> Int
  | ^ These cases do not cover every possible input; for example, `Blank` is not covered.
6 | earned_points Marked(earned, _) = earned
  | ^ These cases do not cover every possible input; for example, `Blank` is not covered.
reason: coverage.non-exhaustive
The message names Blank and labels the incomplete earned_points definition, from its signature through the remaining equation. The wildcard ignored one field of one constructor; it said nothing about the other constructor, and coverage still asks for every constructor. Restoring earned_points Blank = 0 gives that form its own result.

With a learning assistant: Show the assistant the single equation and the complete diagnostic. Ask which words of the message name the missing case and which label the definition. Then explain why ignoring a field of Marked could never cover Blank before asking for feedback.

title: Patterns in depth
section: Following a value two layers deep
text:
Following a value two layers deep
One type’s field may hold another data type’s value. An entry is either a graded answer or a skip:
type Answer =
    Marked(Int, Int)
    | Blank

type Entry =
    Graded(Answer)
    | Skipped

earned_from : Entry -> Int
earned_from Graded(Marked(earned, _)) = earned
earned_from Graded(Blank) = 0
earned_from Skipped = 0

main : Unit -> Int
main () = earned_from (Graded(Marked(42, 50)))
The first pattern reaches through both layers: Graded(Marked(earned, _)) applies only when the entry holds a graded marked answer, and then earned names that answer’s first field. The possible points stay unnamed, and the other two equations keep their own forms. Predict the result for the graded answer shown, then change main’s input to Graded(Blank) and to Skipped, predicting each result before running. The first call reports 42 : Int; the other two report 0 : Int.
Writing both layers in one pattern keeps the equation’s shape next to the value’s shape. Two matches, one per layer, would ask the same question with more machinery.

title: Patterns in depth
section: Patterns built from the values themselves
text:
Patterns built from the values themselves
Bool has two values, and either may stand directly in an equation. The choose function of the fourth lesson matched on its condition; the same function writes as two equations:
pick : Bool -> Int -> Int -> Int
pick true when_true when_false = when_true
pick false when_true when_false = when_false

main : Unit -> Int
main () = pick (20 + 22 == 42) 42 0
The literal patterns true and false select an equation by the condition’s value. Coverage is checked across them as across any other patterns: omit the second equation and the report names false as an uncovered input. The unit value has a literal pattern too, and it has stood in every program so far — main () is an equation whose pattern is (). Predict which equation the call shown selects, then run it; Ash reports 42 : Int.

title: Patterns in depth
section: Stating the type beside the pattern

title: Patterns in depth
text:
Exercise: count the integers
Start from a fresh copy of src/01-earned-points.ash in your scratch directory, and give the program this definition instead:
type Roll =
    Both(Int, Int)
    | One(Int)
    | None
Define count : Roll -> Int that counts the integers a roll carries: Both holds two, One holds one, and None holds none. The count never inspects the integers themselves, so let the wildcard keep every field unnamed. Call count with each form of Roll, predicting all three results before you run them.
Then define add_up : Roll -> Int that adds every integer a roll carries. Name only the fields the addition needs. Compare the two definitions: which equations changed shape, and which stayed the same?

title: Patterns in depth
text:
What a pattern can say
Across these programs, one idea repeats: a pattern describes the shape of the value it matches. The wildcard fills a field without naming it. A nested pattern follows the value’s layers. Literal patterns let Bool and Unit values select the equation for themselves. A stated type gives the pattern something to be checked against. And coverage asks, of every pattern alike, which values still have no equation.
Every value so far has a bounded shape — one answer, one entry, one roll. A data definition may instead refer to the very type it defines, letting one value contain another of the same shape. The next lesson follows that self-reference.

title: Following recursive data
text:
A finite list of integers
The data definitions so far have been shallow. A Found value contains an integer, and a Missing value contains nothing. Once a pattern exposes those fields, the function has reached the end of the value.
Some data grows by repeating one shape. A line of integers may contain a first integer followed by the rest of the line. That rest is itself another line of integers. An algebraic data type can express this repetition: its definition refers to the very type it defines.
Here is a type for such values:
Read the definition one form at a time:
The second field of More is the self-reference. It permits another More value, whose second field may permit another. In the finite lists here, following those rest fields reaches Empty.
The value in main has two More layers. Indentation makes its structure easier to see:
The first layer carries 20. Its rest is a list whose first integer is 22. That second layer’s rest is Empty, so the value is finite. Predict the nested value and its type before running; Ash displays:

title: Following recursive data
text:
type IntList =
    Empty
    | More(Int, IntList)

main : Unit -> IntList
main () = More(20, More(22, Empty))


Empty represents a list with no integers;
More(first, rest) represents one integer followed by another IntList.



More(20,
    More(22,
        Empty))

More(20, More(22, Empty)) : IntList

title: Following recursive data
section: A function with the same shape
text:
A function with the same shape
To add every integer in an IntList, begin as before: give each form in the data definition an equation.
type IntList =
    Empty
    | More(Int, IntList)

sum : IntList -> Int
sum Empty = 0
sum More(first, rest) = first + sum rest

main : Unit -> Int
main () = sum (More(20, More(22, Empty)))
For Empty, there is no integer to add, so the result is 0 — the base case, answered directly, without another call. For More, the pattern gives names to the first integer and the rest of the list. We can add first directly. To find what the entire rest contributes, the function applies itself to that smaller list.
This is a recursive call. It follows the recursive field in the data. For this finite input, count the More layers still to visit at each call. Predict the result before running; Ash reports 42 : Int. Compare the pending additions with this trace:
sum (More(20, More(22, Empty)))
20 + sum (More(22, Empty))
20 + (22 + sum Empty)
20 + (22 + 0)
42
Each call receives one fewer More layer, until Empty supplies 0. The pending additions combine that base result with 22 and then 20. This finite input and the move to its smaller rest explain why this traversal ends. Exhaustive equations alone do not prove that every recursive call terminates.

With a learning assistant: Give the assistant a three-element IntList and your trace of sum. Ask it to check that each recursive call receives exactly the rest field from the preceding value. Keep the arithmetic and final explanation as your work.

title: Following recursive data
text:
The ending form still matters
It may be tempting to write only the More equation because that is where the addition happens:
type IntList =
    Empty
    | More(Int, IntList)

sum : IntList -> Int
sum More(first, rest) = first + sum rest

main : Unit -> Int
main () = sum Empty
Empty is itself a valid IntList, as well as the ending form reached by the finite lists here. Which equation gives it a result? Run this version from content/learn to check that coverage requirement:
$ ash --message-format human --locale en following-recursive-data/src/03-missing-empty.ash
These cases do not cover every possible input; for example, `Empty` is not covered.
  --> /path/to/ash-doc/content/learn/following-recursive-data/src/03-missing-empty.ash:5:1
5 | sum : IntList -> Int
  | ^ These cases do not cover every possible input; for example, `Empty` is not covered.
6 | sum More(first, rest) = first + sum rest
  | ^ These cases do not cover every possible input; for example, `Empty` is not covered.
reason: coverage.non-exhaustive
The message names Empty and labels the incomplete sum definition. Restoring sum Empty = 0 supplies the ending result that the More equation needs when it follows rest. Coverage checks the same promise as before: sum : IntList -> Int must handle every IntList. With recursive data, the non-recursive form also provides the result from which the longer cases can be calculated.

title: Following recursive data
text:
Exercise: count the integers
Start from a fresh copy of src/02-sum.ash in your scratch directory, keeping the data definition. Define length : IntList -> Int by following the two forms of the data:

the length of Empty is 0;
the length of More(first, rest) is one more than the length of rest.

The first field is not needed for this calculation, but its place still appears in the constructor pattern. Test the function with Empty, a one-element list, and the two-element list from the lesson. Predict each result before running the program.
Then compare the definitions of length and sum. Both follow rest; only the expression that combines the first part with the recursive result changes.

title: Following recursive data
text:
Recursion follows self-reference
In these finite lists, every rest holds fewer layers of the same type, so the call that follows it makes progress, and Empty supplies the ending result. The data definition guides the cases; the input and the recursive argument explain why this traversal ends. One equation per constructor, recursing into the data’s own fields, is called structural recursion.
So far, every function has been called by name where it is used. Functions are also values — they can be received, returned, and made for a particular calculation. The next two lessons map what this language declines and then build its missing arithmetic from data; the lesson after those develops functions as values directly.

title: The edges of the language
text:
A note the program cannot carry
The programs so far have grown from a single calculation into data definitions, recursive functions, and matches. Each new form extended what you could say. Every language also draws a boundary around what it admits, and knowing Ash’s boundary prevents surprises: it explains why the book’s idioms look the way they do.
This lesson tours the boundary from the inside. At each stop we attempt something Ash declines, read the compiler’s complete answer, and name the idiom that covers the need. The refusals are deliberate, and every one points at a working alternative.
Other languages let a source file carry notes for its next reader — comments that explain a choice without changing what the program does. Try adding one to the smallest program:
The note is written for a reader; predict how the compiler answers it. Run this program from content/learn:
The message names what it found — the whole // explain this line — and states the rule in words. Its reason line, lex.comment, identifies the message family for later comparison; the sentence above it carries the teaching.
The refusal suggests the idiom. An Ash program explains itself through its signature, its names, and small definitions whose scope is easy to see. Longer explanations live beside the file, in a lesson or a document such as this one. Every chapter you have read follows that arrangement: the prose is the comment’s home.
crumbs: 14  The edges of the language

title: The edges of the language
text:
// explain this
main : Unit -> Int
main () = 1

$ ash --message-format human --locale en edges-of-the-language/src/01-comment.ash
Ash does not support comments.
  --> /path/to/ash-doc/content/learn/edges-of-the-language/src/01-comment.ash:1:1
1 | // explain this
  | ^ Ash does not support comments.
reason: lex.comment
crumbs: 14  The edges of the language

title: The edges of the language
text:
Counting below zero
Ash counts 0, 1, 2, and upward; every integer literal is nonnegative. Suppose a calculation needs one less than zero:
main : Unit -> Int
main () = -1
Predict the compiler’s answer before running it:
$ ash --message-format human --locale en edges-of-the-language/src/02-negative-one.ash
An expression is required here.
  --> /path/to/ash-doc/content/learn/edges-of-the-language/src/02-negative-one.ash:2:11
2 | main () = -1
  |           ^ An expression is required here.
  --> /path/to/ash-doc/content/learn/edges-of-the-language/src/02-negative-one.ash:2:13
2 | main () = -1
  |             ^ Parsing resumes at this boundary.
reason: parse.expected-form
The parser expected an expression after =, and - cannot begin one: a leading minus is not part of an integer literal. The second label marks where parsing resumes; the compiler reports and stops, so a declined program never runs in a damaged state.
Stand the question on its head. Without subtraction, a program seems unable to count downward at all — so where would descent come from? Hold that question; the next stop sharpens it, and the lesson after this one follows it.
crumbs: 14  The edges of the language

title: The edges of the language
text:
The operators Ash declines
The arithmetic in this edition is exactly three operators: + and * on integers, and ==, which asks whether two integers are equal. A reader arriving from another language expects a fourth operation on that list to work:
main : Unit -> Int
main () = 40 - 2
Here 40 is already a complete expression, so predict what the parser expects where - appears. Run it:
$ ash --message-format human --locale en edges-of-the-language/src/03-subtract.ash
A logical line end is required here.
  --> /path/to/ash-doc/content/learn/edges-of-the-language/src/03-subtract.ash:2:14
2 | main () = 40 - 2
  |              ^ A logical line end is required here.
  --> /path/to/ash-doc/content/learn/edges-of-the-language/src/03-subtract.ash:2:17
2 | main () = 40 - 2
  |                 ^ Parsing resumes at this boundary.
reason: parse.expected-form
The message records a completed expression: after 40, only the end of the logical line is expected, and - cannot extend the line. There is no subtraction to type-check because subtraction is not in the grammar — the grammar, not the operand, is what declines.
Comparison meets the same boundary. Try asking whether one integer sits below another:
main : Unit -> Bool
main () = 1 < 2
Predict the message, then run it:
$ ash --message-format human --locale en edges-of-the-language/src/04-less-than.ash
A logical line end is required here.
  --> /path/to/ash-doc/content/learn/edges-of-the-language/src/04-less-than.ash:2:13
2 | main () = 1 < 2
  |             ^ A logical line end is required here.
  --> /path/to/ash-doc/content/learn/edges-of-the-language/src/04-less-than.ash:2:16
2 | main () = 1 < 2
  |                ^ Parsing resumes at this boundary.
reason: parse.expected-form
After 1, the parser again expects the line to end; < plays its role in declarations, not between expressions. What these operators would answer, Ash programs build from data definitions — the next lesson shows the build. The Cases path makes the same move at larger scale: its ordered tree derives comparison by structural recursion over a data-built number type. The boundary also excludes floating-point literals, character literals, and integer literal patterns; the programs in this path need none of them.
crumbs: 14  The edges of the language

title: The edges of the language
text:
Composing conditions
The fourth lesson built decisions from Bool: == produces one, and match spends it. Other languages also offer operators that combine Booleans, and they are written with characters Ash’s alphabet omits:
main : Unit -> Bool
main () = true && false
Predict the answer, then run it:
$ ash --message-format human --locale en edges-of-the-language/src/05-boolean-and.ash
This character cannot begin an Ash token.
  --> /path/to/ash-doc/content/learn/edges-of-the-language/src/05-boolean-and.ash:2:16
2 | main () = true && false
  |                ^ This character cannot begin an Ash token.
reason: lex.unknown-character
This character cannot begin an Ash token.
  --> /path/to/ash-doc/content/learn/edges-of-the-language/src/05-boolean-and.ash:2:17
2 | main () = true && false
  |                 ^ This character cannot begin an Ash token.
reason: lex.unknown-character
The lexer — the stage that splits source into tokens — reports one message per character: & cannot begin a token, so && never reaches the parser. Two unknown characters, two identical reports.
The idiom composes conditions without an operator. A match already selects on a Bool directly, and the choose function of the fourth lesson routes a condition to either of two results; when two conditions must hold together, give the combination a name:
both : Bool -> Bool -> Bool
both first second = match first {
    true => second
    false => false
}

main : Unit -> Bool
main () = both (20 + 22 == 42) (1 * 1 == 1)
Read both as a match on its first condition: when first is true, the combined answer is whatever second is; when first is false, the combination is false. Predict the call’s result before running; Ash answers true : Bool. A condition worth reusing is a condition worth naming.

With a learning assistant: Show the assistant one declined program from this lesson and its complete diagnostic. Ask which stage — lexer, parser, or type checker — produced each labelled part, and what rule its words name. Then explain the label positions back in your own words before asking for feedback.
crumbs: 14  The edges of the language

title: The edges of the language
text:
The operator’s contract
The last stop is the subtlest, because the attempt looks almost legal. + accepts two integer operands; what does the compiler say about an operand of the wrong type?
main : Unit -> Int
main () = true + 1
Predict the message before running it:
$ ash --message-format human --locale en edges-of-the-language/src/07-bool-plus-int.ash
This operator requires an `Int` operand, but this operand has type `Bool`.
  --> /path/to/ash-doc/content/learn/edges-of-the-language/src/07-bool-plus-int.ash:2:11
2 | main () = true + 1
  |           ^ This has type `Bool`.
  --> /path/to/ash-doc/content/learn/edges-of-the-language/src/07-bool-plus-int.ash:2:16
2 | main () = true + 1
  |                ^ This operator requires `Int` operands.
reason: type.operator-operand
Unlike the earlier stops, this program parses; it fails one step later, when types are checked. The two labels restate the operator’s operand contract: the label on true reports what the operand has, and the label on + reports what the operator requires. The fix is the contract itself — give + two Int operands — and when a calculation needs more than three operators can say, an Ash program defines it from data, the move the next lesson makes.
crumbs: 14  The edges of the language

title: The edges of the language
text:
Exercise: predict the boundary
Work in your scratch directory. Here are five tiny programs, each two lines long, separated by blank lines. For each one, predict whether Ash accepts it. For those you predict Ash accepts, predict the value and type it prints; for those you predict it declines, predict which stage answers — lexer, parser, or type checker — and what rule its words name. Then run all five and reconcile each outcome with your prediction.
main : Unit -> Int
main () = 6 * 7

main : Unit -> Bool
main () = 41 + 1 == 42

main : Unit -> Int
main () = 1 // one

main : Unit -> Bool
main () = 1 < 2

main : Unit -> Bool
main () = true == false
For any prediction that missed, read the message’s labels again: each one points at the character or operand where the rule engaged. Finish by writing one more two-line program of your own that Ash accepts and that uses ==; predict its value and type before running it.
crumbs: 14  The edges of the language

title: The edges of the language
text:
The boundary is knowable
