Six attempts, six answers — and each answer named its rule in words: no comments, no negative literals, no subtraction, no ordering operators, no boolean operators, and operator contracts checked before anything runs. Ash declines at the exact stage responsible: the lexer for tokens, the parser for grammar, the type checker for contracts.
The refusals were the lesson; the needs behind them are covered. Notes live beside the program; conditions compose through match and named helpers; and descent and comparison are built from data definitions, as the Cases path’s ordered tree already shows. Every need that arises in this book meets an idiom in its remaining lessons.
One question stays open. With no subtraction and no ordering operators, how does a program count downward or compare two numbers? The next lesson follows that question: it defines a number type from data and builds comparison on top of the definition.
crumbs: 14  The edges of the language

title: Ordering from data
text:
The numbers, built as data
The last lesson left one question standing. With no subtraction and no ordering operators, where do a program’s descent and comparison come from? This lesson answers it: define the numbers as data, and the operations become structural recursion — the same shape the lesson on recursive data established, base case included.
Everything the build uses is already in place: data definitions, pattern matching (wildcards and nested patterns included), and structural recursion.
A data definition can build numbers rather than describe them:
Read the definition one form at a time. Zero is a number — the first one. Next(rest) is the number after another Natural, and its field holds the number it follows. These are the natural numbers of mathematics: zero, then the number after zero, then the number after that, one counting step per layer.
The value in main builds two steps past Zero. Predict the displayed value and its type before running; Ash reports Next(Next(Zero)) : Natural.

title: Ordering from data
text:
type Natural =
    Zero
    | Next(Natural)

main : Unit -> Natural
main () = Next(Next(Zero))

title: Ordering from data
text:
Comparison, one equation per form
To compare two Natural values, first name the answers comparison can give:
type Natural =
    Zero
    | Next(Natural)

type Ordering =
    Less
    | Equal
    | Greater

compare_natural : Natural -> Natural -> Ordering
compare_natural Zero Zero = Equal
compare_natural Zero Next(right) = Less
compare_natural Next(left) Zero = Greater
compare_natural Next(left) Next(right) = compare_natural left right

main : Unit -> Ordering
main () = {
    let two = Next(Next(Zero))
    let three = Next(two)
    compare_natural two three
}
Ordering carries one constructor per outcome, and the function pairs every form of one input with every form of the other. Two Zero values are equal; Zero comes before every Next value, answering Less; every Next value comes after Zero, answering Greater. Two Next values each hide one counting step — removing both outside layers compares the numbers that remain.
This is structural recursion, exactly as the lesson on recursive data defined it: one equation per form, every recursive call receiving a field of the matched value. Here two inputs are matched together, so the call descends into both rests at once.
Ash has no integer literal patterns, so the program builds its values with constructors; the bindings give the compared numbers readable names. Follow the call:
compare_natural two three
compare_natural (Next(Zero)) (Next(Next(Zero)))
compare_natural Zero (Next(Zero))
Less
Each call removes one layer from both sides until a Zero pairing answers directly — the base case. Predict the results of the reversed call, compare_natural three two, and of compare_natural two two before trying them in your scratch copy. Run the program; Ash reports Less : Ordering.

title: Ordering from data
section: The way back and the way down
text:
The way back and the way down
Comparison stays inside Natural; to see the count a value carries, convert it to an Int:
type Natural =
    Zero
    | Next(Natural)

to_int : Natural -> Int
to_int Zero = 0
to_int Next(rest) = 1 + to_int rest

main : Unit -> Int
main () = to_int (Next(Next(Next(Zero))))
The base case names the count of Zero directly: 0; the Next equation asks for the count of the rest first, then adds one for the outside layer. The additions wait on the recursive call:
to_int (Next(Next(Next(Zero))))
1 + to_int (Next(Next(Zero)))
1 + (1 + to_int (Next(Zero)))
1 + (1 + (1 + to_int Zero))
1 + (1 + (1 + 0))
3
Each call hands its result back to the waiting addition, and the full answer is assembled as the calls return — the result is built on the way back from the base case. Predict the program’s report; Ash answers 3 : Int.
The same conversion can carry its count into the calls instead:
type Natural =
    Zero
    | Next(Natural)

to_int : Natural -> Int
to_int Zero = 0
to_int Next(rest) = 1 + to_int rest

to_int_down : Natural -> Int -> Int
to_int_down Zero count = count
to_int_down Next(rest) count = to_int_down rest (count + 1)

main : Unit -> (Int, Int)
main () = {
    let three = Next(Next(Next(Zero)))
    (to_int three, to_int_down three 0)
}
The second parameter holds the count so far: it starts at 0 in the call, each Next equation increases it by one and passes it down, and the base case hands back whatever arrives. A parameter that carries a partial result toward the base case like this is called an accumulator. The trace shows where the work happens now:
to_int_down (Next(Next(Next(Zero)))) 0
to_int_down (Next(Next(Zero))) (0 + 1)
to_int_down (Next(Zero)) ((0 + 1) + 1)
to_int_down Zero (((0 + 1) + 1) + 1)
(((0 + 1) + 1) + 1)
3
No addition waits on a return: each step finishes before the next call begins, and the base case returns the running total. The first function computes on the way back from the base case; this one computes on the way down. The program runs both shapes on the same value and pairs the answers; predict the pair before running it. Ash reports (3, 3) : (Int, Int) — both routes reach the same value.

title: Ordering from data
text:
The pairing no equation answers
Coverage has checked every definition so far: a signature accepting every Natural promises equations for every form. Remove the Zero and Zero equation and the promise breaks exactly where main still asks it a question:
type Natural =
    Zero
    | Next(Natural)

type Ordering =
    Less
    | Equal
    | Greater

compare_natural : Natural -> Natural -> Ordering
compare_natural Zero Next(right) = Less
compare_natural Next(left) Zero = Greater
compare_natural Next(left) Next(right) = compare_natural left right

main : Unit -> Ordering
main () = compare_natural Zero Zero
Run this version from content/learn:
$ ash --message-format human --locale en ordering-from-data/src/05-missing-equal.ash
These cases do not cover every possible input; for example, `Zero Zero` is not covered.
  --> /path/to/ash-doc/content/learn/ordering-from-data/src/05-missing-equal.ash:10:1
10 | compare_natural : Natural -> Natural -> Ordering
   | ^ These cases do not cover every possible input; for example, `Zero Zero` is not covered.
11 | compare_natural Zero Next(right) = Less
   | ^ These cases do not cover every possible input; for example, `Zero Zero` is not covered.
12 | compare_natural Next(left) Zero = Greater
   | ^ These cases do not cover every possible input; for example, `Zero Zero` is not covered.
13 | compare_natural Next(left) Next(right) = compare_natural left right
   | ^ These cases do not cover every possible input; for example, `Zero Zero` is not covered.
reason: coverage.non-exhaustive
The message names the uncovered pairing — Zero against Zero — and labels the whole remaining definition, which was meant to answer it. Restoring compare_natural Zero Zero = Equal keeps the promise.

title: Ordering from data
text:
Exercise: double the number
Start from a fresh copy of src/03-to-int.ash in your scratch directory, keeping the data definition. Define double : Natural -> Natural the structural way: one equation per form of the data, the recursive call receiving the rest. Call double on Next(Next(Zero)) and on Next(Next(Next(Zero))), predicting each result before running.

title: Ordering from data
text:
From data, the operations
Descent and comparison arrived without a single operator. A data definition built the numbers, structural recursion built comparison on top of it, and two process shapes carried a count to an Int and back. The language declined subtraction and ordering operators; the build replaced them with one number type and two operations — comparison and conversion — guarded by the coverage check.
The Cases path makes the same move at larger scale: Searching an ordered tree stores these unary numbers as keys and derives its branch choices from the same four equations.
One step remains for values themselves. Every function so far has stood behind a name, called where it was needed. Functions are also values: they can be given as inputs, produced as results, and made for one particular calculation. The next lesson takes that step.

title: Functions as values
text:
Giving a function as an input
In the lesson on several inputs, the partial call add 20 produced a function. That function could wait for another integer because functions are values in Ash. Like other values, a function can be given as an input, produced as a result, and associated with a name.
This lets one function describe when another calculation should be used. We will begin with a named function, then remove the name, and finally construct a function that remembers an earlier input.
Suppose we want to apply the same integer transformation two times:
The first input to apply_twice has type Int -> Int. The parentheses in (Int -> Int) -> Int -> Int keep that whole function type together. After receiving such a function, apply_twice receives an integer and produces an integer.
In the body, transform stands for the function supplied by the call. Predict the value after its first application and after its second. Run the program; Ash reports 42 : Int. Substituting the supplied function explains the two calls:
No special call syntax is needed for the function parameter; transform number works like every named function call we have written. A function that receives another function, like apply_twice, is called a higher-order function.

title: Functions as values
text:
increment : Int -> Int
increment number = number + 1

apply_twice : (Int -> Int) -> Int -> Int
apply_twice transform number = transform (transform number)

main : Unit -> Int
main () = apply_twice increment 40


apply_twice increment 40
increment (increment 40)
increment 41
42

title: Functions as values
section: Writing a function where it is needed
text:
Writing a function where it is needed
If a small function is used in only one place, a separate definition may hide the calculation rather than clarify it. An anonymous function is a function expression without a source-level name:
apply_twice : (Int -> Int) -> Int -> Int
apply_twice transform number = transform (transform number)

main : Unit -> Int
main () = apply_twice (fn(number) {
    number + 1
}) 40
Read the expression inside the parentheses as “a function of number whose result is number + 1.” Ash knows that apply_twice requires an Int -> Int, so the parameter and result are checked as integers.
Predict whether replacing the named function changes either application. Running again produces 42 : Int: the anonymous body adds one at each call. The choice between a named and anonymous function is about explanation: name a function when the name helps the reader or the calculation is reused; keep a short, local transformation beside its use when that is clearer.

title: Functions as values
text:
Producing a function
A function expression may use a parameter from the surrounding definition. That use remains available after the surrounding call has produced the new function:
make_adder : Int -> Int -> Int
make_adder amount = fn(number) {
    amount + number
}

main : Unit -> Int
main () = make_adder 20 22
make_adder first receives amount. Its result is the anonymous function fn(number) { amount + number }. That function remembers the particular amount from the call that created it; a function value that carries bindings from where it was made is called a closure.
Which input is saved when the function is created, and which arrives when it is called? Predict the final value before running. Ash reports 42 : Int. Trace creation first:
make_adder 20
fn(number) { 20 + number }
Supplying the remaining input continues the calculation:
make_adder 20 22
20 + 22
42
Creating the anonymous function retains 20 without doing its addition. The later call supplies 22, then the body computes the result. This is the earlier partial-call idea written out: creation produces an Int -> Int, and its invocation produces the integer.

title: Functions as values
section: A function parameter requires a function
text:
A function parameter requires a function
Function types preserve the same boundary as other types. The first input to apply_twice cannot be an integer:
apply_twice : (Int -> Int) -> Int -> Int
apply_twice transform number = transform (transform number)

main : Unit -> Int
main () = apply_twice 2 40
Compare the first argument’s type with the parenthesized input contract. Which value would need to be callable? Run this version from content/learn:
$ ash --message-format human --locale en functions-as-values/src/04-not-a-function.ash
This function argument must have type `Int -> Int`, but has type `Int`.
  --> /path/to/ash-doc/content/learn/functions-as-values/src/04-not-a-function.ash:5:23
5 | main () = apply_twice 2 40
  |                       ^ This has type `Int`.
  --> /path/to/ash-doc/content/learn/functions-as-values/src/04-not-a-function.ash:1:15
1 | apply_twice : (Int -> Int) -> Int -> Int
  |               ^ This function requires an argument of type `Int -> Int`.
  --> /path/to/ash-doc/content/learn/functions-as-values/src/04-not-a-function.ash:5:11
5 | main () = apply_twice 2 40
  |           ^ This is the containing function application.
reason: type.argument
The labels connect the integer argument 2 to the function input Int -> Int in the signature, then show the containing call. Replacing 2 with the earlier increment function supplies a callable value of that type. With 40 as its input, applying the increment twice produces 42. The signature tells us not only how many inputs remain, but whether one of those inputs must itself be callable.

title: Functions as values
text:
Exercise: apply three times
Start from a fresh copy of src/01-named-function.ash in your scratch directory, keeping increment.
Define a repetition that goes one step further:
apply_three_times : (Int -> Int) -> Int -> Int
Its body applies transform three times, each call’s result feeding the next. First run it with the named increment and the value 39; then replace increment with an anonymous function that adds one. Trace both programs before running them — they should produce the same integer and make three calls to the supplied function.

title: Functions as values
text:
Calculations as data
A function value carries a calculation that can be used later. A function can receive such a value, call it, or return a new function. An anonymous function describes the calculation at the expression where it is needed, and it may remember names from that surrounding expression.
apply_twice works only with functions from Int to Int, even though its structure does not depend on integers. Our IntList similarly repeats a shape that need not be limited to integer elements. The next lesson asks how one definition can express that independence from a particular type.

title: Definitions for many types
text:
One function, different uses
Several definitions in this path have depended on integers. IntList contains integers, and apply_twice accepts an Int -> Int function. Yet some of their structure does not depend on what the values are. Returning an input unchanged requires no knowledge of its type. Keeping values in a list requires no knowledge of how those values are calculated.
A type parameter gives a name to such an unspecified type. The definition must then work in the same way for every type that may replace the parameter. We will begin with a function whose entire job is to preserve its input.
The identity function returns the value it receives:
The uppercase name A in the signature is a type parameter. Read A -> A as “takes a value of some type and returns a value of that same type.” Nothing in the body assumes that the value is an integer, a Boolean, or any other particular type.
For each call, decide which type replaces A and use that choice for both input and result. Predict the pair’s value and type, then run the program to compare:
The first call chooses Int, and the second chooses Bool. Ash determines those choices from the calls; the source expression does not supply type arguments. There is still one identity definition, with a consistent substitution at each use.

title: Definitions for many types
text:
identity : A -> A
identity value = value

main : Unit -> (Int, Bool)
main () = (identity 42, identity true)


(42, true) : (Int, Bool)

title: Definitions for many types
text:
Data with an element type
A data definition writes its type parameters between angle brackets. Here a box may contain one value of any type:
type Box<A> = Box(A)

main : Unit -> (Box<Int>, Box<Bool>)
main () = (Box(42), Box(false))
In Box<A>, A names the type of the constructor’s field. Replacing A with Int gives Box<Int>, whose constructor carries an integer. Replacing it with Bool gives Box<Bool>, whose constructor carries a Boolean. Box<A> is a parameterized algebraic data type: the same sum-and-product structure as before, with one type left as a parameter.
Predict the complete type of each constructor expression before running the program. These two fields account for the tuple it reports:
Box(42)     : Box<Int>
Box(false)  : Box<Bool>
The two values share the Box shape, but their complete types remain different. A function that accepts Box<Int> cannot therefore be given a Box<Bool> by accident.

title: Definitions for many types
section: A list that leaves its elements open
text:
A list that leaves its elements open
We can now remove the integer-specific part of IntList. The recursive shape stays the same; a parameter names the element type:
pub type List<A> =
    Empty
    | More(A, List<A>)

pub map : (A -> B) -> List<A> -> List<B>
map transform Empty = Empty
map transform More(first, rest) = More(transform first, map transform rest)
This source file defines List<A> in the same way that IntList was defined: the list is either empty or contains a first element followed by another list. The difference is that the first field has type A, and the rest must be a list with that same element type.
The function map introduces two type parameters. Its signature says:

receive a function from A to B;
receive a list whose elements have type A; and
produce a list whose elements have type B.

The equations follow the data definition. Mapping over Empty produces Empty. For More, the supplied function transforms first, while the recursive call transforms the rest. The result constructor combines those two pieces as a List<B>.
Neither equation needs to know what A and B are. It can construct and follow the list, and it can call transform, but only the supplied function knows how one element becomes another.
Both the type and the function are public because another source file will use them:
import lists as Lists

main : Unit -> Lists.List<Int>
main () = Lists.map (fn(number) {
    number + 1
}) (Lists.More(41, Lists.Empty))
Because pub type List<A> makes the type and all its constructors public, the import makes Lists.More and Lists.Empty available through the alias Lists.
The import and qualified names follow the module boundary from the second lesson. Use the input list and the transformation’s type to choose A and B. Then predict the output list by following one More case and its Empty rest. Run the entry beside lists.ash; it reports:
More(42, Empty) : List<Int>
Both parameters are Int here. The transformation produces 42 from 41, while the recursive call preserves the empty tail:
Lists.map increment (Lists.More(41, Lists.Empty))
Lists.More(increment 41, Lists.map increment Lists.Empty)
Lists.More(42, Lists.Empty)
The name increment in this trace stands for the anonymous function in the program.
This one example draws on nearly every lesson so far: a module boundary, a recursive data definition, a function that follows its forms, and a function value that decides how each element changes.

With a learning assistant: Draw the input and output list values from the program above as nested More and Empty forms. First trace and explain how each recursive call follows a smaller rest; ask the assistant to question that explanation one step at a time. After you finish the recursion trace, examine one occurrence of A or B at a time and ask the assistant to check it against your two lists.

title: Definitions for many types
section: When a complete type is required
text:
When a complete type is required
List by itself does not yet describe the type of a value. It is a type constructor: applying it to an element type constructs a complete list type. Ash describes what a type-level name still needs with a kind. List has kind Type -> Type because it needs one type of kind Type; after that application, List<Int> has kind Type.
Bare and partially applied type constructors are valid where the surrounding declaration accepts the remaining function kind. An ordinary function parameter or result position instead requires a type of kind Type. That distinction explains why this signature is rejected:
type List<A> =
    Empty
    | More(A, List<A>)

keep : List -> List
keep list = list

main : Unit -> List<Int>
main () = keep Empty
What kind does List have before receiving an element type, and what kind does each ordinary input and result position require? Run this version from content/learn to compare that mismatch with the labels:
$ ash --message-format human --locale en definitions-for-many-types/src/04-unsaturated-list.ash
This position requires a complete value type (kind `Type`), but has kind `Type -> Type`.
  --> /path/to/ash-doc/content/learn/definitions-for-many-types/src/04-unsaturated-list.ash:5:8
5 | keep : List -> List
  |        ^ Found kind `Type -> Type` here.
  --> /path/to/ash-doc/content/learn/definitions-for-many-types/src/04-unsaturated-list.ash:1:1
1 | type List<A> =
  | ^ This declaration fixes the kind as `Type -> Type`.
2 |     Empty
  | ^ This declaration fixes the kind as `Type -> Type`.
3 |     | More(A, List<A>)
  | ^ This declaration fixes the kind as `Type -> Type`.
reason: kind.expected-type
The message marks the first bare List in keep and relates its function kind to the declaration type List<A>. The parameter position needs a complete value type; applying List to an element type supplies one. The kind rules derive both kinds and require ordinary function domains and results to have kind Type.
Writing keep : List<Int> -> List<Int> would make this particular function integer-specific. Writing keep : List<A> -> List<A> would let the unchanged structure work for any element type, like identity and map.

title: Definitions for many types
text:
Exercise: change the element type
Place fresh copies of src/lists.ash and src/03-list-main.ash beside each other in your scratch directory, and keep the module unchanged. In the entry, define a test for one particular number:
is_42 : Int -> Bool
is_42 number = number == 42
Map is_42 over a two-element List<Int>. Before running, decide which types replace A and B in map, construct the expected List<Bool> value, and trace one map call for each More layer and one for Empty. Update main’s result type to describe the transformation.
Then change the integer elements so one produces true and the other false. The list shape should stay the same while its element type and values change.

title: Definitions for many types
text:
The beginning model
A parameterized definition names the types it does not need to fix. Each use supplies consistent types for those parameters, while the definition follows the same structure. This form of reuse is called parametric polymorphism, or generics. It is one of two principal forms of polymorphism; the other, ad-hoc polymorphism, gives one operation different implementations for different types. Ash provides that form through interfaces and their implementations, developed in the libraries path.
We can now give a fuller answer to the question that began this path. An Ash program is a group of source modules containing definitions. Its expressions produce values; its functions connect calculations; its data definitions name the possible shapes of values; and its patterns guide functions over those shapes. Evaluation begins with main (), and the command-line tool reports the resulting value and type.
The examples have grown from one integer expression to a public, recursive list transformation without changing that central model: definitions describe expressions, and expressions calculate values.
The next two lessons widen the module boundary this chapter used: they choose which public spellings cross it, re-export them through a facade, and keep a type nameable while hiding how its values are built. The continuation chapters then ask which local function bindings can retain this reuse across different input types, and which bindings hold one chosen function value. Continue with module channels.

title: Module channels
text:
Importing one name
Early in this path, the module lesson connected two source files with one channel: a complete import placed every public name of arithmetic.ash under the alias Arithmetic. That client wanted one name and accepted the whole namespace to get it. A module boundary usually offers more than one public name, though, and a client rarely wants all of them, qualified or not. This lesson narrows what crosses the boundary in two directions: importing selected names into a file, and re-exporting selected names through another module.
The earlier program still serves. Create a fresh directory for this program with the same two files:
arithmetic.ash holds the module from that lesson, unchanged:
answer is public; the helper double stays inside the module. This time the entry names the one spelling it wants, in a parenthesized list:
This is a targeted import. Where the complete import bound the whole public namespace under one alias, the targeted import places only the selected public spellings in this file’s file-wide namespaces. The call therefore writes answer () with no qualifier. Nothing else in arithmetic.ash becomes nameable here, not even under an alias.
Each item in the list may take its own alias. Writing import arithmetic (answer as total) brings the same definition in under the name total, so the call becomes total (). The alias changes only this file’s spelling; the definition followed is still answer in arithmetic.ash.
Follow answer into its module as before and predict the value and type of main (). Run the entry from channels:
Ash follows the import, checks both files, and reports:

title: Module channels
text:
channels/
|-- arithmetic.ash
`-- main.ash

double : Int -> Int
double number = number * 2

pub answer : Unit -> Int
answer () = double 21

import arithmetic (answer)

main : Unit -> Int
main () = answer ()



ash main.ash

42 : Int

title: Module channels
section: The boundary answers at the import
text:
The boundary answers at the import
The earlier module lesson tested this boundary at a call: Arithmetic.double was refused because double is private. Naming the helper in the import list tests the same boundary at the channel itself:
import arithmetic (double)

main : Unit -> Int
main () = double 21
Predict first: does naming double in the list make it cross? Run the saved version from content/learn:
$ ash --message-format human --locale en module-channels/src/02-private-import.ash
The declaration `double` is private to its defining module.
  --> /path/to/ash-doc/content/learn/module-channels/src/02-private-import.ash:1:20
1 | import arithmetic (double)
  |                    ^ This name is not accessible here.
  --> /path/to/ash-doc/content/learn/module-channels/src/arithmetic.ash:1:1
1 | double : Int -> Int
  | ^ The inaccessible declaration is here.
reason: resolve.unavailable-export
The words match the rejection the earlier lesson produced for a private call, and the reason is the same, resolve.unavailable-export. What changed is where the label lands: on the import item itself. Naming a private spelling refuses the import, so this file has no double at all. The second label still leads to arithmetic.ash, to the declaration with no pub. A targeted import selects from public spellings only; the import rules define what the list may name.

With a learning assistant: Show the assistant both source files and the complete diagnostic. Ask it to point to the exact spelling the import selected, to the label that refused it, and to explain why the second label lands in arithmetic.ash before suggesting any change.

title: Module channels
text:
Re-exporting selected names
A module can also widen what its own clients receive. Add a third file, reporting.ash, beside the other two:
pub import arithmetic (answer)

pub report : Unit -> Int
report () = answer () + 1
Two things happen on the first line. pub import is a targeted import with pub in front, so inside this file answer is usable unqualified, exactly as a private targeted import would allow. The pub also places the selected spelling in this module’s own public summary: a client that imports reporting receives answer with it. A public import must be targeted — it has no complete as form — and it re-exports exactly the names it selects, nothing more.
Such a module is an ordinary module to its clients, one that passes selected names through — a facade. The client below imports the facade and reaches answer through it:
import reporting (report, answer)

main : Unit -> Int
main () = report () + answer ()
Predict the sum from the two definitions: report () follows the re-exported answer and adds one. Run the entry from channels:
ash main.ash
Both spellings crossed, and the entry reports:
85 : Int
A complete alias import of the facade — import reporting as Reporting — would reach Reporting.report and the re-exported Reporting.answer, because both are public spellings of reporting. It would still not reach Reporting.double: that helper never left arithmetic.ash. And the alias would belong to the importing file alone, exactly as the alias did in the earlier module lesson.

title: Module channels
text:
Exercise: one facade, two modules
Build a scratch program with two small modules side by side: scores.ash offering a public top and a private helper, and limits.ash offering a public maximum and a private helper. Add a facade module that re-exports top from scores and maximum from limits, renaming one of them with its own as clause as it passes through, and keeps both helpers hidden.

Write the three modules and an entry that imports the facade targeted, then predict the entry’s value and type and run it.
Predict which names a complete alias import of the facade would give a client: write each Facade. spelling you expect to reach, and each one you expect to be refused.
Verify the prediction with a client that imports the facade as Facade and calls every spelling you listed.

title: Module channels
section: What crosses, and under whose name
text:
What crosses, and under whose name
Three channels are now known. A complete import places every public name of a module under an alias. A targeted import places selected public spellings in the file-wide namespaces, each renamable with as. A public import re-exports its selected spellings to its own clients. The boundary question is always the same: which public spellings cross, and under whose name?
One more channel exists at this checkpoint: an import item can carry implementation evidence for an interface instead of a name. The libraries path develops it; the name-only channels are what ordinary clients need.
The next lesson turns the boundary around once more: how can a module keep a type nameable while hiding how its values are built?

title: Opaque types
text:
A score built at home
The previous lesson narrowed what crosses a module boundary: a targeted import moves selected public spellings into the importing file. Every spelling moved so far named a function. A boundary can also move a type — but only part of the way. This lesson declares a type whose name crosses to clients while its constructors stay home. A client can then name the type, annotate values with it, and compute with values the provider built, without ever building one itself.
A game keeps a running tally. The module that owns the tally also owns how tally values are made, so it declares the type opaque and offers functions instead of the constructor. Create a fresh directory for this program with the same two files:
score.ash holds the provider:
Read the first line as two decisions. pub places the type name Score in the module’s public summary; opaque keeps its constructors out. The type and its constructor share the spelling Score, as they did in the data lesson; inside this module both remain available, and the three functions use the constructor freely. make builds a tally from an integer, add consumes one tally and builds the next, and total reads a tally back into an integer. Every construction happens in this file. The visibility rules define what each visibility mode exports.
The targeted import names the type alongside the functions, so the client can annotate a binding with it:
The type name Score crossed the boundary with the functions, and the annotation let score : Score names it. Follow the block: make 10 builds a tally of ten, add ... 5 asks the provider for the next tally, and total reads it back into an integer. Predict the value and type of the block, then run the entry from score:
Ash follows the import, checks both files, and reports:

title: Opaque types
text:
score/
|-- score.ash
`-- main.ash

pub opaque type Score = Score(Int)

pub make : Int -> Score
make points = Score(points)

pub add : Score -> Int -> Score
add (Score points) extra = Score(points + extra)

pub total : Score -> Int
total (Score points) = points


import score (Score, make, add, total)

main : Unit -> Int
main () = {
    let score : Score = add (make 10) 5
    total score
}

ash main.ash

15 : Int

title: Opaque types
text:
The boundary refuses the constructor
The client named the type in an annotation. What about the constructor that shares its spelling? A client may try to name it too:
import score (Score)

main : Unit -> Score
main () = Score(42)
Predict first: the import names Score, a public spelling — does the constructor cross with the name? Run the saved version from content/learn:
$ ash --message-format human --locale en opaque-types/src/02-constructing.ash
The constructor `Score` belongs to an opaque type and is not accessible here.
  --> /path/to/ash-doc/content/learn/opaque-types/src/02-constructing.ash:4:11
4 | main () = Score(42)
  |           ^ This name is not accessible here.
  --> /path/to/ash-doc/content/learn/opaque-types/src/score.ash:1:25
1 | pub opaque type Score = Score(Int)
  |                         ^ The inaccessible declaration is here.
reason: resolve.opaque-constructor
The import succeeded and the signature main : Unit -> Score is accepted; the refusal lands one line lower, on the term Score(42). The first label marks that term — “This name is not accessible here.” The second label leads into score.ash, and its column lands on the constructor after the =, not on the type name earlier in the line: the declaration the client cannot reach is the constructor, which opaque withholds.
The reason line also distinguishes this refusal from the previous lesson’s. Naming a private spelling in an import list refused the import itself, with resolve.unavailable-export: that spelling never crossed. Here the type name did cross, and resolve.opaque-constructor refuses the constructor itself. A constructor can appear in a pattern as well; the exercise below asks whether the boundary answers differently there.

With a learning assistant: Show the assistant both source files and the complete diagnostic. Ask it to point to the label that refused the spelling and to the exact declaration the second label marks inside score.ash, then to explain why the import line itself was accepted — before suggesting any change.

title: Opaque types
text:
Changing what a value contains
The provider’s side of the boundary can move without disturbing the client’s. Suppose the provider learns that the tally must also count how many times add ran — say, to report an average later. The representation grows a second integer, while every spelling the client named stays as it was. In a fresh copy of the program, the provider becomes:
pub opaque type Score = Score(Int, Int)

pub make : Int -> Score
make points = Score(points, 0)

pub add : Score -> Int -> Score
add (Score(points, additions)) extra = Score(points + extra, additions + 1)

pub total : Score -> Int
total (Score(points, _)) = points
Inside the module, construction and matching follow the new definition; add now carries a running count of additions. Outside, nothing about the client changes: same import list, same annotation, same calls. The client beside the revised provider is the earlier file, byte for byte, and it still reports 15 : Int.
Because the client never wrote the constructor, the new field has no spelling to break; only the provider’s own equations mention what a Score contains. Had the type been declared with plain pub type, its constructors would be public spellings too, and every client that built or matched values through them would have to change with the representation.

title: Opaque types
text:
Exercise: grow the provider
Start from fresh copies of src/score.ash and src/01-main.ash beside each other in your scratch directory.

The provider next offers scale : Score -> Int -> Score, which multiplies the stored points by the given integer. Add it to the provider, building the result with the provider’s own constructor as add does, and keep the other functions unchanged. Then, in the client, scale make 10 by 3 and read its total; predict the value and type, then run.
In a fresh client that imports (Score, total), attempt the construction twice: once in a term, as the rejected program above does, and once in a match pattern. Predict whether the two refusals name the same reason, run both, and explain each capture’s labels in your own words.

title: Opaque types
section: The name crosses, the constructors stay
text:
The name crosses, the constructors stay
Three channels for moving names across a boundary are now known: a complete import, a targeted import, and a public re-export. One visibility rule decides what a moved name carries with it — a type name can cross without its constructors. The provider owns how values of its type are built; its clients own what they do with them. The libraries path develops the full provider discipline this enables, and the Cases path protects an ordered dictionary the same way at larger scale in Protecting the dictionary invariant.
One question remains on this path: which local bindings can be reused across different types, and which hold one chosen function value? The next chapter develops it. Continue with Generalizing local functions.

title: Generalizing local functions
text:
Give each use its own type choice
The previous chapter gave a global identity function the signature A -> A, and each use chose its own type for A. A block can hold that kind of reusable function too — when the binding is written one way. Written another way, the same body yields one monomorphic function value — one fixed type for every use. Two functions that return their inputs can carry different reuse contracts, and the difference lies in how the local binding is written and checked.
The first program binds an anonymous function with no annotation:
Ash infers that the input and result must have the same type. Nothing fixes that type to Int or Bool, and it does not belong to an enclosing binding. The compiler leaves it open for each use of identity. This is called local generalization.
Predict the function type needed by each use and the resulting pair’s type. From this lesson’s src directory, run:
At the first occurrence, identity has the chosen type Int -> Int. At the second, it has Bool -> Bool. Both choices come from the same definition.
This rule applies when an unannotated let binds one name and its initializer is syntactically an anonymous function. It generalizes only still-open type choices that do not come from the surrounding environment. It does not make every local binding polymorphic.

title: Generalizing local functions
Generalizing local functions
text:
An annotation chooses one contract
The next program supplies an ordinary function type explicitly:
main : Unit -> (Int, Bool)
main () = {
    let identity : Int -> Int = fn(value) {
        value
    }
    (identity 42, identity true)
}
Compare the annotation’s input with each supplied argument. Can both uses meet that one contract? Keep this lesson’s src directory as the working directory for its diagnostic commands:
$ ash --message-format human --locale en 02-annotated-identity.ash
This function argument must have type `Int`, but has type `Bool`.
  --> /path/to/ash-doc/content/learn/generalizing-local-functions/src/02-annotated-identity.ash:6:28
6 |     (identity 42, identity true)
  |                            ^ This has type `Bool`.
  --> /path/to/ash-doc/content/learn/generalizing-local-functions/src/02-annotated-identity.ash:6:19
6 |     (identity 42, identity true)
  |                   ^ This function requires an argument of type `Int`.
  --> /path/to/ash-doc/content/learn/generalizing-local-functions/src/02-annotated-identity.ash:6:19
6 |     (identity 42, identity true)
  |                   ^ This is the containing function application.
reason: type.argument
The labels connect true to the integer argument required by identity. The annotation checks one type; it introduces no new type parameters. Remove it to recover the first program’s eligible binding, or keep the annotation and use the function only with integers.
A global signature can introduce parameters. A local annotation does not have that role, even if an enclosing definition already has a parameter whose name can appear in the annotation.

title: Generalizing local functions
section: A call produces one function value
text:
A call produces one function value
This time the initializer is a call:
make_identity : Unit -> A -> A
make_identity () = fn(value) {
    value
}

main : Unit -> (Int, Bool)
main () = {
    let identity = make_identity ()
    (identity 42, identity true)
}
make_identity itself is polymorphic. Each occurrence chooses one type for A, but its returned function is bound by a call initializer, not by the eligible anonymous-function syntax. That binding keeps one shared choice. Which use fixes the function’s input, and can the other use keep that choice?
$ ash --message-format human --locale en 03-returned-function.ash
This function argument must have type `Int`, but has type `Bool`.
  --> /path/to/ash-doc/content/learn/generalizing-local-functions/src/03-returned-function.ash:9:28
9 |     (identity 42, identity true)
  |                            ^ This has type `Bool`.
  --> /path/to/ash-doc/content/learn/generalizing-local-functions/src/03-returned-function.ash:9:19
9 |     (identity 42, identity true)
  |                   ^ This function requires an argument of type `Int`.
  --> /path/to/ash-doc/content/learn/generalizing-local-functions/src/03-returned-function.ash:9:19
9 |     (identity 42, identity true)
  |                   ^ This is the containing function application.
reason: type.argument
The diagnostic again marks a Boolean supplied to an integer function. The cause is now the shared inferred type of the returned function, rather than an explicit annotation. Ash does not inspect the factory’s body and treat its result as though the local initializer had been an anonymous function.
If we need two separately chosen function values, call the factory twice:
make_identity : Unit -> A -> A
make_identity () = fn(value) {
    value
}

main : Unit -> (Int, Bool)
main () = {
    let integer_identity = make_identity ()
    let boolean_identity = make_identity ()
    (integer_identity 42, boolean_identity true)
}
There are now two factory occurrences. Predict whether their type choices must agree, and whether the pair can satisfy main’s result type:
$ ash 04-separate-creations.ash
(42, true) : (Int, Bool)
Each occurrence of make_identity supplies its own choice. Alternatively, write the local anonymous function directly when one generalized definition expresses the intended reuse.
The similar function bodies have different places for choosing types:



Binding
Where the type is chosen




Direct unannotated anonymous function (01)
At each use


Annotated function (02)
In the one declared local type


One factory result (03)
Shared by uses of that returned value


Separate factory results (04)
Independently at each factory call

title: Generalizing local functions
text:
Keep captured types fixed
A local function can capture an enclosing value while leaving its own input open. The program below saves one value and pairs it with every input:
pair_with : A -> ((A, Int), (A, Bool))
pair_with saved = {
    let pair = fn(value) {
        (saved, value)
    }
    (pair 42, pair true)
}

main : Unit -> ((Bool, Int), (Bool, Bool))
main () = pair_with false
Within pair_with, the type of saved is the enclosing parameter A. The local definition cannot choose a different type for that captured value. It can generalize its new input type, which is independent of saved. Predict the type of both fields in each pair before running:
$ ash 05-captured-input.ash
((false, 42), (false, true)) : ((Bool, Int), (Bool, Bool))
Both pairs retain the same Boolean in their first field. Their second fields have different types. Generalization preserves connections to enclosing values rather than inventing a new type for each capture.

title: Generalizing local functions
section: Passing a function chooses an ordinary function type
text:
Passing a function chooses an ordinary function type
A generalized name can be used as an argument too:
apply_twice : (A -> A, A) -> A
apply_twice (transform, value) = transform (transform value)

main : Unit -> (Int, Bool)
main () = {
    let identity = fn(value) {
        value
    }
    (apply_twice (identity, 42), apply_twice (identity, true))
}
Each apply_twice call chooses one A. Its transform parameter is one ordinary A -> A function for that call; it is not a parameter that may be called at unrelated types within the body. The two occurrences of identity are instantiated separately before they meet those parameter contracts. Predict the two results and identify which one function type each transform parameter uses throughout its call:
$ ash 06-function-arguments.ash
(42, true) : (Int, Bool)
This is the rank-1 boundary: general type choices belong to global signatures and eligible local definitions. Ordinary function parameters and results do not contain another layer of polymorphic contract. A tuple or an application initializer likewise does not acquire generalization merely by storing a function.
The block rules specify eligible bindings, and the inference rules specify which variables remain fixed. Every inference choice must eventually be solved or generalized; an unused name does not excuse an unresolved type.

title: Generalizing local functions
Generalizing local functions
text:
Exercise: locate the type choice
For each task, make a fresh copy of its named source in a scratch directory outside this lesson’s src tree. Predict the observation, then run that copy from its directory.

Change 01-local-identity.ash to return three uses, with integer, Boolean, and unit inputs. Update the entry result type before running it.
In 04-separate-creations.ash, give both functions integer inputs. Explain why two separately chosen types may still turn out to be equal.
Change pair_with false to pair_with 7 in 05-captured-input.ash and update main’s result type. Predict which fields change type.
In 06-function-arguments.ash, replace one identity argument with a function that adds one. Trace the two calls inside apply_twice.

A local function’s reuse comes from its binding and its connections to the enclosing environment. We can now distinguish a generalized definition from one stored function value. The next chapter asks how local definitions can refer to themselves and to one another while being initialized safely.

title: Defining local recursion
text:
Start with the preceding scope
Ordinary local bindings extend a block one step at a time. A later function can use an earlier value, but a definition cannot normally use its own new name or one introduced later. Recursive functions need a different scope: all names in their group must be available together.
Giving names that scope also creates an initialization question. A function body can wait until a later call. A data initializer that immediately tries to use an unfinished value cannot make the same promise.
In 01-sequential-bindings.ash, add_base captures an already bound integer:
base is in scope while the anonymous function is checked. Identify that saved value separately from the later argument, then predict their sum. Run from this lesson’s src directory:
The new name add_base enters scope after its initializer, the same sequential rule every lesson has used so far.

title: Defining local recursion
Defining local recursion
text:
Name a local recursive calculation
02-local-sum.ash keeps a list traversal close to the value it uses:
type Scores = End
    | Item(Int, Scores)

main : Unit -> Int
main () = {
    let bonus = 1
    let rec sum : Scores -> Int = fn(values) {
        match values {
            End => 0
            Item(value, rest) => value + bonus + sum rest
        }
    }
    sum (Item(20, Item(20, End)))
}
let rec makes sum available in its own initializer and the rest of the block. Its annotation is required: the recursive calls must already have a contract while the body is checked. The body may also capture the preceding bonus binding.
The initializer creates a function; it does not run the match yet. The call after the group starts the traversal. Each Item contributes its score plus one, then the recursive call follows rest. End contributes zero. Predict the total, distinguishing the captured bonus from the score supplied by each recursive argument:
$ ash 02-local-sum.ash
42 : Int
Here termination follows from the finite input and the move to its smaller rest. The rec keyword itself does not prove that a function stops.
Recursive annotations describe one type per member. They do not introduce local type parameters or apply the preceding lesson’s generalization rule. An enclosing type parameter can still appear where it is already in scope.
