section: Put mutually dependent functions in one group

title: Defining local recursion
section: Build a cycle without traversing it forever

title: Defining local recursion
section: The initializer must provide its data shape
text:
The initializer must provide its data shape
A bare self-reference does not construct a node:
type Trail = Step(Int, Trail)

main : Unit -> Int
main () = {
    let rec trail : Trail = trail
    0
}
Compare this initializer’s outer form with the constructor-root requirement. What node would it construct before trying to retain its own reference?
$ ash --message-format human --locale en 06-unsafe-root.ash
This recursive data initializer must start with a fully applied constructor of its declared nominal type.
  --> /path/to/ash-doc/content/learn/defining-local-recursion/src/06-unsafe-root.ash:5:29
5 |     let rec trail : Trail = trail
  |                             ^ This recursive data initializer must start with a fully applied constructor of its declared nominal type.
  --> /path/to/ash-doc/content/learn/defining-local-recursion/src/06-unsafe-root.ash:5:5
5 |     let rec trail : Trail = trail
  |     ^ This declaration introduces the recursive group.
  --> /path/to/ash-doc/content/learn/defining-local-recursion/src/06-unsafe-root.ash:5:21
5 |     let rec trail : Trail = trail
  |                     ^ The recursive member's type is declared here.
reason: recursion.unsafe-root
The message identifies the initializer, its recursive group, and its declared nominal type. There is no constructor-rooted value to initialize. Write Step(42, trail) to build a node that retains its own reference, or use an ordinary nonrecursive binding when no cycle is needed. The unused result of the group does not make unsafe initialization acceptable.
A constructor root is necessary, but references beneath it must be guarded too:
type Trail = Step(Int, Trail)

keep : Trail -> Trail
keep value = value

main : Unit -> Int
main () = {
    let rec trail : Trail = Step(42, keep trail)
    0
}
The outer constructor is present. Follow the recursive occurrence beneath it: is the reference stored directly, or passed through a calculation that initialization checking does not allow?
$ ash --message-format human --locale en 07-forced-reference.ash
This recursive value cannot be passed through this expression during initialization.
  --> /path/to/ash-doc/content/learn/defining-local-recursion/src/07-forced-reference.ash:8:38
8 |     let rec trail : Trail = Step(42, keep trail)
  |                                      ^ This recursive value cannot be passed through this expression during initialization.
reason: recursion.unguarded-use
keep is an ordinary call. Passing the unfinished trail through it crosses a form that initialization checking does not permit. Returning the argument unchanged does not make the call a constructor. Replace keep trail with the direct field trail to retain the reference without calling a function on it.
The recursive-group rules define both checks; the execution rules explain reservation and initialization of the recursive data locations. Neither rule authorizes arbitrary recursive integers, implicit delays, or a promise that later traversals terminate.

title: Defining local recursion
text:
Practice: separate construction from use
For each task, make a fresh copy of its named program in a scratch directory outside this lesson’s src tree. Run the copy from that directory.

Change bonus and the input list in 02-local-sum.ash. Trace which values come from capture and which come from each recursive argument.
Add one Next to two in 03-mutual-functions.ash. Predict both results by tracing the alternating calls before running.
Start from 03-mutual-functions.ash and exchange its two member declarations. Keep let rec on the first and and on the second. Explain whether scope changes.
Extend 05-guarded-cycle.ash to observe exactly three scores. Predict which node supplies the third, and keep a fixed observation bound.

A recursive group gives its names one shared scope, with explicit contracts and safe initialization: functions delay their bodies until called, and constructor fields can retain guarded links. What happens after initialization still depends on the program’s calls and data. With this boundary understood, the effects and library paths can build on local functions without assuming they are all polymorphic or that every recursive structure is a finite list.

title: Where Ash goes next
text:
Behavior a definition states
One model carried this path from its first file to its last: definitions describe expressions, and expressions calculate values. The programs grew from a single expression to recursive data, module boundaries, and text, and the model stayed put through every lesson.
Ash has features this path never needed, and three of them are worth meeting before you leave it. Each extends the model rather than replacing it, and each belongs to a path that continues after this one. This closing lesson shows all three working in small programs you can run. None asks you to learn its machinery; each asks you to recognize the shape and follow the pointer to the path that develops it.
Definitions for many types closed with a promise. Parametric polymorphism fixes one definition for every type; the other principal form, ad-hoc polymorphism, gives one operation different implementations for different types. Ash provides that form through interfaces, and 01-twice.ash shows the whole mechanism at once:
Twice<A> names a capability: for a type A, a value can be doubled into a pair. The implementation supplies that capability for Int. The signature of replicate records its need in where Twice<A>, and its body calls double as an ordinary function. When main calls replicate 21, checking fixes A to Int, and the implementation for Int answers. These are the interface and implementation forms the checker verifies.
Predict the displayed pair before running. From this lesson’s src directory:
The need was stated in the signature and satisfied without passing the behavior as an argument. The libraries path develops interfaces and their implementation evidence, starting from this shape in choosing implementation evidence.

title: Where Ash goes next
Where Ash goes next
Where Ash goes next
text:
A cell a scope owns
The third feature gives one scope an owned place to hold an integer while a calculation runs. 03-cell-tally.ash acquires such a cell, replaces its contents, and reads them back:
import @builtin.cell as Cell

main : Unit -> Int
main () = resource cell<R> tally = 0 {
    let ignored = Cell.write (tally, 7)
    Cell.read tally
}
import @builtin.cell as Cell makes the compiler-owned cell operations available under the alias Cell. The resource cell<R> tally = 0 { ... } form acquires a cell holding 0 and runs its body with tally naming the cell; the scope owns the cell’s release when the body finishes. Cell.write replaces the cell’s integer, and Cell.read copies the current one out. The cell rules describe the acquisition and its owned scope.
Predict the copied integer, then run from this lesson’s src directory:
$ ash 03-cell-tally.ash
7 : Int
The write replaced the initial 0 before the read, so the body returns 7. The effects path develops scoped cells after its handler chapters, in counting with a cell.

title: Where Ash goes next
text:
Practice: choose a different answer
Make a fresh copy of 02-scale-price.ash in a scratch directory outside this lesson’s src tree, and run the copy from there. Change the handler’s clause so it answers with the requested factor plus ten rather than the factor times three. Predict the program’s result before running your copy, then identify which line chooses the answer and which line only requests it.
Nothing in these programs breaks the path’s model. An interface states a need in a signature; an effect states a need in a row; a resource scope owns a cell while expressions calculate values inside it. The three features extend the model rather than replace it, and the libraries path and the effects path develop them in order, each building on this path’s definitions, signatures, and runs.
Good luck in the paths ahead, and predict before you run.

title: Design library abstractions in Ash
text:
Lessons in order
This path asks how reusable source libraries can state the behavior and type structure they need, then carry those abstractions across module boundaries. It continues from the complete Learn Ash path. Finish that path first so functions, parameterized definitions, public declarations, and source imports are already familiar. The lessons are written for readers growing from beginner toward intermediate.
Use the ash command prepared by the repository’s shared setup. Each lesson keeps its program in a src directory. Run the displayed commands from that directory. Relative imports resolve from the importing source file’s directory, so keep sibling library files beside their clients.
The diagnostic reading notes explain the shell prompt, English output, and source-path convention. Rejection commands also run from the lesson’s src directory.
For practice, start each task in a fresh scratch directory outside the lesson’s canonical src tree. Copy the named entry and its required sibling modules together, keeping their filenames. Run the copied entry from that scratch directory. Begin the next task with fresh copies, so an earlier edit does not change the boundary you are testing.
For each boundary, use the same cycle:

title: Design library abstractions in Ash
text:
Choosing implementation evidence — separate an imported constrained name from the public implementation fact that satisfies its concrete requirement.
Forwarding capability evidence — carry public names and implementation authorization through a facade without redefining the capability.
Accepting a type constructor — use an explicit function kind when an abstraction applies a type constructor to different element types.
Giving a method local type parameters — instantiate one interface method at unrelated element types while retaining one complete implementation requirement.
Determining interface results — use one total forward edge to complete an interface obligation before implementation selection.
Requiring element behavior — derive container behavior from explicit element prerequisites.
Wrapping a representation — use explicit newtype conversions and nominal interface behavior.
Supplying scoped evidence — combine local nominal types with sequential exact method evidence.

title: Choosing implementation evidence
text:
A name is not implementation evidence
Suppose a library needs to compare two values. It could accept a comparison function every time, but then every caller must carry that choice as an ordinary value. Sometimes the library instead needs to state, “this operation works when equality behavior is available for the value type.”
Ash represents that boundary with an interface requirement. The library can describe the required operation, provide an implementation for a particular type, and keep the requirement visible on any definition that uses it. A client then chooses which public implementation facts are available in its module.
Choosing the implementation by type, rather than fixing one in the definition, is ad-hoc polymorphism — the form the Learn path promised at the close of Definitions for many types. An interface is Ash’s form of the literature’s type class.
Read the library source, equality.ash:
Equal<A> names a capability for a type A. Its method says that equality behavior accepts two values of that type and produces a boolean. The implementation supplies the complete method set for Equal<Int>; it does not introduce an ordinary source name for the implementation itself. These are the interface and implementation forms that the checker verifies.
The signature of same keeps its dependency explicit:
The value type still says that same accepts a pair and returns a boolean. The where Equal<A> clause adds the evidence same needs in order to use equal. While Ash checks the body of same, that declared requirement is the abstract evidence for the call. The library does not have to choose a concrete implementation for every possible A.
This gives us two separate questions at a client boundary:
Begin with a client that imports only the constrained definition:
The pair supplies two integers. Which complete Equal<A> requirement does that create? Before running the client, predict whether importing same also makes the library’s public implementation available.
Run the entry from this lesson’s src directory:
Ash exits with status 1 and writes this message on standard error.
The import made the spelling same available, so name resolution reached the call and its constrained scheme. Ordinary typing also fixed A to Int from the pair of integer arguments. The remaining obligation is therefore the complete application Equal<Int>.
But a targeted name item selects no implementation facts. Ash reports the unsatisfied obligation at the call and relates it to the imported same item, the declaration that introduced the requirement, and the owning Equal interface. It does not expose the public but unselected implementation as though that fact were ambient. This behavior follows the separate name and implementation import channels and the rules for an unsatisfied evidence obligation.

title: Choosing implementation evidence
text:
import equality (same)

main : Unit -> Bool
main () = same((21, 21))


$ ash --message-format human --locale en 02-name-only.ash
No available evidence satisfies this interface requirement.
  --> /path/to/ash-doc/content/libraries/choosing-implementation-evidence/src/02-name-only.ash:4:11
4 | main () = same((21, 21))
  |           ^ No available evidence satisfies this interface requirement.
  --> /path/to/ash-doc/content/libraries/choosing-implementation-evidence/src/equality.ash:9:5
9 | pub same : (A, A) -> Bool where Equal<A>
  |     ^ This declaration introduced the interface requirement.
  --> /path/to/ash-doc/content/libraries/choosing-implementation-evidence/src/02-name-only.ash:1:18
1 | import equality (same)
  |                  ^ This import made the declaration available.
  --> /path/to/ash-doc/content/libraries/choosing-implementation-evidence/src/equality.ash:1:1
1 | pub interface Equal<A> {
  | ^ This interface participates in the failing evidence selection.
2 |     equal : (A, A) -> Bool
  | ^ This interface participates in the failing evidence selection.
3 | }
  | ^ This interface participates in the failing evidence selection.
reason: constraint.unsatisfied

title: Choosing implementation evidence
text:
Select the required fact
Now add an implementation item beside the name item:
import equality (same, impl Equal)

main : Unit -> Bool
main () = same((21, 21))
The new item selects public implementation facts for Equal. Use the integer arguments to identify the required application, then follow the matching method body in equality.ash. What boolean will the client produce? Run it to compare with your prediction:
ash 01-selected.ash
Ash reports:
true : Bool
The selected method compares 21 == 21, which produces true. same uses that method to compare its pair and returns the boolean unchanged.
The two clients differ only by , impl Equal. The item resolves the public interface spelling in equality.ash and selects its public implementation facts, but it binds no source name. Once ordinary typing fixes the call’s requirement to Equal<Int>, the selected Equal<Int> fact is the unique matching concrete evidence.
That order matters. impl Equal does not choose a result by inspecting the values at runtime. Checking first determines the complete interface application and then selects evidence from the facts explicitly available in the client module. After validation, Ash lowers selected evidence to ordinary Core functions and applications. Imports, implementation identities, and checking registries do not become runtime operations; evaluation performs no runtime interface lookup.
The cost of this boundary is one explicit requirement on the library definition and one explicit selection channel at the client. In return, the library can describe the behavior it needs without accepting a comparator in every value-level call, and the importing module makes its available implementation evidence visible in source.

title: Choosing implementation evidence
section: Practice: change one boundary at a time
text:
Practice: change one boundary at a time
Start each task with fresh copies of equality.ash and 01-selected.ash together in a scratch directory, as described in the library path’s setup.

Change the selected client’s arguments to 21 and 22. Predict the boolean before running it, then explain why the selected fact is unchanged.
Remove pub from the implementation in equality.ash. Predict what the client can select, then run it. Follow the diagnostic’s labels and explain which declaration or import you would change to repair it.
Replace impl Equal with the ordinary name item Equal. The interface name is now available in the client, but is its implementation fact available? Predict what the message will explain and where its labels will point, then check it.

When you explain each result, keep the four roles separate: the interface names required behavior, the implementation supplies that behavior for Int, the where clause records the library definition’s need, and impl Equal selects public implementation facts for the client module. The next chapter asks how those names and facts can reach a client through a facade.

title: Forwarding capability evidence
text:
What do public names carry?
The previous lesson made a client choose Equal<Int> directly from the source that defines it. A larger program may not want every client to depend on that source. It may place a smaller public boundary in front of several libraries and let clients depend on that boundary instead.
Such a boundary is called a facade. An Ash facade can re-export public names, but equality behavior needs more than names. The implementation owner, facade, and client form a route: the owner publishes an implementation fact, the facade authorizes that fact for its dependents, and the client selects it. We can observe what each hop contributes without writing another equality implementation.
Begin with the same equality.ash source used in the previous lesson:
This source still owns the Equal interface, its Int implementation, and the constrained same definition. The facade will not copy any of those declarations.
First read names_only_facade.ash, which contains one public targeted import:
The import makes the three selected names available in the facade and stages them for its public summary. A later client reaches the original declarations through those spellings: re-export preserves each defining identity rather than creating a forwarding declaration. But ordinary name items select no implementation facts. These are separate rules in Ash’s imports and namespaces.
Use that facade from 02-names-only.ash:
Before running it, follow the name route. The client imports same from the facade, and the facade publicly imported same from the equality owner. The call can therefore reach the constrained definition. Now ask a different question: which source item selected Equal<Int> implementation evidence for this client?
Run the entry from this lesson’s src directory:
Ash exits with status 1 and writes this message on standard error.
Typing the integer pair fixes the call’s requirement to Equal<Int>, but no implementation item supplied a candidate. The diagnostic places its sole primary label on the same call. Its related labels identify the client’s import and the original same and Equal declarations in equality.ash. There is no facade-owned copy to identify, and the unselected implementation is not exposed. The constraint-selection rules make an eligible concrete obligation with no available source constraint.unsatisfied.

title: Forwarding capability evidence
text:
pub import equality (Equal, equal, same)


import names_only_facade (same)

main : Unit -> Bool
main () = same((21, 21))


$ ash --message-format human --locale en 02-names-only.ash
No available evidence satisfies this interface requirement.
  --> /path/to/ash-doc/content/libraries/forwarding-capability-evidence/src/02-names-only.ash:4:11
4 | main () = same((21, 21))
  |           ^ No available evidence satisfies this interface requirement.
  --> /path/to/ash-doc/content/libraries/forwarding-capability-evidence/src/equality.ash:9:5
9 | pub same : (A, A) -> Bool where Equal<A>
  |     ^ This declaration introduced the interface requirement.
  --> /path/to/ash-doc/content/libraries/forwarding-capability-evidence/src/02-names-only.ash:1:27
1 | import names_only_facade (same)
  |                           ^ This import made the declaration available.
  --> /path/to/ash-doc/content/libraries/forwarding-capability-evidence/src/equality.ash:1:1
1 | pub interface Equal<A> {
  | ^ This interface participates in the failing evidence selection.
2 |     equal : (A, A) -> Bool
  | ^ This interface participates in the failing evidence selection.
3 | }
  | ^ This interface participates in the failing evidence selection.
reason: constraint.unsatisfied

title: Forwarding capability evidence
text:
Forward the implementation route
capability_facade.ash differs by one import item:
pub import equality (Equal, equal, same, impl Equal)
impl Equal binds no source name. In this public import, it selects the equality owner’s public Equal facts and adds their authorization routes to the facade’s public implementation closure. The route retains its hop back to the defining source and preserves the original implementation identity. The facade still contains no interface, function, or implementation body.
The client must select the route that the facade made public:
import capability_facade (same, impl Equal)

main : Unit -> Bool
main () = same((21, 21))
Trace the implementation route from this client through the facade to equality.ash. Which item authorizes each hop, and which complete requirement does the integer pair create? Predict the comparison’s boolean, then run it:
ash 01-forwarded.ash
Ash reports:
true : Bool
The result comes from the original method’s 21 == 21 comparison. same receives that method and returns its answer; the facade adds no calculation.
There are two explicit implementation items. The public item in the facade authorizes the route for later dependents. The private item in the client selects that authorized fact into the client’s effective implementation environment. Ordinary typing fixes Equal<Int>, the route leads to the original implementation, and its method compares the two integers.
This routing is static. A public import does not construct a runtime facade object, register an implementation, or arrange dynamic dispatch. After Ash validates the selected route, it lowers evidence to ordinary Core functions and applications. The evaluator performs no runtime interface lookup.
The source adds one import hop and an explicit selector at each boundary that forwards or consumes the capability. The invariant is visible in source: names and implementation authorization travel through independent items. The facade gains a stable public boundary without duplicating the interface, constrained function, implementation identity, or method body.

title: Forwarding capability evidence
text:
Practice: inspect each hop
Start each task with fresh copies in a scratch directory. For tasks one, two, and four, copy equality.ash, capability_facade.ash, and 01-forwarded.ash together. For task three, copy equality.ash, names_only_facade.ash, and 02-names-only.ash instead.

Remove impl Equal only from capability_facade.ash, leaving the client selector in place. Predict whether the failure occurs while resolving the import or while satisfying the call, then run it. This is a different boundary from the lesson’s name-only client.
Remove impl Equal only from 01-forwarded.ash. Predict whether the facade’s public authorization is enough for this call, then check and explain the observation through the two imports.
Add the ordinary name Equal to 02-names-only.ash’s import. Predict what the call requires and what the new item supplies, then run it and explain the message’s labels.
Change pub import to import in capability_facade.ash. Identify which facts remain usable inside that facade. Predict what its client can import, then check your prediction.

Both facades contain a single import line, and neither copies a declaration; what differed was whether impl Equal rode the public boundary and was selected again at the client. The next lesson asks how a library abstraction can accept a type constructor such as Option, rather than only a completed type such as Int.

title: Accepting a type constructor
text:
State the constructor’s kind
The first two library lessons worked with the completed type Int and the complete requirement Equal<Int>. Some abstractions need a different input. They should work with Option<Int>, Option<Bool>, and every other application of Option without being tied to one element type.
To describe that boundary, distinguish a completed type from a type constructor. Int and Option<Int> are types that values can have. Bare Option still needs one type argument. Ash records that difference with kinds.
This complete program defines keep, which returns a constructed value without changing it:
Type is the kind of a completed value type. Type -> Type is the kind of a constructor that accepts one Type and produces another. Because Option accepts its element type and produces Option<A>, bare Option has kind Type -> Type.
The annotation gives F the same shape:
The parameter A omits an annotation, so its kind is Type. Applying F to A consumes that input and leaves the completed type F<A>. Both the domain and result of keep are therefore valid value types. These relationships follow Ash’s rules for kinds, monotypes, and schemes.
At the call in main, which constructor replaces F, and which element type replaces A? Follow keep’s body to predict both the returned value and its completed type. Run the program from this lesson’s src directory:
Ash reports:
At this call, ordinary typing chooses F = Option and A = Int. keep does not inspect either type argument or the Some value. It returns the same Option<Int> value it received.

title: Accepting a type constructor
Accepting a type constructor
text:
Read the omitted declaration
The omitted annotation on A fixed its kind to Type. The same rule applies to every omitted declaration kind; Ash does not infer a function kind from use. The parallel program removes F’s annotation:
type Option<A> =
    None
    | Some(A)

keep<F, A> : F<A> -> F<A>
keep value = value

main : Unit -> Option<Int>
main () = keep(Some(42))
Before running it, locate the first type application that needs F to have a function kind. Which declaration fixes the kind that application receives?
$ ash --message-format human --locale en 02-omitted-kind.ash
The applied type has kind `Type` and cannot take type arguments.
  --> /path/to/ash-doc/content/libraries/accepting-type-constructors/src/02-omitted-kind.ash:5:14
5 | keep<F, A> : F<A> -> F<A>
  |              ^ Found kind `Type` here.
  --> /path/to/ash-doc/content/libraries/accepting-type-constructors/src/02-omitted-kind.ash:5:6
5 | keep<F, A> : F<A> -> F<A>
  |      ^ This declaration fixes the kind as `Type`.
reason: kind.not-applicable
Ash exits with status 1 and writes this message on standard error.
The message states the cause directly: the applied type has kind Type and cannot take type arguments. The primary label marks the first F<A> application, and the related label points to F’s declaration, which fixes that kind.
Applying a type requires a function kind. The declared F has kind Type, so it cannot accept A. Adding the annotation changes the declaration, not a runtime operation. Kind annotations and type arguments are checked statically and do not become values.
Kind arrows associate to the right. Type -> Type -> Type therefore means Type -> (Type -> Type): a constructor that accepts one type and leaves a constructor waiting for one more. Parentheses are needed for a parameter that instead accepts a one-argument constructor, such as (Type -> Type) -> Type. The exact forms come from Ash’s kind grammar.

title: Accepting a type constructor
text:
Practice: follow the remaining kind
Start each task with a fresh copy of 01-explicit-kind.ash in a scratch directory.

Reason about replacing Option with a two-parameter type Pair<A, B> and giving F the kind Type -> Type -> Type. Apply F to one type on paper and state the kind that remains. Explain which context could accept it; this task does not ask for a partial application in a value-type position.
Replace Option with Pair<A, B>. Revise keep to accept its two-argument constructor and apply it to both element types in its domain and result. Construct a pair in main and update its result annotation. Predict the value and type, then run the complete program and explain the kinds.
Change F back to an omitted-kind parameter. Predict which application is rejected before running the program.
Try to use bare Option as main’s result type. Predict whether its kind satisfies that value boundary, then run it and follow the causal labels.

The two keep programs differed by one annotation, and the runs turned on it: with F : Type -> Type the call returned its Option<Int> value unchanged; without it, checking stopped at the first type application. The next lesson uses this constructor parameter inside an interface method that has its own type parameters.

title: Giving a method local type parameters
text:
Declare the method’s changing types
The previous lesson gave F the kind Type -> Type, so a definition could accept a type constructor and apply it to an element type. A reusable mapping operation needs another degree of freedom: the same operation must change F<Int> into F<Bool> at one call and F<Bool> into F<Int> at another.
An interface parameter describes the type constructor whose implementation is required. A method may declare additional type parameters for the types that vary from one occurrence to the next.
Read the interface and its constrained consumer in api.ash:
F belongs to the interface. The complete application Functor<F> records the implementation requirement. By contrast, A and B belong only to map. They describe one occurrence’s input and output element types and create no separate interface requirement.
map_pair uses map once with each transformation function. The function and container arguments determine each occurrence’s element types. Both occurrences retain the same Functor<F> requirement. Ash gives the interface vector and then the method’s ordered parameters fresh type choices at each occurrence, as specified by the interface method typing rule.
Supply one implementation in carrier.ash:
The implementation head fixes the interface parameter to the Box type constructor. The implementation method remains generic in the method’s two local types: it unwraps a Box<A>, applies the supplied A -> B function, and wraps the resulting B. Its equations do not need to repeat the interface’s parameter spellings.
Now select that implementation from the entry:
Use to_bool and to_int to identify A and B at the two map calls. Then follow the implementation: unwrap, apply the supplied function, and wrap. Predict both fields of the returned tuple before running from this lesson’s src directory:
Ash reports:
The first call unwraps Box(42), compares its integer with 42, and wraps true. Its method arguments are A = Int and B = Bool. The second unwraps Box(true), maps that boolean to 42, and wraps the integer; there A = Bool and B = Int. This accounts for both the values and the tuple’s reported type.
The entry selects one Functor<Box> fact. That evidence supplies map for both method-local instantiations; it does not select a new implementation for each element-type pair. The method’s type operations and the selected interface evidence are static. After checking, generated evidence lowers to ordinary functions and erased type operations, not runtime type inspection or dynamic interface lookup. The boundary is described by Ash’s interface evidence lowering and generated evidence evaluation.
crumbs: 26  Giving a method local type parameters

title: Giving a method local type parameters
crumbs: 26  Giving a method local type parameters

title: Giving a method local type parameters
section: An omitted list binds no local types
text:
An omitted list binds no local types
A method’s parameter list must declare every type variable in its signature outside the interface’s parameters. An omitted list binds none. The rejected source removes that list but leaves the method type unchanged:
interface Functor<F : Type -> Type> {
    map : (A -> B, F<A>) -> F<B>
}
F still belongs to the interface. Which remaining names need method-local binders? Locate their signature before running this source:
$ ash --message-format human --locale en 02-missing-method-parameters.ash
Method type parameters must be explicitly declared in the method's parameter list.
  --> /path/to/ash-doc/content/libraries/giving-method-local-type-parameters/src/02-missing-method-parameters.ash:2:5
2 |     map : (A -> B, F<A>) -> F<B>
  |     ^ Method type parameters must be explicitly declared in the method's parameter list.
  --> /path/to/ash-doc/content/libraries/giving-method-local-type-parameters/src/02-missing-method-parameters.ash:1:19
1 | interface Functor<F : Type -> Type> {
  |                   ^ An interface parameter is declared here.
reason: interface.method-parameter
Ash exits with status 1 and writes this message on standard error.
An omitted method parameter list is not an inference request: it binds no method-local type parameters. The signature therefore contains the unlisted names A and B. The diagnostic’s primary label covers the complete map signature, and its related label points to the declared interface parameter F. Adding <A, B> makes the method type’s non-interface variables an ordered declared set. These binding rules come from method parameter resolution.
This is rank-1 method polymorphism at an interface boundary. Each occurrence instantiates the method scheme to a monotype; source code cannot store an uninstantiated method scheme in a value, write forall, or pass a polymorphic method as an ordinary argument.
crumbs: 26  Giving a method local type parameters

title: Giving a method local type parameters
section: Practice: separate the two parameter roles
text:
Practice: separate the two parameter roles
Start each task with fresh copies of api.ash, carrier.ash, and 01-map-pair.ash together in a scratch directory.

Use map twice at the same Int -> Bool element types. Adjust map_pair’s domain and result, and the entry’s arguments and annotation, to agree with those calls. Predict the resulting pair and identify what stays polymorphic even though both occurrences choose the same local arguments.
Reverse the written method parameters to <B, A> without changing the signature. Predict the output and explain what parameter order records.
Add an unused method parameter C. Predict the binding error before running the source.
Remove impl Functor only from the entry import. Predict whether the declared method parameters supply what this call needs, then run it and explain the diagnostic’s labels through the separate parameter roles.

In the entry’s two calls, map ran once at Int -> Bool and once at Bool -> Int, and the single selected Functor<Box> fact supported both: the element types varied, the requirement did not. The next lesson asks how one known interface argument can determine another before evidence selection.
crumbs: 26  Giving a method local type parameters

title: Determining interface results
text:
Declare the forward relationship
The previous lesson used one complete requirement, Functor<Box>, while each map occurrence chose its own method-local types. Some interfaces relate two arguments even when an operation reveals only one of them. A measurement operation might receive a key type while its implementation fixes a dependent interface type that never appears in the method’s value type. That dependent type need not be the type of the value the method returns.
Ash can state one forward determination edge on an interface. The edge says which known arguments may determine the remaining arguments before Ash selects implementation evidence.
Read the relation and one implementation in measurement.ash:
Measure has the complete ordered parameter vector <Key, Result>. The where Key -> Result clause partitions it into a nonempty determinant and its dependent complement. This arrow is a static relationship between interface arguments, not a function from Key values to Result values.
Without a determination edge, every interface parameter must occur in each method type. Here only the determinant Key is required. Result may be absent from measure : Key -> Int because a source for the known key can fill it before selection. These conditions come from Ash’s interface well-formedness rules.
The published implementation is one such source. Its head records both arguments of the complete Measure application, while the method signature states what value a call returns.

title: Determining interface results
Determining interface results
section: Select a source for the known key
text:
Select a source for the known key
The successful client imports the method name and independently selects the published implementation fact:
import measurement (measure, impl Measure)

main : Unit -> Int
main () = measure(true)
Identify the key fixed by true, then the dependent argument supplied by the selected implementation. Predict the method’s returned value and type separately from those interface arguments. Run from this lesson’s src directory to compare the observation:
ash 01-selected.ash
Ash reports:
42 : Int
The method body returns 42. Its Key -> Int signature promises an integer result. Result is Unit in the implementation’s interface application; that type is not the method’s returned value type.
The argument true fixes Key = Bool without guessing. The selected source with that key improves the pending obligation by filling Result = Unit. Ash can then select the complete Measure<Bool, Unit> implementation and run its measure method.
The sequence matters:
known Bool key -> determine Unit -> select Measure<Bool, Unit>
Determination changes only static evidence checking. It creates no result-type projection, runtime search, or dynamic mapping from Bool to Unit. Checked evidence still lowers to ordinary functions and erased type operations.

title: Determining interface results
section: A known key is not enough by itself
text:
A known key is not enough by itself
Now leave the same method call and ordinary import in place, but omit the implementation selector:
import measurement (measure)

main : Unit -> Int
main () = measure(true)
The call and its Int result annotation have not changed. Which interface argument remains unanswered without the selected source? Predict whether the checker can reach a complete evidence requirement, then run this entry:
$ ash --message-format human --locale en 02-name-only.ash
The types in this interface requirement are not sufficiently determined to select evidence.
  --> /path/to/ash-doc/content/libraries/determining-interface-results/src/02-name-only.ash:4:11
4 | main () = measure(true)
  |           ^ The types in this interface requirement are not sufficiently determined to select evidence.
  --> /path/to/ash-doc/content/libraries/determining-interface-results/src/measurement.ash:2:5
2 |     measure : Key -> Int
  |     ^ This declaration introduced the interface requirement.
  --> /path/to/ash-doc/content/libraries/determining-interface-results/src/02-name-only.ash:1:21
1 | import measurement (measure)
  |                     ^ This import made the declaration available.
  --> /path/to/ash-doc/content/libraries/determining-interface-results/src/measurement.ash:1:1
1 | pub interface Measure<Key, Result> where Key -> Result {
  | ^ This interface participates in the failing evidence selection.
2 |     measure : Key -> Int
  | ^ This interface participates in the failing evidence selection.
3 | }
  | ^ This interface participates in the failing evidence selection.
reason: constraint.ambiguous
Ash exits with status 1 and writes this message on standard error.
The call still fixes the key to Bool, but no selected implementation source is available to determine Result. The obligation therefore remains incomplete when its evidence scope closes. This is constraint.ambiguous, not constraint.unsatisfied: Ash has not reached a complete application for which it could establish that no candidate exists. The checked-evidence rules do not invent the dependent type or infer it from an implementation that the client did not select.
In the first lesson, the missing selector left a complete Equal<Int> requirement unsatisfied. Here the key is known but the dependent argument is still unresolved. The two messages identify different stages of checking.
The diagnostic’s primary label covers the measure occurrence. Its related labels point to the client’s name import, the original method declaration, and the complete Measure interface declaration. Together they retain the path from the ambiguous call back to the relation that owns its obligation. Restoring impl Measure makes the published source available to determine the dependent argument and satisfy the resulting complete requirement.

title: Determining interface results
text:
Practice: trace completeness before selection
Start each task with fresh copies of measurement.ash and 01-selected.ash together in a scratch directory.

Change the implementation key and call argument from Bool to Int. Identify which source occurrence fixes the determinant. Predict the value and type before running the entry.
Keep the selector but add a second published implementation with the same Bool key and a different dependent type. Predict the checking outcome, then use its labels to explain the interface’s invariant.
Change the method signature to return Result, and update the implementation body and entry result annotation to agree with that contract. Predict the value and type, then run it. Explain what the edge records when ordinary result typing also exposes the dependent argument.
Remove the determination clause. Identify which interface parameter the method type mentions, predict the checking outcome, and follow its labels.

In the two runs the call itself never changed. true gave the checker its key, the selected source filled Result, and the program returned 42; without that source, the same call stopped with its obligation still incomplete. The next chapter asks how container behavior can depend on its elements, so selecting one implementation may require further evidence.

title: Requiring element behavior
text:
Retain the concrete element behavior
The first library lesson compared integers through Equal<Int>. A container can also support equality, but its implementation must explain what makes its elements equal. A box cannot obtain that behavior merely because its element type is written as a parameter.
We will derive box equality by unwrapping two boxes and asking for equality of their contents. The resulting implementation has a prerequisite. A client must make both the container implementation and the needed element behavior available.
Keep the familiar interface, integer implementation, and constrained helper in equality.ash:
same requires Equal<A> and forwards that evidence to the method call. The integer implementation satisfies Equal<Int>. It says nothing yet about boxes, even boxes containing integers.

title: Requiring element behavior
Requiring element behavior
text:
Derive the container implementation
boxes.ash owns the box type and supplies its equality rule:
pub import equality (Equal, equal)

pub type Box<A> = Box(A)

pub impl<A> Equal<Box<A>> where Equal<A> {
    equal (Box(left), Box(right)) = equal (left, right)
}
Read the header from the outside inward. impl<A> names the head’s type parameter. Equal<Box<A>> is the interface application being implemented. where Equal<A> is the evidence needed to implement it.
The method patterns expose left and right, both of type A. Their equality call uses the declared prerequisite. The method cannot assume integer operations because A is rigid while the implementation is checked. Its argument type is fixed by substituting Box<A> into the interface contract.
The public import forwards the interface and method names. It does not import or re-export the integer implementation. The public box implementation is a separate fact whose prerequisite must be satisfied when a client selects it. All parameter names in a prerequisite must already occur in the head; prerequisites do not introduce new unknown element types.

title: Requiring element behavior
section: Supply both facts at the use
text:
Supply both facts at the use
The entry explicitly selects the two public implementations:
import equality (same, impl Equal)
import boxes (Box, impl Equal)

main : Unit -> (Bool, Bool)
main () = (same (Box(42), Box(42)), same (Box(20), Box(22)))
Write the complete requirement for the first same call. Follow the box implementation’s prerequisite to the selected element method, then use that method on each pair’s unwrapped contents. Predict both booleans before running from this lesson’s src directory:
$ ash 01-box-equality.ash
(true, false) : (Bool, Bool)
The first pair has equal contents and the second does not. The ordinary constructor shapes are the same; the element method supplies the distinction.
For same (Box(42), Box(42)), the evidence request follows this path:

The argument fixes A in same to Box<Int>.
Equal<Box<Int>> matches the generic box implementation with its parameter set to Int.
Substituting that choice into its prerequisite gives Equal<Int>.
The selected integer implementation satisfies that prerequisite.

The resulting box method receives integer equality and uses it on the two unwrapped values. The second call uses the same evidence path with different integer contents.

title: Requiring element behavior
section: A selected container rule still needs its prerequisite
text:
A selected container rule still needs its prerequisite
02-missing-prerequisite.ash removes only the integer implementation selector:
import equality (same)
import boxes (Box, impl Equal)

main : Unit -> (Bool, Bool)
main () = (same (Box(42), Box(42)), same (Box(20), Box(22)))
The box implementation is still selected. Trace its prerequisite from the first call: where does evidence become unavailable? Predict which call and declarations the message will connect, then run this entry:
$ ash --message-format human --locale en 02-missing-prerequisite.ash
No available evidence satisfies this interface requirement.
  --> /path/to/ash-doc/content/libraries/requiring-element-behavior/src/02-missing-prerequisite.ash:5:12
5 | main () = (same (Box(42), Box(42)), same (Box(20), Box(22)))
  |            ^ No available evidence satisfies this interface requirement.
  --> /path/to/ash-doc/content/libraries/requiring-element-behavior/src/equality.ash:9:5
9 | pub same : (A, A) -> Bool where Equal<A>
  |     ^ This declaration introduced the interface requirement.
  --> /path/to/ash-doc/content/libraries/requiring-element-behavior/src/02-missing-prerequisite.ash:1:18
1 | import equality (same)
  |                  ^ This import made the declaration available.
  --> /path/to/ash-doc/content/libraries/requiring-element-behavior/src/equality.ash:1:1
1 | pub interface Equal<A> {
  | ^ This interface participates in the failing evidence selection.
2 |     equal : (A, A) -> Bool
  | ^ This interface participates in the failing evidence selection.
3 | }
  | ^ This interface participates in the failing evidence selection.
  --> /path/to/ash-doc/content/libraries/requiring-element-behavior/src/02-missing-prerequisite.ash:2:1
2 | import boxes (Box, impl Equal)
  | ^ This import made the selected implementation available.
  --> /path/to/ash-doc/content/libraries/requiring-element-behavior/src/boxes.ash:5:1
5 | pub impl<A> Equal<Box<A>> where Equal<A> {
  | ^ Evidence selection followed this implementation.
6 |     equal (Box(left), Box(right)) = equal (left, right)
  | ^ Evidence selection followed this implementation.
7 | }
  | ^ Evidence selection followed this implementation.
  --> /path/to/ash-doc/content/libraries/requiring-element-behavior/src/boxes.ash:6:5
6 |     equal (Box(left), Box(right)) = equal (left, right)
  |     ^ This implementation method supplies the selected evidence.
  --> /path/to/ash-doc/content/libraries/requiring-element-behavior/src/equality.ash:1:1
1 | pub interface Equal<A> {
  | ^ This interface participates in the failing evidence selection.
2 |     equal : (A, A) -> Bool
  | ^ This interface participates in the failing evidence selection.
3 | }
  | ^ This interface participates in the failing evidence selection.
reason: constraint.unsatisfied
The message starts at the constrained use, relates it to same’s declaration, and follows the imported box implementation. That implementation is available, but its substituted Equal<Int> prerequisite has no evidence in this entry’s effective environment. Importing same by name does not admit that fact.
Restore impl Equal in the import from equality. This repairs the missing element behavior without changing the generic container rule. A library may also deliberately forward public implementation facts through a facade, as in the earlier forwarding lesson; the route must still be explicit.

title: Requiring element behavior
section: Follow nested prerequisites toward a base case
text:
Follow nested prerequisites toward a base case
The same generic implementation handles a box inside another box:
import equality (same, impl Equal)
import boxes (Box, impl Equal)

main : Unit -> Bool
main () = same (Box(Box(42)), Box(Box(42)))
Write the complete requirements from the outer box to the element type. Separately count the box layers each value must lose during execution. Predict the boolean before running this nested comparison:
$ ash 03-nested-boxes.ash
true : Bool
Selection follows Equal<Box<Box<Int>>>, then Equal<Box<Int>>, then Equal<Int>. Each generic step removes one Box layer from the requirement. Execution similarly unwraps each layer before comparing the integer values. The implementation is reused with different complete arguments; its own method body remains checked once against its declared generic contract.
For an interface without a determination edge, the complete argument vector is its selection key. With an edge, only the determinant positions form the key, as in the preceding determination lesson. Prerequisites do not provide a second way to choose between competing implementations.

title: Requiring element behavior
section: Require structural progress from a generic prerequisite
text:
Require structural progress from a generic prerequisite
For a generic prerequisite still containing parameters, compare its selection key with the head’s key. The vectors must have equal width. Each prerequisite component must equal or be a strict syntactic part of the corresponding head component, and at least one must be strictly smaller. This rule checks structural progress in the requirement, not the method’s calculation.
Consider keeping the box type in the prerequisite:
type Box<A> = Box(A)

interface Equal<A> {
    equal : (A, A) -> Bool
}

impl<A> Equal<Box<A>> where Equal<Box<A>> {
    equal pair = true
}

main : Unit -> Unit
main () = ()
Compare the two Box<A> key arguments. Which part of the progress requirement can this header satisfy, and which part remains unmet? Run the source:
$ ash --message-format human --locale en 04-no-decrease.ash
This generic prerequisite does not have a strictly smaller selection key than the implementation head.
  --> /path/to/ash-doc/content/libraries/requiring-element-behavior/src/04-no-decrease.ash:7:29
7 | impl<A> Equal<Box<A>> where Equal<Box<A>> {
  |                             ^ This generic prerequisite does not have a strictly smaller selection key than the implementation head.
  --> /path/to/ash-doc/content/libraries/requiring-element-behavior/src/04-no-decrease.ash:7:9
7 | impl<A> Equal<Box<A>> where Equal<Box<A>> {
  |         ^ Each prerequisite key argument must equal or be a strict syntactic subterm of its corresponding head argument, with at least one strict decrease.
reason: impl.prerequisite-not-decreasing
The labels compare Box<A> with the unchanged Box<A> prerequisite. The prerequisite repeats the head instead of removing a constructor layer. In the working implementation, A is a strict part of Box<A>, so the prerequisite makes structural progress.
This admission rule applies to nonground prerequisites: those still containing parameters. A fully concrete prerequisite is exempt from this decrease comparison, but evidence selection still detects cycles of complete requirements. The rule does not prove that arbitrary method bodies terminate.

title: Requiring element behavior
section: A specialized implementation is not an override
text:
A specialized implementation is not an override
Available implementation heads must be coherent: two distinct heads cannot match the same complete application. A prerequisite does not give one head lower priority. Consider adding a separate rule for integer boxes:
import equality (Equal, equal, impl Equal)

type Box<A> = Box(A)

impl<A> Equal<Box<A>> where Equal<A> {
    equal (Box(left), Box(right)) = equal (left, right)
}

impl Equal<Box<Int>> {
    equal (Box(left), Box(right)) = left == right
}

main : Unit -> Unit
main () = ()
Find an application that both heads can match. Predict which declarations the checker must compare before it can accept this module, then run it:
$ ash --message-format human --locale en 05-overlap.ash
This implementation can match the same interface application as an earlier available implementation.
  --> /path/to/ash-doc/content/libraries/requiring-element-behavior/src/05-overlap.ash:9:12
9 | impl Equal<Box<Int>> {
  |            ^ This implementation can match the same interface application as an earlier available implementation.
  --> /path/to/ash-doc/content/libraries/requiring-element-behavior/src/05-overlap.ash:5:9
5 | impl<A> Equal<Box<A>> where Equal<A> {
  |         ^ The earlier implementation is defined here.
reason: impl.overlap
Both heads can match Equal<Box<Int>>. The diagnostic identifies the later head and the earlier generic one. Having a prerequisite does not make the generic rule lower priority. Source order, import order, and apparent specificity do not select a winner.
Keep one coherent implementation for that key. Here the generic implementation already obtains integer behavior through its prerequisite, so remove the specialized declaration. If a wrapper needs a distinct meaning, give it a distinct nominal type; the next chapter develops that choice.

title: Requiring element behavior
section: Put an implementation with an owner
text:
Put an implementation with an owner
An implementation belongs in a module that owns its interface or an outer nominal type in its selection key. The box module qualifies through its own type even though Equal comes from another module. Examine this client:
import equality (Equal)
import boxes (Box)

impl Equal<Box<Int>> {
    equal (Box(left), Box(right)) = left == right
}

main : Unit -> Unit
main () = ()
Locate the defining modules of Equal and the outer Box type. Does this client define either one? Predict whether its method body can repair an ownership failure, then run the source:
$ ash --message-format human --locale en 06-foreign-owner.ash
This module owns neither the interface nor an outer nominal type in the implementation's selection key. Dependent arguments and nested nominal types do not establish ownership.
  --> /path/to/ash-doc/content/libraries/requiring-element-behavior/src/06-foreign-owner.ash:4:6
4 | impl Equal<Box<Int>> {
  |      ^ This module owns neither the interface nor an outer nominal type in the implementation's selection key. Dependent arguments and nested nominal types do not establish ownership.
  --> /path/to/ash-doc/content/libraries/requiring-element-behavior/src/06-foreign-owner.ash:4:6
4 | impl Equal<Box<Int>> {
  |      ^ This selected interface belongs to another module.
reason: impl.orphan
The declaration is rejected before its body matters. Place this responsibility in the module owning Equal or the module owning the outer Box, retaining only one implementation for overlapping keys. Importing a type does not transfer ownership of its declaration.
For a determined interface, only the selection-key arguments can establish this nominal ownership. A nominal appearing solely in a dependent result, or nested beneath a foreign outer constructor, does not establish an owner. The implementation rules govern admission and coherence; evidence selection governs the subsequent prerequisite search.

title: Requiring element behavior
text:
Practice: follow the required behavior
Start each task with fresh copies in a scratch directory. For tasks one and two, copy 03-nested-boxes.ash, equality.ash, and boxes.ash together. For tasks three and four, copy 01-box-equality.ash with those two libraries.

Change one innermost integer in 03-nested-boxes.ash. Trace the complete requirements and predict the boolean and which method makes the final decision, then run it.
Add another Box layer to both arguments in 03-nested-boxes.ash. Predict the result and count the unwrapping steps before running it. Explain which complete requirements reuse the generic declaration.
Add Equal<Bool> to equality.ash, using exhaustive Boolean patterns. Compare two Boolean boxes through same in the copied entry and adjust its arguments as needed. Predict the result, then check it.
Explain why removing the prerequisite from the box implementation would leave its method unable to compare arbitrary elements.

One generic declaration served every layer: the nested run reached the integer fact through two unwrappings, and the rejected sources each broke a guard on that same path — selected evidence, a shrinking key, coherent heads, an owning module. The next chapter gives an existing representation a new nominal meaning without allocating an ordinary constructor wrapper.

title: Wrapping a representation
text:
Compare two nominal declarations
Two quantities may both be stored as integers while meaning different things to a program. A nominal type lets their contracts keep that distinction. An ordinary data constructor can carry the integer. A newtype can give the same representation a distinct type without adding a runtime wrapper.
The type distinction remains real: construction and unwrapping are explicit, and interface behavior belongs to the nominal type rather than being inherited from its representation.
01-data-and-newtype.ash constructs one value of each form:
Tagged is ordinary data with one constructor and one integer field. Points is a newtype whose sole, same-spelled constructor takes one representation value. Both are distinct from Int and from each other. Use the rendering rule to predict the two printed fields and their types. Run from this lesson’s src directory:
The tool renders ordinary data with its constructor. It renders the newtype’s representation while retaining Points in the reported type. Seeing an integer in that output does not mean the source type has become Int.

title: Wrapping a representation
text:
type Tagged = Tagged(Int)
newtype Points = Points(Int)

main : Unit -> (Tagged, Points)
main () = (Tagged(42), Points(42))

$ ash 01-data-and-newtype.ash
(Tagged(42), 42) : (Tagged, Points)

title: Wrapping a representation
text:
Cross the representation boundary explicitly
The representation does not make Points equal to Int in a function contract. Consider this call:
newtype Points = Points(Int)

add_one : Int -> Int
add_one value = value + 1

main : Unit -> Int
main () = add_one (Points(41))
Identify the argument expression’s type and the domain that add_one requires. Predict whether the application meets that contract, then run it:
$ ash --message-format human --locale en 02-no-coercion.ash
This function argument must have type `Int`, but has type `Points`.
  --> /path/to/ash-doc/content/libraries/wrapping-a-representation/src/02-no-coercion.ash:7:19
7 | main () = add_one (Points(41))
  |                   ^ This has type `Points`.
  --> /path/to/ash-doc/content/libraries/wrapping-a-representation/src/02-no-coercion.ash:3:11
3 | add_one : Int -> Int
  |           ^ This function requires an argument of type `Int`.
  --> /path/to/ash-doc/content/libraries/wrapping-a-representation/src/02-no-coercion.ash:7:11
7 | main () = add_one (Points(41))
  |           ^ This is the containing function application.
reason: type.argument
The labels connect the supplied Points value to the Int parameter contract. The compiler does not insert an implicit conversion. If the operation should accept and return points, write that contract and expose the representation with a constructor pattern:
newtype Points = Points(Int)

add_one : Points -> Points
add_one (Points(value)) = Points(value + 1)

main : Unit -> Points
main () = add_one (Points(41))
Follow the pattern, integer addition, and explicit construction. What amount does the function return, and which nominal type does its contract retain? Predict both before running this version:
$ ash 03-explicit-conversion.ash
42 : Points
The pattern Points(value) unwraps the integer. Integer addition computes the new amount, and Points(value + 1) wraps it explicitly. The one constructor pattern covers all values of Points, so no second case is needed.

title: Wrapping a representation
section: Give the nominal type its own behavior
text:
Give the nominal type its own behavior
Suppose raw integers are rewards directly, while each point is worth ten reward units. Separate implementations make that interpretation explicit:
newtype Points = Points(Int)

interface Reward<A> {
    reward : A -> Int
}

impl Reward<Int> {
    reward value = value
}

impl Reward<Points> {
    reward (Points(value)) = value * 10
}

main : Unit -> (Int, Int)
main () = (reward 4, reward (Points(4)))
Write the complete Reward requirement for each argument, then follow the matching method. Predict the two reward amounts before running the program:
$ ash 04-distinct-behavior.ash
(4, 40) : (Int, Int)
The raw integer method returns 4; the points method computes 4 * 10 and returns 40. The two arguments select different complete requirements: Reward<Int> and Reward<Points>. Their representations do not merge their implementation identities. Unlike the overlapping integer-box rules in the previous lesson, these two nominal keys cannot match one another.
Now remove only the points implementation:
newtype Points = Points(Int)

interface Reward<A> {
    reward : A -> Int
}

impl Reward<Int> {
    reward value = value
}

main : Unit -> Int
main () = reward (Points(4))
Which complete requirement does this argument create? Compare it with the remaining implementation head and predict whether evidence is available:
$ ash --message-format human --locale en 05-no-inherited-evidence.ash
No available evidence satisfies this interface requirement.
  --> /path/to/ash-doc/content/libraries/wrapping-a-representation/src/05-no-inherited-evidence.ash:12:11
12 | main () = reward (Points(4))
   |           ^ No available evidence satisfies this interface requirement.
  --> /path/to/ash-doc/content/libraries/wrapping-a-representation/src/05-no-inherited-evidence.ash:4:5
4 |     reward : A -> Int
  |     ^ This declaration introduced the interface requirement.
  --> /path/to/ash-doc/content/libraries/wrapping-a-representation/src/05-no-inherited-evidence.ash:3:1
3 | interface Reward<A> {
  | ^ This interface participates in the failing evidence selection.
4 |     reward : A -> Int
  | ^ This interface participates in the failing evidence selection.
5 | }
  | ^ This interface participates in the failing evidence selection.
reason: constraint.unsatisfied
The method occurrence needs Reward<Points>. The message relates that use to the interface contract; the available integer implementation satisfies a different requirement. Restore the explicit points implementation from the preceding example. If the intended calculation is instead the integer reward, unwrap first and call the method on that integer deliberately.
Neither wrapping nor unwrapping copies interface evidence. The evidence rules preserve nominal identity through selection.

title: Wrapping a representation
section: Choose who may construct and unwrap
text:
Choose who may construct and unwrap
The module tickets.ash keeps its constructor behind an opaque public type:
pub opaque newtype Ticket = Ticket(Int)

pub issue : Int -> Ticket
issue value = Ticket(value)

pub number : Ticket -> Int
number (Ticket(value)) = value
The module owns Ticket, so issue may construct it and number may unwrap it. pub opaque newtype exports the type name but withholds the constructor. The functions’ own pub declarations export issue and number. A transparent pub newtype would also export its constructor; a declaration without pub would keep its name private.
This client uses the operations that the module exposes:
import tickets as Tickets

main : Unit -> Int
main () = Tickets.number (Tickets.issue 42)
Follow the public operations from the input integer to the ticket and back. Does the client need to name a constructor along that route? Predict its result before running it:
$ ash 06-opaque-client.ash
42 : Int
issue wraps 42 inside its defining module, and number unwraps that ticket there. The client observes the returned integer using only those operations. The complete import makes the public operations and type name available. Constructor access is a separate boundary. This second client attempts to cross it directly:
import tickets as Tickets

main : Unit -> Tickets.Ticket
main () = Tickets.Ticket(42)
The signature and expression use the same spelling in different roles. Which role needs constructor access, and which public declaration grants or withholds it? Predict the source occurrence the message will identify:
$ ash --message-format human --locale en 07-hidden-constructor.ash
The constructor `Ticket` belongs to an opaque type and is not accessible here.
  --> /path/to/ash-doc/content/libraries/wrapping-a-representation/src/07-hidden-constructor.ash:4:19
4 | main () = Tickets.Ticket(42)
  |                   ^ This name is not accessible here.
  --> /path/to/ash-doc/content/libraries/wrapping-a-representation/src/tickets.ash:1:29
1 | pub opaque newtype Ticket = Ticket(Int)
  |                             ^ The inaccessible declaration is here.
reason: resolve.opaque-constructor
The message identifies the constructor use and the declaration that makes it opaque. Replace Tickets.Ticket(42) with Tickets.issue 42 to construct through the public operation. The result may retain type Tickets.Ticket; the hidden constructor is what the client cannot use.
The module visibility rules allow the type in main’s signature while withholding the expression constructor. A client must use issue, not construct or pattern-match the opaque representation itself. Opacity controls source access; it does not add a wrapper allocation or make printed values a security boundary.

title: Wrapping a representation
text:
Parameterize the representation
A newtype can leave its representation type open:
newtype Recorded<A> = Recorded(A)

unwrap : Recorded<A> -> A
unwrap (Recorded(value)) = value

main : Unit -> (Int, Bool)
main () = (unwrap (Recorded(42)), unwrap (Recorded(true)))
Identify each constructed value’s complete Recorded type, then follow its unwrap call. Predict the pair’s values and types before running it:
$ ash 08-parameterized-wrapper.ash
(42, true) : (Int, Bool)
Each pattern exposes its representation and unwrap returns that value, so the pair retains the integer and boolean. Recorded<Int> and Recorded<Bool> are different applications of the same nominal constructor. Each unwrap use substitutes one element type through both its parameter and result. This follows the same parameter rules used by ordinary data; it adds no implicit conversion between the two applications.

title: Wrapping a representation
text:
Account for the wrapper’s cost
The allocation claim comes from the language’s lowering and execution rules, not from the printed values above. Construction lowers to a checked wrap conversion, and a newtype pattern lowers to an unwrap conversion. The compiler validates the relation between the nominal type and its representation before those conversions erase.
The execution rule enters a validated conversion’s child without allocating a wrapper cell, comparing a tag, or copying the representation. If the representation is an ordinary data value, its own construction still allocates normally. Other work in the program, such as tuple construction or function calls, retains its ordinary costs. Allocation-free wrapping does not mean the whole program performs no allocation.
The pinned evaluator’s module_newtype_wrapper_allocates_no_constructor_cell test checks this distinction directly: it wraps an ordinary Box value and asserts that the heap contains exactly one cell, belonging to that representation. The lowering rules establish why no ordinary constructor node is emitted for the newtype wrapper. The source-level type distinction has already been checked before this runtime erasure.

title: Wrapping a representation
text:
Practice: preserve meaning across conversion
Start each task with a fresh copy in a scratch directory: use 04-distinct-behavior.ash for tasks one and two, 08-parameterized-wrapper.ash for task three, and 01-data-and-newtype.ash for task four.

Change the point multiplier in 04-distinct-behavior.ash. Explain which implementation and tuple field it affects. Predict the pair, then run it.
Add a second newtype over Int with a different domain meaning. Give it an explicit Reward implementation and extend main to compare all three rewards. Update its tuple annotation, predict the values, and run it.
Use Recorded with a tuple representation in 08-parameterized-wrapper.ash. Update the entry result annotation to agree with the unwrapped value. Predict that value and type before running it.
Replace newtype Points with an ordinary one-constructor data declaration. Predict the value display and nominal type, then compare the observation. Explain the representation cost through the lowering and execution rules; explain separately whether either declaration makes the type equal to Int.

Across the runs, the integer inside never changed what the type meant: add_one kept the Points contract, the two reward calls selected different implementations for the same representation, and the opaque constructor stayed out of the client’s reach. The next chapter brings that nominal distinction into one local scope and supplies exact behavior there.

title: Supplying scoped evidence
text:
Consume a local distinction inside its block
A module newtype gives a representation a meaning shared by that module’s clients. Sometimes a calculation needs a distinction only within one block. A local newtype gives the following code a nominal identity without making that identity part of the block’s outward contract.
Once that local type exists, the block may supply exact interface behavior for it. The supplied methods can use values already available there. Their availability follows the source scope, and selected methods become ordinary functions used by the checked calculation.
01-local-value.ash introduces Points only for the remainder of main’s body:
The representation is Int, as for the module newtype in the preceding chapter. Construction and the pattern explicitly cross that boundary. The local identity must stay out of the block’s outward type. Follow the pattern and arithmetic to predict the returned amount, then identify what type leaves the block. Run from this lesson’s src directory:
The pattern unwraps 40, and the body adds two to return 42 : Int. No Points identity occurs in that result type.
A local declaration is sequential: its nominal type and constructor enter the following scope together. It has no pub form and cannot become a recursive group member. Its identity belongs to this lexical declaration; executing the block does not allocate a fresh runtime identity or a resource owner.

title: Supplying scoped evidence
Supplying scoped evidence
section: A closure may retain a value without exposing its type
text:
A closure may retain a value without exposing its type
02-returned-closure.ash returns a calculation over a captured local value:
make_adder : Int -> Int -> Int
make_adder amount = {
    newtype Offset = Offset(Int)
    let offset = Offset(amount)
    fn(value) {
        match offset {
            Offset(saved) => saved + value
        }
    }
}

main : Unit -> Int
main () = make_adder 40 2
The result of make_adder 40 has type Int -> Int. The returned function captures offset and unwraps it when called, but its parameter and result do not expose Offset. Predict the amount retained when make_adder receives 40, then the result when that returned function receives 2. Run it:
$ ash 02-returned-closure.ash
42 : Int
The closure unwraps its saved 40 and adds its argument 2, producing 42. This is an ordinary retained value and closure. The local newtype has no release obligation. Its representation may remain in a function environment when the function’s outward type is independent of the local nominal identity.
Returning the local value itself crosses a different boundary:
main : Unit -> Int
main () = {
    let escaped = {
        newtype Token = Token(Int)
        Token(42)
    }
    0
}
Compare the inner block’s result type with the outward function type of make_adder. Which expression exposes a local identity beyond its declaration’s scope here? Predict whether leaving escaped unused changes that boundary:
$ ash --message-format human --locale en 04-identity-escape.ash
This type or effect row exposes a local nominal type outside its scope.
  --> /path/to/ash-doc/content/libraries/supplying-scoped-evidence/src/04-identity-escape.ash:5:9
5 |         Token(42)
  |         ^ This type or effect row exposes a local nominal type outside its scope.
  --> /path/to/ash-doc/content/libraries/supplying-scoped-evidence/src/04-identity-escape.ash:4:9
4 |         newtype Token = Token(Int)
  |         ^ This scope owns the local nominal type.
reason: type.local-nominal-escape
The escaping expression has type Token, and the related label identifies the declaration whose scope would end. The unused name escaped does not hide that outward type. Return an unwrapped integer, or an identity-free function such as make_adder’s result.
The check includes function domains and results, aggregate members, schemes, requirements, and effect rows. Returning a local value together with a function that unwraps it does not create an implicit package hiding the identity. The local nominal rules define this boundary.

title: Working with effects and scoped resources
text:
Lessons in order
A function can request behavior that a surrounding handler supplies. This path begins with that exchange, then develops how a program describes its effects and keeps control and resource access within their scopes.
Finish Learn Ash first. The opening lesson uses its functions, signatures, values, and pattern bindings; it needs no library or algorithm Case as a prerequisite. The lessons are written for readers growing from beginner toward intermediate.
Use the ash command from the repository’s shared setup. The buffer chapter builds native executables; earlier chapters use ordinary ash execution. Each lesson keeps complete programs in its src directory. Change into that directory before running the commands shown in the lesson. For the first one:
Read the calculation, predict its result, and run it. When the result differs from your prediction, follow the request and the answer before changing the program. The diagnostic reading notes explain the command prompt, English messages, and displayed source paths.
Before the scoped-cell chapter, read the existing implementation-evidence lesson. It supplies the interface vocabulary used by resource providers. The effects chapters otherwise follow in order and introduce the concepts each later chapter needs.

title: Working with effects and scoped resources
text:
Requesting a value — declare an effect, read a closed effect row, request a value, and supply it through a handler.
Following effect contracts — follow effects through calls and distinguish requesting now from returning a function that requests later.
Preserving callback effects — give a callback’s effect row a parameter and explain known effects beside an open tail.
Choosing a handler — trace nested handlers, exact effect instances, and later closure calls.
Resuming a calculation — separate operation answers from results and consume continuations once.
Stopping a calculation — compare pure outcomes, resumption, and discard on a finite list.
Counting with a cell — use acquired cell access and compare it with a pure accumulator.
Keeping access in scope — follow dependencies through handles, closures, tuples, and requests.
Running cleanup — trace cleanup on normal completion and checked abandonment.
Transforming publications — use hook roots and registrations with checked callback lifetimes.
Acquiring a buffer — distinguish acquisition outcomes from checked buffer operations.
Combining effects and scopes — combine policy, state, early stopping, and cleanup in one calculation.
