title: Requesting a value
text:
Pass the bonus as an argument
A score might combine points earned with a bonus chosen for the round. The calculation needs that bonus, but it need not decide what the bonus is. So far, we have supplied values like this through function arguments. An effect gives us another way: the calculation requests a value, and a surrounding handler answers the request. The programming-language literature calls this request-and-handler arrangement algebraic effects.
We will keep the calculation small enough to follow each step. First we will pass the bonus directly. Then we will request it and see how different handlers supply different answers.
Here is the argument-based version in 01-explicit.ash:
The pair supplies both inputs. Follow how matching it binds points and bonus, then work out the addition. Predict the value and its type before running the program from this lesson’s src directory:
main supplies 40 as the earned points and chooses 2 as the round’s bonus. score uses those inputs to calculate 40 + 2, producing 42. The integer result agrees with its declared result type, Int.
This version already solves the problem. Keep it in mind as we change how the calculation obtains the bonus. The addition itself will stay the same.
crumbs: Working with effects and scoped resources

title: Requesting a value
text:
score : (Int, Int) -> Int
score (points, bonus) = points + bonus

main : Unit -> Int
main () = score (40, 2)

$ ash 01-explicit.ash
42 : Int
crumbs: Working with effects and scoped resources

title: Requesting a value
crumbs: Working with effects and scoped resources

title: Requesting a value
text:
Answer the request
The expression handle (score 40) with Bonus { ... } evaluates score 40 under a handler for Bonus. Its amount clause answers an amount request. ignored binds the operation’s Unit input; the clause does not use it.
resume 2 supplies 2 as the operation’s answer and continues the calculation that was waiting for it. The waiting work is the addition in score.
Trace the call and predict the resulting score before running it:

score 40 begins evaluating its addition.
perform Bonus.amount () requests the missing integer.
The handler’s amount clause answers through resume 2.
The addition finishes as 40 + 2.

$ ash 02-handled.ash
42 : Int
The handler chooses 2, and score uses it in 40 + 2. The resumed calculation produces 42, which is also this handler’s result. The value matches the argument-based version, but score now obtains the bonus through a request instead of receiving it in its argument.
A handler must supply a clause for every operation in its effect. Bonus has only amount, so this handler is complete. The clause also has a responsibility to consume the suspended continuation exactly once on every normally completing path. Here it does so with its single resume. A continuation is the work suspended at the request; resuming it supplies the answer that work needs. We will examine other control choices later.
The handler accounts for the calculation’s Bonus requirement, and its clause adds no further effect requirement. That is why main can retain the signature Unit -> Int. As with the pure signatures used in Learn, omitting the row means it is empty: calling the function must leave no effects for its caller to handle. The row describes requirements, not a second value returned by the function.
The specification’s effect rules describe these request, handler, and resumption boundaries. Its computation types and effect rows describe the signature notation, and its handler evaluation rules describe how the answer continues the suspended calculation.

title: Requesting a value
section: A row records a need; it does not answer it
text:
A row records a need; it does not answer it
What if we call score without a handler? In 04-unhandled.ash, the signature of main records the Bonus requirement that this call leaves outward:
effect Bonus {
    amount : Unit -> Int
}

score : Int -> Int ! {Bonus}
score points = points + (perform Bonus.amount ())

main : Unit -> Int ! {Bonus}
main () = score 40
Follow the call from main to the request in score. Which part of this program could supply the missing integer? Compare the two versions of main: does recording {Bonus} supply an answer, or describe a need that remains? Run the file to inspect what happens at the program’s entry:
$ ash --message-format human --locale en 04-unhandled.ash
Calling `main` must require no effects from its caller.
  --> /path/to/ash-doc/content/effects/requesting-a-value/src/04-unhandled.ash:8:1
8 | main : Unit -> Int ! {Bonus}
  | ^ This is the local `main` declaration.
reason: entry.main-effects
There is no handler here to answer the request. The message points at the local main declaration, whose ! {Bonus} records the requirement left by calling score. Ash’s entry contract rejects this unanswered ordinary effect: there is no source caller outside the program’s entry to handle it. The tool can install an interpretation for certain declared native effects, but Bonus is an ordinary effect requiring our handler. The file is rejected before the calculation runs. entry.main-effects identifies this entry-contract rejection.
Restore the handled main from 02-handled.ash, including its Unit -> Int signature, and run the file again. The handler supplies the answer and removes the outward requirement. Merely erasing ! {Bonus} would not answer the request or make the calculation pure.
crumbs: Working with effects and scoped resources

title: Requesting a value
section: Practice: choose a different scoring rule
text:
Practice: choose a different scoring rule
Start each task from a fresh copy of 02-handled.ash, so changes from one task do not affect the next.
Suppose the round’s rules change so the handler grants 7. Before running the program, trace the request and predict the score; then identify which source line supplies the bonus and which line uses it.
Next, change score so it doubles the earned points before adding the requested bonus, keeping the handler unchanged. Predict, run, and explain the new result.
Finally, write the equivalent pure version with an explicit bonus argument. Where does each version receive the bonus, and which part chooses its value?
You now have two ways to supply the same calculation with a value. An argument passes it directly. An effectful calculation requests it, records that need in its row, and continues when a handler resumes it with an answer.
This example puts one call inside one handler. The next question is how the requirement travels when one function calls another, or returns a function that will make the request later.
crumbs: Working with effects and scoped resources

title: Following effect contracts
text:
Follow the request through calls
In the previous lesson, score requested a bonus and main supplied a handler. A larger calculation may reach score through other functions. Each caller must account for the request, even when its own body contains no perform.
There is another distinction to make when a function returns a function. Does the request happen while making that function, or when calling it later? The position of the effect row in the signature tells us which call needs a handler.
01-call-chain.ash adds two calls around the familiar score calculation:
Start at main and follow total 40, then round_score 40, then score 40. Only score contains a request, but each call needs that request answered before it can return. This is why all three signatures contain ! {Bonus}. An effect row describes the requirements of calling the function, including work done through other calls.
Trace the answer back from the handler through the addition and the two callers. Predict the result, then run the file from this lesson’s src directory:
The handler around total 40 supplies 2 when the calculation reaches the request. The addition produces 42, and the two callers return that same value. Neither caller writes perform; each still requires that request to be answered.
None of these functions needs a separate handler merely because it calls an effectful function. It may pass the requirement outward through its contract. Here main handles it, leaving the entry computation with an empty row.
crumbs: Working with effects and scoped resources

title: Following effect contracts
crumbs: Working with effects and scoped resources

title: Following effect contracts
section: A pure contract cannot hide a request
text:
A pure contract cannot hide a request
In 04-missing-row.ash, only the signature of total changes. It now promises a pure call:
effect Bonus {
    amount : Unit -> Int
}

score : Int -> Int ! {Bonus}
score points = points + (perform Bonus.amount ())

round_score : Int -> Int ! {Bonus}
round_score points = score points

total : Int -> Int
total points = round_score points

main : Unit -> Int
main () = handle (total 40) with Bonus {
    amount ignored => resume 2
}
Compare total’s new signature with the contract of the function it calls. Can that body meet the promise of a pure call? Keep the handler in main in view while you run the file and inspect where Ash reports the mismatch:
$ ash --message-format human --locale en 04-missing-row.ash
This function body requests effects outside its declared effect row.
  --> /path/to/ash-doc/content/effects/following-effect-contracts/src/04-missing-row.ash:12:16
12 | total points = round_score points
   |                ^ This function body requests effects outside its declared effect row.
reason: effect.row-union-ambiguous
The label points at round_score points, the call that brings the requirement into total. The words of the message explain the mismatch: the body requests an effect outside the declared row. Ash checks total against its own signature. The handler in main can answer the eventual request, but it does not repair that definition’s incorrect promise. Restore ! {Bonus} on total, as in 01-call-chain.ash, and the contract again describes what the body does.
This diagnostic uses effect.row-union-ambiguous. Here the source contains only closed rows; the message identifies a body that exceeds its declared row. Read the explanation and source label rather than assuming that the reason code alone describes the particular mistake.
crumbs: Working with effects and scoped resources

title: Following effect contracts
section: Practice: place the handler around the work
text:
Practice: place the handler around the work
Start each task from a fresh copy of its named program in this lesson’s src directory.
Add another function between total and round_score in 01-call-chain.ash, writing its signature before its body. Does the new function need an effect row? Run it to confirm your answer.
In 02-request-later.ash, change the remembered points and the handler’s answer. Predict the result and identify which call makes the request.
In 03-request-now.ash, call calculate () twice and return both results as a tuple. Do those later calls request another bonus? Run the program and explain the result from the saved values.
An effectful contract follows the work that can make the request. Ordinary callers carry the requirement outward until a handler answers it. A returned function carries its later requirements in its own function type.
We can now describe a particular effectful function accurately. The next question is how a reusable helper can call functions with different effects without fixing its contract to Bonus.

title: Preserving callback effects
text:
Start with a pure callback
A function such as apply_twice does not need to know what calculation its argument performs. It calls the supplied function twice. But its signature still has to account for any effects those calls require.
We will start with a pure callback, then pass the bonus calculation from the previous lessons. This creates a reason to make the effect row a parameter, just as Learn made an element type a parameter of a reusable definition.
A callback is an ordinary function passed to another function to be called there. In 01-pure-callback.ash, increment is the callback:
Start with the inner call, function value, and use its result as the input to the outer call. Predict what applying increment twice does to the starting value, then run the file from this lesson’s src directory:
The first call turns 40 into 41. The second uses that result and produces 42. Neither call requests an effect.
The tuple parameter contains a pure function of type Int -> Int and its starting integer. apply_twice also promises a pure result computation. Those promises agree with increment.
crumbs: Working with effects and scoped resources

title: Preserving callback effects
text:
apply_twice : (Int -> Int, Int) -> Int
apply_twice (function, value) = function (function value)

increment : Int -> Int
increment value = value + 1

main : Unit -> Int
main () = apply_twice (increment, 40)

$ ash 01-pure-callback.ash
42 : Int
crumbs: Working with effects and scoped resources

title: Preserving callback effects
section: An effectful callback needs a different contract
text:
An effectful callback needs a different contract
Now try supplying score. 02-pure-contract.ash installs a handler around the call, but leaves the pure signature of apply_twice unchanged:
effect Bonus {
    amount : Unit -> Int
}

score : Int -> Int ! {Bonus}
score points = points + (perform Bonus.amount ())

apply_twice : (Int -> Int, Int) -> Int
apply_twice (function, value) = function (function value)

main : Unit -> Int
main () = handle (apply_twice (score, 40)) with Bonus {
    amount ignored => resume 2
}
Compare score’s signature with the function component of apply_twice’s tuple parameter. Which requirement does each row describe? Keep the outer handler in view as you check whether the supplied function fits that parameter:
$ ash --message-format human --locale en 02-pure-contract.ash
This function argument must have type `(Int -> Int, Int)`, but has type `(Int -> Int ! {Bonus}, Int)`.
  --> /path/to/ash-doc/content/effects/preserving-callback-effects/src/02-pure-contract.ash:12:31
12 | main () = handle (apply_twice (score, 40)) with Bonus {
   |                               ^ This has type `(Int -> Int ! {Bonus}, Int)`.
  --> /path/to/ash-doc/content/effects/preserving-callback-effects/src/02-pure-contract.ash:8:15
8 | apply_twice : (Int -> Int, Int) -> Int
  |               ^ This function requires an argument of type `(Int -> Int, Int)`.
  --> /path/to/ash-doc/content/effects/preserving-callback-effects/src/02-pure-contract.ash:12:18
12 | main () = handle (apply_twice (score, 40)) with Bonus {
   |                  ^ This is the containing function application.
reason: type.argument
The first label identifies the supplied argument. The second points back to the tuple parameter in apply_twice’s signature, and the third identifies the whole call. Together they show where the effectful function meets a pure function requirement.
score has type Int -> Int ! {Bonus}, while the helper requires Int -> Int. The outer handler can answer a request made during a valid calculation; it does not change the helper’s required argument type. The callback contract has to describe the function being supplied.
The message names Bonus in the supplied function’s nonempty row. The callback may request a bonus; the helper’s pure callback contract permits no such request.
We could specialize apply_twice to Bonus. Instead, its body gives us a more useful contract: it needs whatever effects the supplied function needs.
crumbs: Working with effects and scoped resources

title: Preserving callback effects
crumbs: Working with effects and scoped resources

title: Preserving callback effects
section: Add a known effect to the callback’s row
text:
Add a known effect to the callback’s row
A different helper might call its callback once and then request a bonus of its own. Its result must include both requirements. In 04-known-effect.ash, add_bonus writes the known effect beside the tail:
effect Bonus {
    amount : Unit -> Int
}

add_bonus<R : EffectRow> : (Int -> Int ! {| R}, Int) -> Int ! {Bonus | R}
add_bonus (function, value) = (function value) + (perform Bonus.amount ())

increment : Int -> Int
increment value = value + 1

main : Unit -> Int
main () = handle (add_bonus (increment, 40)) with Bonus {
    amount ignored => resume 2
}
The callback has row {| R}. The helper’s result has row {Bonus | R}: the known Bonus instance together with the remaining effects represented by R. This notation also records that R excludes that exact Bonus instance. The tail is the remainder, not an unknown row that might duplicate the known member.
The addition uses the callback’s result and the helper’s own requested bonus. Follow the callback first and the request second, then predict their sum:
$ ash 04-known-effect.ash
43 : Int
Here the callback is pure, so R becomes empty. increment 40 produces 41, and the handler supplies 2 for the helper’s request. Adding them produces 43; only the helper introduces a Bonus requirement.
The tail’s exclusion also limits which callbacks this helper accepts. A callback that itself requests Bonus cannot supply that tail. We will examine that call after checking why the known member is needed in the result row.
crumbs: Working with effects and scoped resources

title: Preserving callback effects
section: Do not guess what an unknown tail contains
text:
Do not guess what an unknown tail contains
05-unknown-union.ash drops the known member from the result row:
effect Bonus {
    amount : Unit -> Int
}

add_bonus<R : EffectRow> : (Int -> Int ! {| R}, Int) -> Int ! {| R}
add_bonus (function, value) = (function value) + (perform Bonus.amount ())

increment : Int -> Int
increment value = value + 1

main : Unit -> Int
main () = handle (add_bonus (increment, 40)) with Bonus {
    amount ignored => resume 2
}
The body still combines the callback’s unknown row with a Bonus request. Compare the result signature with the preceding version. Does it establish that the tail excludes the known effect being added? Inspect the rejected expression:
$ ash --message-format human --locale en 05-unknown-union.ash
This expression combines effect rows that have no most general union.
  --> /path/to/ash-doc/content/effects/preserving-callback-effects/src/05-unknown-union.ash:6:31
6 | add_bonus (function, value) = (function value) + (perform Bonus.amount ())
  |                               ^ This expression combines effect rows that have no most general union.
reason: effect.row-union-ambiguous
The label identifies the expression combining the two requirements. This message uses the same reason code seen for the incorrect closed contract in the preceding lesson, but its explanation concerns an unknown row union. The signature neither includes Bonus explicitly nor establishes that R excludes it. Ash does not invent that exclusion to make the union work. Restore {Bonus | R} in the result signature, as in 04-known-effect.ash. That states the known requirement and the restriction on the remaining tail.
The effect-row rules govern these unions and exclusions. Known members form an unordered set: their written order does not select handlers or order requests. The type checker also needs enough information about open tails; it cannot assume facts about an unconstrained tail merely because one particular call uses a pure callback.
crumbs: Working with effects and scoped resources

title: Preserving callback effects
section: Respect the tail’s exclusion at a call
text:
Respect the tail’s exclusion at a call
Now try the bonus-requesting score as the callback to add_bonus. 06-excluded-callback.ash retains the known member beside the result tail and passes score to the helper:
effect Bonus {
    amount : Unit -> Int
}

add_bonus<R : EffectRow> : (Int -> Int ! {| R}, Int) -> Int ! {Bonus | R}
add_bonus (function, value) = (function value) + (perform Bonus.amount ())

score : Int -> Int ! {Bonus}
score points = points + (perform Bonus.amount ())

main : Unit -> Int
main () = handle (add_bonus (score, 40)) with Bonus {
    amount ignored => resume 2
}
Read the row in score’s signature, then substitute it for R in the helper’s callback type. Can that substitution satisfy the exclusion recorded by {Bonus | R}? Run the file to inspect the call boundary:
$ ash --message-format human --locale en 06-excluded-callback.ash
This computation requires an effect excluded from the row tail. An effect written before a row tail cannot also occur in that tail with the same type arguments.
  --> /path/to/ash-doc/content/effects/preserving-callback-effects/src/06-excluded-callback.ash:12:29
12 | main () = handle (add_bonus (score, 40)) with Bonus {
   |                             ^ This computation requires an effect excluded from the row tail. An effect written before a row tail cannot also occur in that tail with the same type arguments.
  --> /path/to/ash-doc/content/effects/preserving-callback-effects/src/06-excluded-callback.ash:5:28
5 | add_bonus<R : EffectRow> : (Int -> Int ! {| R}, Int) -> Int ! {Bonus | R}
  |                            ^ This type is required here.
reason: effect.row-exclusion
The first label points at the supplied callback and its starting value. The related label points at the helper’s required callback type. The message explains why matching them fails: the known effect cannot also occur in the tail with the same type arguments.
score requires {Bonus}. Matching that callback against Int -> Int ! {| R} would put Bonus into R. The helper’s result row {Bonus | R} requires that R exclude that same instance, so this substitution cannot satisfy the contract.
Use the pure increment callback from 04-known-effect.ash to satisfy this contract. Its empty row fits R, leaving only the helper’s own Bonus request. If the helper is intended to share Bonus with its callback, its callback contract must include that known effect explicitly as well.
This is a restriction on substituting a row into a contract. It does not mean that a calculation can request a given effect only once: apply_twice already requested the bonus twice using one effect-row member.

title: Preserving callback effects
text:
Practice: preserve the callback’s contract
Use a fresh copy of 03-open-row.ash for each of the first two tasks, and a fresh copy of 04-known-effect.ash for the third. Keep the copies in this lesson’s src directory.
Rename apply_twice to apply_three_times and make it call its callback three times. Predict both results before running. Does the row need to change?
Now add a pure Boolean callback that exchanges true and false, and use the same apply_twice definition with it. Which value-type and row arguments does this use supply? Run it to check.
In 04-known-effect.ash, change the handler’s bonus and the initial points. Trace the callback first and the helper’s request second; predict the result without changing either function’s contract.
A reusable helper can leave its value type and its effect requirements open. The repeated row parameter connects what the callback needs to what the helper needs. A known member beside that tail adds a requirement and makes an exclusion explicit.
So far each successful effectful calculation has used one handler for Bonus. Next we can ask which handler receives a request when handlers are nested or when a program uses different effect instances.

title: Choosing a handler
text:
A local answer inside an outer calculation
The preceding lessons put each request under one handler. A calculation can also have a local rule inside a broader rule. To predict its result, follow where the request happens and identify the nearest handler for that exact effect instance.
An effect instance consists of the declaring effect and its type arguments. Two handlers with the same target can answer differently. Two effects with the same spelling need not be the same target.
In 01-nested.ash, the first request has a local handler. The second request comes after that local scope has finished:
For each perform, identify the matching handler that still surrounds it. Follow where the local scope finishes before predicting the sum, then run the file from this lesson’s src directory:
The inner handler supplies 2. The later request uses the still-surrounding handler and receives 10, so the addition produces 12.
Both requests name Bonus.amount. The handler evaluation rules select the nearest matching handler at the point of each request. The effect row does not list an order of handlers.

text:
Practice: trace the request before changing the answer
Start each task from a fresh copy of its named program in this lesson’s src directory. Keep left.ash and right.ash beside the module-example copy so its relative imports still find the same declarations.
In 01-nested.ash, change only the inner answer. Which part of the sum changes? Run the program to check.

Rename the Left import alias in 05-module-identities.ash and update its uses. Does renaming change either answer? Predict before running.
In 06-returned-function.ash, change the handler around request (). Its result combines one saved value with the new answer; predict the new result.
The nearest matching handler answers a request from its body; its own clauses can request behavior from outside that handler. Exact declaration identity and type arguments determine what matches. We can now follow a request to its clause. Next we will follow what happens when that clause resumes the waiting calculation.

title: Resuming a calculation
text:
Follow the waiting work
A request pauses some work. Its handler clause can supply the operation’s answer through resume, but that answer is not necessarily the value returned by resume itself. Resuming runs the waiting calculation; when that work finishes, its result comes back to the clause.
We will follow two requests in one calculation, then examine why the right to resume cannot be ignored, reused, or saved in another function.
Round supplies an integer bonus and a Boolean choice. In 01-resumed-result.ash, the bonus clause does more work after resuming:
The first request needs an integer; resume 2 supplies it and continues at the binding of bonus. Follow that work through the enabled request and the match. Before running, predict what value returns to result, then what the bonus clause returns after adding 100. Run the file from this lesson’s src directory:
The enabled clause supplies true, so the match computes 40 + 2. That result returns to the bonus clause, which still has its addition to do:
For the other operation, resume true takes a Boolean answer but returns an integer result. The operation signature controls the answer supplied to resume. The handler’s result contract controls the resumed computation and the clause result.
Resumption continues after the request. It does not start the body again or repeat work before that request. Handlers in the suspended segment are restored as the work continues, which is why the later enabled request still uses the Round handler. The handler evaluation rules describe this return to the clause after the resumed work finishes.

title: Resuming a calculation
text:
Cover the whole operation API
A handler supplies exactly one clause for every operation in its target API. 02-missing-operation.ash uses a body that only requests bonus. Compare the declared operations with the clauses: which requirement remains uncovered?
effect Round {
    bonus : Unit -> Int
    enabled : Unit -> Bool
}

main : Unit -> Int
main () = handle (perform Round.bonus ()) with Round {
    bonus ignored => resume 2
}
Check that comparison against the diagnostic:
$ ash --message-format human --locale en 02-missing-operation.ash
This handler must contain exactly one clause for every operation of the handled effect.
  --> /path/to/ash-doc/content/effects/resuming-a-calculation/src/02-missing-operation.ash:7:11
7 | main () = handle (perform Round.bonus ()) with Round {
  |           ^ This handler must contain exactly one clause for every operation of the handled effect.
8 |     bonus ignored => resume 2
  | ^ This handler must contain exactly one clause for every operation of the handled effect.
9 | }
  | ^ This handler must contain exactly one clause for every operation of the handled effect.
reason: effect.handler-coverage
The diagnostic labels the incomplete handler. Add an enabled clause that resumes with a Boolean, as in 01-resumed-result.ash. Coverage belongs to the API, not just to operations reached by one chosen input.
crumbs: Working with effects and scoped resources

title: Resuming a calculation
text:
Consume the continuation once
The waiting work is the continuation. A selected clause receives the right to consume it exactly once on every normally completing path. Returning an ordinary integer does not consume it. 03-missing-resume.ash demonstrates that difference with a smaller API:
effect Bonus {
    amount : Unit -> Int
}

main : Unit -> Int
main () = handle (perform Bonus.amount ()) with Bonus {
    amount ignored => 2
}
At the end of this clause, has the waiting calculation received an answer? Identify what remains unconsumed before reading the message:
$ ash --message-format human --locale en 03-missing-resume.ash
This path can finish without resuming or safely discarding the continuation.
  --> /path/to/ash-doc/content/effects/resuming-a-calculation/src/03-missing-resume.ash:7:23
7 |     amount ignored => 2
  |                       ^ This path can finish without resuming or safely discarding the continuation.
reason: effect.resume-not-consumed
The label points at the clause that finishes while leaving its continuation unused. Replace its 2 with resume 2 to continue the waiting calculation. The message also names safe discard, which the next lesson will introduce.
Once resumed, the same continuation cannot be used again. Trace its state through the two uses in 04-repeated-resume.ash:
effect Bonus {
    amount : Unit -> Int
}

main : Unit -> Int
main () = handle (perform Bonus.amount ()) with Bonus {
    amount ignored => {
        let result = resume 2
        resume result
    }
}
Which use encounters a continuation that has already been consumed?
$ ash --message-format human --locale en 04-repeated-resume.ash
This path has already resumed or discarded the continuation; it cannot do so again.
  --> /path/to/ash-doc/content/effects/resuming-a-calculation/src/04-repeated-resume.ash:9:9
9 |         resume result
  |         ^ This path has already resumed or discarded the continuation; it cannot do so again.
reason: effect.resume-already-consumed
The second resume is the error. Return result there instead; using an ordinary returned integer does not require another resumption.

title: Stopping a calculation
text:
Return an outcome directly
A list of scores can contain a marker meaning that processing should stop. Use zero as that marker. We want the total before the marker, and we want to leave later items unprocessed.
A pure function can express that decision by returning an outcome. An effect lets the calculation request the decision from a handler. We will compare the two approaches before using discard to stop the waiting work.
01-pure-outcome.ash uses the finite recursive data and accumulated total introduced in Learn and the list Cases:
End completes the calculation. An Item with value zero returns Stopped immediately. Every other item adds to the total and continues with its tail. Trace the list 20, 0, 99: which items contribute to the accumulated total, and which tail is left untouched? Predict the outcome before running the file from this lesson’s src directory:
The first item adds 20; the next item selects Stopped with that total. The call never recurses into the tail containing 99. The constructors make the result meaningful to this program. Their names do not give them any special failure or control behavior in Ash.
crumbs: Working with effects and scoped resources

title: Stopping a calculation
text:
type Scores = End
    | Item(Int, Scores)
type Outcome = Finished(Int)
    | Stopped(Int)

sum_scores : (Scores, Int) -> Outcome
sum_scores (End, total) = Finished total
sum_scores (Item(value, rest), total) = match value == 0 {
    true => Stopped total
    false => sum_scores (rest, total + value)
}

main : Unit -> Outcome
main () = sum_scores (Item(20, Item(0, Item(99, End))), 0)

$ ash 01-pure-outcome.ash
Stopped(20) : Outcome

title: Counting with a cell
text:
Read a value, then change the cell
The preceding list calculation carried its total through ordinary arguments. Sometimes a calculation needs several helpers to read and update one shared count. A scoped cell provides that access while one surrounding scope owns the cell’s release.
Before this chapter, work through choosing implementation evidence. It distinguishes a method’s interface requirement from the evidence needed to call it. Cell acquisition supplies a particular sealed form of that evidence.
01-read-and-write.ash starts with one cell containing zero:
@builtin.cell is a compiler-owned module. The import gives its public names the alias Cell; the alias itself is an ordinary name chosen by this program.
resource cell<R> counter = 0 { ... } acquires the cell and runs its body. Within the body, counter is a handle of type Cell.Handle<R>. The scope introduces R to distinguish this acquisition. Reading returns a copied integer; writing changes the cell and returns Unit.
alias provides access to the same cell as counter. Predict both fields of the returned pair: does changing the cell also change the integer already bound to before? Run the file from this lesson’s src directory:
before keeps the copied 0; writing 1 through alias changes the cell, so the later read returns 1. The aliases do not own separate releases. The resource scope owns one release when its body finishes. The returned pair contains ordinary integers and needs no cell access after that scope has closed.
crumbs: Working with effects and scoped resources

title: Counting with a cell
section: Keep the pure count for comparison
text:
Keep the pure count for comparison
02-pure-count.ash counts a finite list without mutable state:
type Scores = End
    | Item(Int, Scores)

count : (Scores, Int) -> Int
count (End, total) = total
count (Item(value, rest), total) = count (rest, total + 1)

main : Unit -> Int
main () = count (Item(20, Item(0, Item(99, End))), 0)
Every Item contributes one, including an item whose score is zero. The accumulator is the number of items already visited. At End, it is the final count. Trace the list and predict that count, including the item with score zero:
$ ash 02-pure-count.ash
3 : Int
There are three Item constructors, so the count is 3. Zero counts as an item here; this traversal has no stopping rule. This is still a suitable way to count a list. The cell version will let us compare the same result with a different way of carrying the count.

title: Counting with a cell
text:
State the helper’s evidence requirement
A caller’s resource scope does not erase the contract required by a helper’s own definition. 04-missing-provider.ash records the read effect but omits its provider requirement:
import @builtin.cell as Cell

read_count : Cell.Handle<R> -> Int ! {Cell.Ops<R>}
read_count counter = Cell.read counter

main : Unit -> Int
main () = resource cell<R> counter = 0 {
    read_count counter
}
The call sits inside an acquisition, but the helper’s definition must state what it needs for every use. Compare its signature with visit’s: what requirement can the caller supply only if the helper declares it?
$ ash --message-format human --locale en 04-missing-provider.ash
No available evidence satisfies this interface requirement.
  --> /path/to/ash-doc/content/effects/counting-with-a-cell/src/04-missing-provider.ash:4:22
4 | read_count counter = Cell.read counter
  |                      ^ No available evidence satisfies this interface requirement.
  --> @builtin.cell:7:1
7 | read : Handle<R> -> Int ! {Ops<R>}
  | ^ This declaration introduced the interface requirement.
  --> /path/to/ash-doc/content/effects/counting-with-a-cell/src/04-missing-provider.ash:1:1
1 | import @builtin.cell as Cell
  | ^ This import made the declaration available.
  --> @builtin.cell:6:1
6 | pub interface Provider<R> {
  | ^ This interface participates in the failing evidence selection.
7 | read : Handle<R> -> Int ! {Ops<R>}
  | ^ This interface participates in the failing evidence selection.
8 | write : (Handle<R>, Int) -> Unit ! {Ops<R>}
  | ^ This interface participates in the failing evidence selection.
9 | }
  | ^ This interface participates in the failing evidence selection.
reason: constraint.unsatisfied
The first label identifies the method call without evidence. The label on read’s builtin declaration identifies the method that introduced the requirement. The import label explains how that declaration became available by name; the final group shows the Provider<R> interface participating in the failed selection. @builtin.cell names compiler-owned source rather than a missing file in your checkout.
Add where Cell.Provider<R> to read_count’s signature, following visit in 03-cell-count.ash. The helper then declares the requirement that the resource body can supply at its call. An effect row and an interface requirement answer different questions: what operation may be requested, and what evidence the method needs.

section: Practice: track the count and its access
text:
Practice: track the count and its access
Start each task with fresh copies of its named programs in a scratch directory outside this lesson’s src tree, and run the copies from that directory.
Add another item to the lists in 02-pure-count.ash and 03-cell-count.ash. Predict their results. How does each version represent the intermediate state?

Change visit in 03-cell-count.ash to count only nonzero scores, keeping the updates inside the branch that counts an item. Make the same counting choice in 02-pure-count.ash and compare the two versions.
A cell handle provides reusable access during one owned scope. The scope supplies the provider and operation interpreter and owns release; copies of a read integer are ordinary values. Next we will examine which values can leave that scope and which ones still retain access to the cell.

title: Keeping access in scope
text:
Return a calculation over a copied integer
A resource scope owns release, but its result can outlive that scope. The question is what the result retains. An integer read from a cell is a copy. A handle, or a function that retains the handle, still depends on access to the cell.
We will compare those results, then follow the same distinction through a tuple and an effect request. A type annotation alone does not describe every resource dependency stored in a value.
01-copied-result.ash reads a cell before returning a function:
Inspect what calculate captures: does its body need the handle, or only the integer already read? Predict its result when later () runs after the resource scope ends. Run from this lesson’s src directory:
The closure keeps the copied 41 and adds one, producing 42. The scope releases the cell before later () runs; the closure needs no access to it. This is the same split the handler-selection lesson drew for closures: captured values travel with the function, while a request inside its body answers to the handler in place when the function is called.

title: Keeping access in scope
section: A returned handle would outlive its owner
text:
A returned handle would outlive its owner
03-handle-escape.ash attempts to keep the handle after the resource body ends:
import @builtin.cell as Cell

main : Unit -> Int
main () = {
    let leaked = resource cell<R> counter = 0 {
        counter
    }
    0
}
What would leaked retain after the closing brace? Compare it with the copied integer retained by the first example:
$ ash --message-format human --locale en 03-handle-escape.ash
This value or computation depends on a resource that would be out of scope.
  --> /path/to/ash-doc/content/effects/keeping-access-in-scope/src/03-handle-escape.ash:6:9
6 |         counter
  |         ^ This value or computation depends on a resource that would be out of scope.
  --> /path/to/ash-doc/content/effects/keeping-access-in-scope/src/03-handle-escape.ash:5:18
5 |     let leaked = resource cell<R> counter = 0 {
  |                  ^ This resource is acquired here and must remain within its scope.
6 |         counter
  | ^ This resource is acquired here and must remain within its scope.
7 |     }
  | ^ This resource is acquired here and must remain within its scope.
reason: type.resource-escape
The first label identifies the escaping value and the related label identifies its acquisition. The unused name leaked does not make that escape valid. Return Cell.read counter instead when the outside code needs only the count.
Wrapping the handle in a function does not solve the problem. 04-closure-escape.ash returns a function that would read the closing cell:
import @builtin.cell as Cell

main : Unit -> Int
main () = {
    let leaked = resource cell<R> counter = 0 {
        let later : Unit -> Int ! {Cell.Ops<R>} = fn(ignored) {
            Cell.read counter
        }
        later
    }
    0
}
Follow later’s captured value back to its owner. Could that function perform its read after the owner closes?
$ ash --message-format human --locale en 04-closure-escape.ash
This value or computation depends on a resource that would be out of scope.
  --> /path/to/ash-doc/content/effects/keeping-access-in-scope/src/04-closure-escape.ash:9:9
9 |         later
  |         ^ This value or computation depends on a resource that would be out of scope.
  --> /path/to/ash-doc/content/effects/keeping-access-in-scope/src/04-closure-escape.ash:5:18
5 |     let leaked = resource cell<R> counter = 0 {
  |                  ^ This resource is acquired here and must remain within its scope.
6 |         let later : Unit -> Int ! {Cell.Ops<R>} = fn(ignored) {
  | ^ This resource is acquired here and must remain within its scope.
7 |             Cell.read counter
  | ^ This resource is acquired here and must remain within its scope.
8 |         }
  | ^ This resource is acquired here and must remain within its scope.
9 |         later
  | ^ This resource is acquired here and must remain within its scope.
10 |     }
   | ^ This resource is acquired here and must remain within its scope.
reason: type.resource-escape
The error is at the returned later value. Compare the correction in 01-copied-result.ash: read inside the scope, then capture only the copied integer. Alternatively, call the access-retaining function while the owner still surrounds it, as in 02-live-access.ash.

Practice: identify the retained value
For each task, start with a fresh copy of its named program in a scratch directory outside this lesson’s src tree. Run your copy from that directory.

title: Running cleanup
text:
Preserve the body result, then observe the action
A calculation may need to record that a scope has finished, even when a handler stops its body early. cleanup action { body } gives the scope one obligation: invoke the retained action when closing it. The action is an ordinary function from Unit to Unit; the obligation belongs to the scope.
We will use a live cell as a log. Appending digit one means multiplying its current value by ten and adding one. This makes action order visible without introducing external output operations.
01-normal-completion.ash writes nine in its body and appends one on closing:
On normal completion, cleanup saves the body’s value, invokes the action, and then returns the saved value. Predict the pair’s fields separately: what does the body return, and what does the log contain after append_one? Run from this lesson’s src directory:
The body returns 42 after writing 9; the action changes the log to 9 * 10 + 1, or 91. Its Unit result is set aside, preserving the body’s 42. The cleanup evaluation rules describe these two steps. The cell owner surrounds the cleanup and the final read, so the action has live access when it runs. Its function type records that access’s operation row. Cleanup does not require its action to be pure.

title: Running cleanup
text:

For each task, make a fresh copy of its named program in a scratch directory outside this lesson’s src tree, then run the copy from that directory.

A cleanup scope retains one action and owns its invocation. Normal return preserves the body’s value; abandonment closes the owned scopes before the clause continues. Both paths must respect the resources and handlers available at closing. Next we will use scoped handlers to transform publications through several registered functions.

title: Transforming publications
text:
Transform in registration order
A score may pass through several adjustments: add one point, then double the result. We could compose two functions directly. A hook gives surrounding scopes a way to register those transformations while the calculation publishes an ordinary typed value.
A hook API is an effect with exactly one operation named publish, whose input and result types are structurally equal under the declaration’s own parameters, before substituting arguments at a use. hook establishes a root with an identity transformation. Each register adds a transformer for its body’s scope.
In 01-transform-order.ash, the outer registration increments and the inner registration doubles:
Publication uses ordinary perform syntax. It applies the outer transformation first, then the inner one. Predict the two intermediate values for payload 3 before running from this lesson’s src directory:
Increment changes 3 to 4; double changes 4 to 8. The hook evaluation rules describe this outer-to-inner chain. Each transformer is an ordinary Int -> Int function. Registration evaluates the transformer expression once and retains the resulting function for that scope. It does not call the transformer until a publication reaches it.

title: Transforming publications
section: Qualify the API before specializing it
text:
Qualify the API before specializing it
04-invalid-api.ash declares a conversion with different input and result parameters:
effect Convert<A, B> {
    publish : A -> B
}

main : Unit -> Int
main () = hook Convert<Int, Int> {
    perform Convert<Int, Int>.publish 3
}
Compare A and B in the declaration before substituting Int. Does this API meet the hook requirement, regardless of this particular use?
$ ash --message-format human --locale en 04-invalid-api.ash
An API used by `hook` or `register` must declare exactly one operation, `publish`, whose parameter and result types are equal before type arguments are substituted.
  --> /path/to/ash-doc/content/effects/transforming-publications/src/04-invalid-api.ash:6:16
6 | main () = hook Convert<Int, Int> {
  |                ^ An API used by `hook` or `register` must declare exactly one operation, `publish`, whose parameter and result types are equal before type arguments are substituted.
reason: type.hook-api
Even though this use supplies Int for both parameters, the declaration does not promise one unchanged payload type. Its domain is A and its result is B. Qualification happens before use-site substitution. Use a declaration such as Adjust, whose publish : Int -> Int has equal input and result types, or a one-parameter API with publish : A -> A.
The diagnostic points at the target that fails qualification. Changing only the callback or publication value would not repair the API declaration.

title: Acquiring a buffer
text:
Read an initially zero byte
A cell scope begins with an integer value. A native buffer must first acquire space for a requested number of bytes. That acquisition can fail before its body starts. Successful acquisition followed by normal body completion wraps the body’s value in Success, even when that value is itself a Failure.
The buffer API also returns ordinary outcomes for checked reads and writes. We will keep those outcomes separate: acquiring a buffer successfully does not guarantee that every operation on it succeeds.
The buffer library calls the native allocator. Its programs need a generated executable, built on Linux x86-64 GNU with the selected Rust toolchain and a native linker. Keep ASH_LIBRARIES from the shared setup in this terminal; it points at the selected Ash checkout’s libraries directory. ASH_NATIVE_CACHE lets these builds reuse their compiled dependencies. The ffi root connects imports to that directory. Building reports the executable’s absolute path; running it prints the value without a type suffix. The main signature still states the result type checked during compilation.
01-zeroed-bytes.ash acquires four bytes and reads index zero:
@ffi.native_buffer imports the source buffer library through the ffi root. Buffer.Buffer<R> names its declared resource family. Like a cell, an acquired buffer has a handle, an exact provider relation, an operation interpreter, and one scope owning release. Its bytes start at zero.
Buffer.Outcome<A> has ordinary constructors Success(A) and Failure(Error). Its errors include InvalidLength, AllocationFailed, InvalidIndex, and InvalidByte. A read at a valid index returns Success containing the byte. Identify the two expressions producing outcome layers here: the read and the surrounding acquisition. Predict both before running from this lesson’s src directory:
The inner Success(0) is the read outcome. The outer Success says acquisition succeeded and the body returned that value normally. The buffer is released before that outer successful result is returned.
Code must match the outcomes it needs; these constructors do not throw exceptions or automatically stop surrounding work.

text:
import @ffi.native_buffer as Buffer

main : Unit -> Buffer.Outcome<Buffer.Outcome<Int>>
main () = resource Buffer.Buffer<R> bytes = 4 {
    Buffer.read (bytes, 0)
}


$ ash build --output ./buffer-example \
    --cargo-target-dir "$ASH_NATIVE_CACHE" \
    --root ffi="$ASH_LIBRARIES" 01-zeroed-bytes.ash
/path/to/ash-doc/content/effects/acquiring-a-buffer/src/buffer-example

title: Acquiring a buffer
section: Check the write before using its result
text:
Check the write before using its result
02-write-and-read.ash writes one byte, then reads the same position:
import @ffi.native_buffer as Buffer

main : Unit -> Buffer.Outcome<Buffer.Outcome<Int>>
main () = resource Buffer.Buffer<R> bytes = 4 {
    match Buffer.write (bytes, 1, 42) {
        Buffer.Success(()) => Buffer.read (bytes, 1)
        Buffer.Failure(error) => Buffer.Failure error
    }
}
For four bytes, valid indices are zero through three; valid byte values are zero through 255. A successful write returns Buffer.Success(()), and its match then reads index one. If the write failed, the other branch would return that error instead. Predict which branch this write selects, then the read’s value and its acquisition wrapper:
$ ash build --output ./buffer-example \
    --cargo-target-dir "$ASH_NATIVE_CACHE" \
    --root ffi="$ASH_LIBRARIES" 02-write-and-read.ash
/path/to/ash-doc/content/effects/acquiring-a-buffer/src/buffer-example
$ ./buffer-example
Success(Success(42))
The body chooses an ordinary outcome, and acquisition wraps that body result. These wrappers answer different questions and are not flattened.
crumbs: Working with effects and scoped resources

title: Acquiring a buffer
text:
Acquisition failure skips the body
A length must be positive and within the provider’s addressable bound. 03-acquisition-failure.ash requests zero bytes and uses a cell to record whether the body runs:
import @ffi.native_buffer as Buffer

import @builtin.cell as Cell

main : Unit -> (Buffer.Outcome<Int>, Int)
main () = resource cell<C> entered = 0 {
    let result = resource Buffer.Buffer<R> bytes = 0 {
        let ignored = Cell.write (entered, 1)
        42
    }
    (result, Cell.read entered)
}
Use the positive-length requirement to decide whether the body is entered. Predict the acquisition outcome and the cell’s final value separately:
$ ash build --output ./buffer-example \
    --cargo-target-dir "$ASH_NATIVE_CACHE" \
    --root ffi="$ASH_LIBRARIES" 03-acquisition-failure.ash
/path/to/ash-doc/content/effects/acquiring-a-buffer/src/buffer-example
$ ./buffer-example
(Failure(InvalidLength), 0)
Zero is invalid, so no buffer is acquired and the body never writes to entered. The result is Failure(InvalidLength) and the cell remains 0. This failure comes from acquisition, before any body value exists.
A valid length can also fail because allocation is unavailable. The program must be able to handle AllocationFailed; this example uses invalid length because it gives a deterministic observation. A provider requirement grants access inside a successful acquisition, not a promise that allocation always succeeds.
crumbs: Working with effects and scoped resources

title: Acquiring a buffer
text:
Check indices and byte values
For a length of two, the valid indices are zero and one. 04-invalid-index.ash attempts to read index two:
import @ffi.native_buffer as Buffer

main : Unit -> Buffer.Outcome<Buffer.Outcome<Int>>
main () = resource Buffer.Buffer<R> bytes = 2 {
    Buffer.read (bytes, 2)
}
The length is valid, but is the read index within its bounds? Predict the read’s outcome and whether the enclosing acquisition still returns Success:
$ ash build --output ./buffer-example \
    --cargo-target-dir "$ASH_NATIVE_CACHE" \
    --root ffi="$ASH_LIBRARIES" 04-invalid-index.ash
/path/to/ash-doc/content/effects/acquiring-a-buffer/src/buffer-example
$ ./buffer-example
Success(Failure(InvalidIndex))
Acquisition succeeded and the body returned normally, but its value was the read’s Failure(InvalidIndex). This is an ordinary returned value: the tool prints it and exits with status 0. Changing the index to one gives a valid read of the initially zero byte.
A byte value must be between zero and 255. 05-invalid-byte.ash records both the write outcome and a later read in ordinary data:
import @ffi.native_buffer as Buffer

type Checked = Checked(Buffer.Outcome<Unit>, Buffer.Outcome<Int>)

main : Unit -> Buffer.Outcome<Checked>
main () = resource Buffer.Buffer<R> bytes = 2 {
    let written = Buffer.write (bytes, 0, 256)
    Checked(written, Buffer.read (bytes, 0))
}
Predict both fields of Checked. If the write is outside the byte range, what will a later read find at the unchanged position?
$ ash build --output ./buffer-example \
    --cargo-target-dir "$ASH_NATIVE_CACHE" \
    --root ffi="$ASH_LIBRARIES" 05-invalid-byte.ash
/path/to/ash-doc/content/effects/acquiring-a-buffer/src/buffer-example
$ ./buffer-example
Success(Checked(Failure(InvalidByte), Success(0)))
Checked is our data constructor for the two observations. The invalid write leaves the byte unchanged, so the later read still returns zero. Use a value within the byte range to make the write succeed. Numeric bounds are checked when operations run; the Int type does not prove them in advance.

title: Acquiring a buffer
text:
Keep nested acquisition outcomes distinct
06-nested-acquisition.ash acquires an outer buffer successfully, then tries to acquire an invalid inner one:
import @ffi.native_buffer as Buffer

main : Unit -> Buffer.Outcome<Buffer.Outcome<Int>>
main () = resource Buffer.Buffer<R> outer = 1 {
    resource Buffer.Buffer<S> inner = 0 {
        Buffer.length outer
    }
}
Trace entry into each body. Which acquisition can return a value without running its body, and what will the outer body return and wrap?
$ ash build --output ./buffer-example \
    --cargo-target-dir "$ASH_NATIVE_CACHE" \
    --root ffi="$ASH_LIBRARIES" 06-nested-acquisition.ash
/path/to/ash-doc/content/effects/acquiring-a-buffer/src/buffer-example
$ ./buffer-example
Success(Failure(InvalidLength))
The inner body does not run. The outer body returns the inner failure as an ordinary value, then the outer scope releases its buffer and wraps that value in Success. Its shape resembles a failed read in an acquired buffer, but its cause is the inner acquisition. Follow the expression producing each outcome rather than guessing from the constructor alone.
These examples separate the producer of each outcome layer:








Example
Acquisition result
Body’s returned value




Zero length (03)
Invalid length
Body never entered


Invalid index (04)
Success(...)
Read’s Failure(InvalidIndex)


Invalid byte (05)
Success(...)
Checked with both access outcomes


Nested acquisition (06)
Success(...)
Inner Failure(InvalidLength)



All six generated programs so far return ordinary values with exit status 0, including those containing Failure. The buffer evaluation rules keep acquisition, access outcomes, and normal release distinct.

title: Acquiring a buffer
section: A success wrapper cannot export access
text:
A success wrapper cannot export access
The lifetime rules from cells still apply. 07-handle-escape.ash tries to return a buffer handle from its owner:
import @ffi.native_buffer as Buffer

main : Unit -> Int
main () = {
    let leaked = resource Buffer.Buffer<R> bytes = 2 {
        bytes
    }
    0
}
What would the success wrapper retain if its body returned bytes? Apply the dependency rule from the resource-scope lesson before reading this source rejection:
$ ash --message-format human --locale en --root ffi="$ASH_LIBRARIES" 07-handle-escape.ash
This value or computation depends on a resource that would be out of scope.
  --> /path/to/ash-doc/content/effects/acquiring-a-buffer/src/07-handle-escape.ash:5:54
5 |     let leaked = resource Buffer.Buffer<R> bytes = 2 {
  |                                                      ^ This value or computation depends on a resource that would be out of scope.
6 |         bytes
  | ^ This value or computation depends on a resource that would be out of scope.
7 |     }
  | ^ This value or computation depends on a resource that would be out of scope.
  --> /path/to/ash-doc/content/effects/acquiring-a-buffer/src/07-handle-escape.ash:5:18
5 |     let leaked = resource Buffer.Buffer<R> bytes = 2 {
  |                  ^ This resource is acquired here and must remain within its scope.
6 |         bytes
  | ^ This resource is acquired here and must remain within its scope.
7 |     }
  | ^ This resource is acquired here and must remain within its scope.
reason: type.resource-escape
The returned handle would depend on the closed acquisition, even inside its success wrapper. The primary label covers the body returning that handle; the related label begins at the acquisition that owns it. Return copied data, such as a read outcome, while keeping all handle access inside the resource body.
The buffer rules define these outcomes, dependencies, and release boundaries. The client acquires scoped access and returns ordinary data; the library owns native allocation and release. No client pointer or manual release is needed for this calculation.

Practice: identify which operation failed
For each task, make a fresh copy of its named program in a scratch directory outside this lesson’s src tree. Predict the outcome, then build and run the copy from its directory with the same ffi root.

title: Combining effects and scopes
text:
Keep the scoring rule visible
We can now give the list calculation one complete contract. Each nonzero item earns its points plus a requested bonus. Zero stops processing. The result reports the completed or partial score, the number of items visited, and how many times the processing scope closed.
The calculation uses features already introduced separately: a policy effect, a scoped counter, a stopping handler, and a cleanup action. We will derive its responsibilities from the earlier pure calculation, then trace a normal run and an early stop through the same code.
The pure comparison in 00-pure-calculation.ash passes the bonus directly. It uses the data declarations from the sibling scoring.ash shown next:
For each nonzero item, add its value and the bonus to the accumulator. At zero, return Stopped total; at End, return Finished total. Trace the two items with bonus 2 and predict the outcome. Run from this lesson’s src directory, where the sibling module already supplies the data declarations:
The two contributions are 20 + 2 and 22 + 2. Their total reaches End, which constructs Finished(46).
The effectful version keeps that arithmetic and stopping point. It changes how the bonus is obtained, makes visits observable, and gives scope completion its own action.

title: Combining effects and scopes
text:
import scoring as Scoring

sum_scores : (Scoring.Scores, Int, Int) -> Scoring.Outcome
sum_scores (Scoring.End, total, bonus) = Scoring.Finished total
sum_scores (Scoring.Item(value, rest), total, bonus) = match value == 0 {
    true => Scoring.Stopped total
    false => sum_scores (rest, total + value + bonus, bonus)
}

main : Unit -> Scoring.Outcome
main () = sum_scores (Scoring.Item(20, Scoring.Item(22, Scoring.End)), 0, 2)

$ ash 00-pure-calculation.ash
Finished(46) : Outcome

title: Combining effects and scopes
text:
Run the completed calculation
01-finished.ash sits beside the module and supplies a bonus of two:
import scoring as Scoring

main : Unit -> (Scoring.Outcome, Int, Int)
main () = {
    let values = Scoring.Item(20, Scoring.Item(22, Scoring.End))
    handle (Scoring.run values) with Scoring.Bonus {
        amount ignored => resume 2
    }
}
Predict each report field separately. Compute the score from item contributions, count the visit requests, and identify when the cleanup runs. Remember that resuming a bonus request continues after it without repeating the preceding visit:
$ ash 01-finished.ash
(Finished(46), 2, 1) : (Outcome, Int, Int)
The two items earn 22 and 24, giving the pure version’s score of 46. Each was visited once, and normal completion invoked on_close once. The other two fields expose the visit and completion behavior we added. Importing the module does not initialize those cells; each call to run executes its own acquisitions.
Read the outward contracts from the inside out:







Boundary
Requirements still needed outside it




sum_scores
Bonus, Stop, and Visit


The visit handler
Bonus, Stop, and access to visited


The cleanup and stop handler
Bonus and access to the two live cells


The two resource scopes
Bonus


The entry’s bonus handler
None



Cleanup’s cell access contributes to the effects of closing, including when closing happens during discard. The resource scopes supply those exact cell interpreters. Bonus remains public because the entry chooses its policy; Stop and Visit remain private implementation choices.

title: Explore algorithms and effects in Ash
text:
How to work through a case
The Learn Ash path builds the language model needed here: modules, functions, patterns, recursive data, higher-order functions, and parameterized definitions. Complete its first seventeen lessons before beginning these cases. The cases are written for intermediate and advanced readers: the algorithm cases assume comfort with recursive data and higher-order functions, and the later cases assume the effects path. Keep the same ash executable available through the shared setup.
The Cases path asks what changes when a program must do more than produce the right value. Each chapter begins with a recursive representation, makes an algorithmic choice visible in complete Ash programs, and then accounts for the work and retained data caused by that choice. Later cases change the representation when an operation or invariant demands it.
The short effect Cases then apply the effects path to scoped state, replaceable dependencies, scripted sessions, search budgets, checked byte storage, and hook pipelines. Each isolates one concept in a small program; its introduction names the relevant effects prerequisites.
The application Cases continue through finite models. A batch retains its primary outcome alongside ordered completion reports, then gives the caller an explicit policy for interpreting them. An order calculation compares explicit pricing functions, selected imported evidence, and locally supplied policies whose methods retain a tariff. An immutable world joins component stores by entity identifier, then compares direct and generic movement while preserving the original snapshot. A journal compares cancellation with explicit compensation, then uses saved snapshots and commit flags to restore staged state across nested scopes. An event pipeline compares internal snapshots with an explicit public view, then separates the public shape from the application policy that keeps sensitive values out of it. A controller checks a proposed batch against its own artifact and allowed positions before returning a decision, then compares rejection with cancellation. A sorter charges comparisons before performing them and returns either a complete stable ordering or cancellation. An independent reference exposes how the insertion position preserves the original order of ties. A tagged frame pairs golden byte lists with a scoped direct decoder, keeping logical input length separate from allocated capacity and copied messages separate from live buffer access.
Start in this directory so the commands in each chapter match your shell:
The diagnostic reading notes explain the shell prompt, English output, and source-path convention used in rejection transcripts. Run those commands from this same Cases directory.
Use the same cycle for each observation:
The checked-in programs remain the canonical observations. Restore a source after experimenting if you want to compare it with the chapter again.

title: Explore algorithms and effects in Ash
text:
Cases in order

Folding recursive lists — separate a list traversal from the operations supplied to a strict right fold.
Building finite lists — use a transition and a structural measure to produce a complete eager list.
Accumulating list results — use accumulator state to avoid repeated append traversal while preserving the same reversed value.
Representing a dictionary as a list — use explicit equality for selective lookup, contrast its work with a strict fold, and observe older dictionary versions retained behind new front entries.
Folding branching data — fold both branches, compare equal-size trees with different heights, and contrast selective search with whole-tree fold work.
Searching an ordered tree — pass an explicit comparator to ordered lookup and insertion, state the descendant invariant, and observe why an unbalanced tree provides no logarithmic guarantee.
Abstracting key order — replace repeated comparator arguments with an Order<K> requirement and explicitly select the implementation evidence used by each client.
Protecting the dictionary invariant — keep Dictionary nameable while hiding its constructors, and combine that opacity with explicitly selected ordering evidence.
Guaranteeing logarithmic retrieval — maintain an opaque persistent red-black representation whose ordering and color invariants bound height while preserving the dictionary API.
Resuming tree traversal — use an opaque eager iterator whose private frames retain unfinished in-order work, then distinguish one step’s worst-case cost from one linear traversal’s amortized frame work.
Implementing a persistent FIFO frontier — split logical order between a front and reversed rear, transfer eagerly only when removal needs it, and bound list-node work along one successor history.
Choosing a search frontier — hold one shared search transition fixed, let LIFO return a longer path and FIFO return the shortest path, guard the cycle by marking before addition, and account for logical pending entries separately.
Numbering a tree’s leaves — compare explicit state passing with a fresh-number request handled by a scoped cell.
Measuring tree-search comparisons — measure the same lookup in two tree shapes through a handler.
Supplying an order’s dependencies — run one calculation under regular, promotional, and unavailable responses.
Running a scripted session — keep domain transitions pure while a handler supplies commands and builds the transcript.
Bounding search work — request permission before each nonempty expansion and distinguish exhaustion from absence.
Compressing parent paths — compare reads and writes with and without compression in a scoped buffer.
Reading a bounded byte message — separate parsing from a scoped cursor, and distinguish truncation from acquisition failure.
Controlling a hook pipeline — combine local hook transformations with ordinary policy and trace handlers; connect the synchronous pipeline to reactive composition.
Preserving outcomes through cleanup — retain the body outcome and ordered completion reports, distinguish reporting from merely constructing an error, and choose a caller policy explicitly.
Supplying a local pricing policy — distinguish money from quantity, supply methods that capture a tariff, and retain a quote closure whose exposed type contains no local identity.
Querying an immutable world — join position and velocity stores by entity identifier, select component evidence explicitly, and preserve the original world through repeated movement.
Rolling back a cancellable journal — distinguish control abandonment from restoring state, record commitment with explicit flags, and compare nested snapshots and surviving cleanup interpreters.
Redact before publication — project an explicit public event, observe internal snapshots around redaction, and distinguish the payload type boundary from the application secrecy policy.
Check proposed edits — validate a complete proposal against an independent model and controller-owned inputs, then distinguish edit authorization from continuation consumption.
Cancel a stable sort — preserve input order among ties, request permission before each comparison, and distinguish a complete sorted result from cancelled work.
Round-trip a tagged frame — check golden encoding and decoding independently, distinguish logical length from capacity, and return copied messages from scoped buffer access.

title: Folding recursive lists
text:
Replacing the list forms
The beginning path ended with map, a function whose equations follow the two forms of List<A>. Other list calculations repeat that shape. A sum returns zero for Empty and combines the first integer with the sum of rest. A length returns zero for Empty and combines one with the length of rest. Only their ending values and combinations differ.
A fold names this repeated traversal. It receives the result for Empty and a function that combines one element with the already folded rest. The list still determines where recursion goes; the two supplied values determine what the traversal means for one algorithm.
Every list in this chapter is finite: a chain of More values ending in Empty. The cost statements describe calculations that reach a result; the supplied functions in the examples return for every element.
The shared module begins with the list from the final Learn Ash lesson. It adds Option<A> so a later observation can distinguish an empty list from one with a first element.
Read the type of fold from left to right. Its first input is a combiner. The combiner receives an element of type A, then a result of type B, and returns another B. The second input supplies the B for Empty. After those choices, fold can turn a List<A> into a B.
The equations mirror the datatype:
This definition is a right fold: the result for the rest becomes the combiner’s second input. fold is not special Ash syntax or a built-in operation. It is an ordinary higher-order function checked by the function-application rules and placed in recursive scope by the global-definition rules used throughout the beginning path.
Each algorithm chooses one replacement for each list form:
The nested anonymous functions in each definition match A -> B -> B: the outer function receives first, and the function it returns receives the folded rest. length does not need the element, but its combiner still receives that position because every More carries one.

title: Folding recursive lists
section: One traversal definition, two integer results
text:
One traversal definition, two integer results
The first entry gives the same three-element list to sum and length. Both functions reuse the fold definition, but each call starts its own traversal:
import lists as Lists

main : Unit -> (Int, Int)
main () = {
    let numbers = Lists.More(1, Lists.More(2, Lists.More(3, Lists.Empty)))
    (Lists.sum numbers, Lists.length numbers)
}
Before running it, replace the list forms by the choices in the table. For the sum, the calculation has this shape:
combine 1 (combine 2 (combine 3 0))
1 + (2 + (3 + 0))
6
For the length, the elements do not enter the arithmetic:
combine 1 (combine 2 (combine 3 0))
1 + (1 + (1 + 0))
3
Run the entry from content/cases:
ash folding-recursive-lists/src/01-fold.ash
The result keeps both predictions together:
(6, 3) : (Int, Int)
One fold over this list selects the recursive equation three times, so it calls its supplied combiner three times. The complete entry runs two folds—one for sum and one for length—and therefore makes six combiner calls. For a calculation that reaches a result, one fold over a finite list with n More forms completes exactly n combiner calls; these two folds together complete 2 * n. Empty selects the base equation and causes no combiner call. Here one combiner call means one complete evaluation of combine first folded_rest, not each unary application step within it.
crumbs: Explore algorithms and effects in Ash

title: Folding recursive lists
text:
Rebuilding or retaining elements
A fold can also produce another list. map constructs one More result for every input element. filter constructs More only when keep first is true; otherwise it returns the already filtered rest without another More.
The next entry uses the same input for both operations:
import lists as Lists

increment : Int -> Int
increment number = number + 1

is_42 : Int -> Bool
is_42 number = number == 42

main : Unit -> (Lists.List<Int>, Lists.List<Int>)
main () = {
    let numbers = Lists.More(41, Lists.More(42, Lists.More(43, Lists.Empty)))
    (Lists.map increment numbers, Lists.filter is_42 numbers)
}
Predict the two shapes before running the entry. map should preserve all three More positions and change their values to 42, 43, and 44. filter should retain only the input value equal to 42:
ash folding-recursive-lists/src/02-map-filter.ash
Ash reports:
(More(42, More(43, More(44, Empty))), More(42, Empty)) : (List<Int>, List<Int>)
For a completed calculation over a finite input with n elements, map constructs n output More values. If the predicate retains r elements, filter constructs r output More values. These counts follow the constructor expressions in the two combiners. A completed filter still applies its predicate to all n input elements because the fold calls its combiner n times. The pinned constructor evaluation rule allocates a constructor cell when a payload constructor is applied. The counts describe the output More cells attributable to these functions, not an exact number of heap bytes.
crumbs: Explore algorithms and effects in Ash

title: Folding recursive lists
section: Why the first result still visits the rest
text:
Why the first result still visits the rest
Finding the first element may appear to need only the outer More. The first_and_visits combiner makes a different property observable: it returns the current first while adding one to the visit count carried back from the rest.
import lists as Lists

main : Unit -> (Lists.Option<Int>, Int)
main () = Lists.first_and_visits(
    Lists.More(42, Lists.More(43, Lists.More(44, Lists.Empty)))
)

(Some(42), 3) : (Option<Int>, Int)
The result follows from strict evaluation. The folded_rest binding evaluates its initializer before the block continues, so the recursive fold becomes a value before combine first folded_rest is evaluated. The dynamic binding rules and application rules make both steps explicit.
Each recursive call therefore depends on the result of the call for rest. For a finite list with n More forms, this right fold creates a linear chain of n recursive dependencies. Returning only the first value does not make the traversal short-circuit. A selective algorithm needs a recursive definition that decides whether to follow rest before it makes that recursive call; changing only this fold’s combiner is too late.

title: Folding recursive lists
section: The base and combiner share one result type
text:
The base and combiner share one result type
The type variable B connects three places in fold: the base, the combiner’s second input, and the final result. A combiner returning Bool therefore requires a Boolean base. This complete entry deliberately supplies integer 0 instead:
import lists as Lists

wrong : Int -> Bool -> Bool
wrong first folded_rest = first == 42

main : Unit -> Bool
main () = Lists.fold wrong 0 (Lists.More(42, Lists.Empty))

Replace 0 with false to make the base and combiner agree; this one-element fold then returns true. The rejection follows the rule that checks an application argument against the function’s domain.

title: Building finite lists
text:
From a state step to a list form
The preceding case used fold to consume a finite list. Its input already had every More and the ending Empty; the recursive equations replaced those forms with a result. Production starts from a different question. Given one state, what value should appear now, which state should follow, and when should the list end?
An unfold separates that question from the recursion that constructs the list. A transition examines the current state and returns one of two steps:
This chapter uses only finite production. Its concrete transition follows a smaller part of a recursive natural number until it reaches Zero. The generic unfold type does not by itself establish that every possible transition will eventually return Stop.
The shared module defines two recursive representations and one step representation. Natural describes the remaining number of emissions. List<A> describes the result. Step<S, A> connects them without choosing either representation: S is the state type, and A is the emitted element type.
The equations for unfold translate steps into list forms. Stop becomes Empty. Emit(value, next_state) produces the list for next_state, then places value in front of that result. The transition decides what one step means; unfold owns the repeated application and list construction.
These are ordinary Ash types, matches, and recursive global definitions. The static pattern and match rules check the two Step arms and make their payload bindings available only in the matching arm. The global-definition rules make every local global scheme available before any body is checked, so unfold can refer to itself. It is neither special syntax nor a built-in list producer.
The concrete repeat_step supplies the missing policy. At Zero, it returns Stop. At Next(rest), it emits the selected integer and uses rest as the next state.

Producing three values
The first entry constructs a state with three Next forms. Predict the step and list form selected at each state before running it.
import lists as Lists

Next(Next(Next(Zero))) -> Emit(42, Next(Next(Zero)))
Next(Next(Zero))       -> Emit(42, Next(Zero))
Next(Zero)             -> Emit(42, Zero)
Zero                   -> Stop

section: Why three elements require four transitions
