Why three elements require four transitions
The output alone shows three constructed elements, but it hides the final question that discovers the end. unfold_counted keeps the ordinary step protocol and mirrors the traversal only to expose how many times it applies the transition. Its Stop arm reports one application. An Emit arm adds one to the count returned by the next state.
import lists as Lists

main : Unit -> (Lists.List<Int>, Int)
main () = {
    let three = Lists.Next(Lists.Next(Lists.Next(Lists.Zero)))
    Lists.unfold_counted (Lists.repeat_step 42) three
}

(More(42, More(42, More(42, Empty))), 4) : (List<Int>, Int)
For a completed production from a state with n Next forms, repeat_step causes n transitions that return Emit and one transition that returns Stop. The source-level total is therefore n + 1 transition applications. The n emitting arms construct n result More values.
The pinned dynamic match rules evaluate the scrutinee once and enter only the first matching arm. Here the scrutinee is transition state, so each recursive call contributes one transition application and selects one arm. The count describes this source operation; it does not claim a duration or a number of machine instructions.

title: Building finite lists
section: The producer supplies the termination argument
text:
The producer supplies the termination argument
The type of unfold connects each returned next state to its input state type:
(S -> Step<S, A>) -> S -> List<A>
That connection prevents a transition from changing to an unrelated state type. It does not say that the next state is smaller. The termination argument for these entries comes from the equations for repeat_step:

Zero returns Stop without another state.
Next(rest) returns the direct rest field as its next state.
A finite seed contains only finitely many enclosing Next forms before Zero.

Each recursive call therefore receives one fewer Next form, and the base form stops production. This is a property of repeat_step and its finite inputs, not of every function with the same type.
For example, a transition could emit a value while returning its unchanged state:
repeat_without_progress value state = Emit(value, state)
This sketch is intentionally non-executable and is not run. Generic unfold would keep asking the same question, so strict evaluation would not produce a completed result. Ash accepting a transition type is not a proof that the transition reaches Stop.

title: Building finite lists
section: Eager production before a following map
text:
Eager production before a following map
Inside unfold, the produced_rest binding evaluates its initializer before the block continues to More(value, produced_rest). Production therefore reaches Stop and returns outward through every recursive binding before the outermost call can return its complete list. The pinned dynamic binding rules make that initializer-before-remainder order explicit.
The next entry creates a second boundary. Its produced binding completes the entire unfold application before the block enters the following map call. It returns both results so the observation retains the produced list beside the mapped list.
import lists as Lists

increment : Int -> Int
increment value = value + 1

main : Unit -> (Lists.List<Int>, Lists.List<Int>)
main () = {
    let three = Lists.Next(Lists.Next(Lists.Next(Lists.Zero)))
    let produced = Lists.unfold (Lists.repeat_step 42) three
    let mapped = Lists.map increment produced
    (produced, mapped)
}

ash building-finite-lists/src/03-map-produced-list.ash

(More(42, More(42, More(42, Empty))), More(43, More(43, More(43, Empty)))) : (List<Int>, List<Int>)
The preceding case established the count: a completed map over a finite list constructs one output More for every input More. The direct map here preserves that source relationship in its nonempty equation, More(transform first, mapped_rest). After this unfold constructs three More values, map constructs three additional More values. The dynamic application rules evaluate a constructor’s argument before allocating its payload constructor cell. Together with the explicit recursive bindings, that rule supports the construction order used in this account.
These are counts of constructor expressions completed by these definitions. They do not determine exact heap bytes, elapsed time, host stack use, or a compiler optimization. The example relies on strict evaluation throughout; it introduces no lazy data, infinite data, or generic fold/build fusion interface.

text:
One state type throughout the unfold
The final entry supplies a Boolean where the selected transition requires a Natural state:
import lists as Lists

main : Unit -> Lists.List<Int>
main () = Lists.unfold (Lists.repeat_step 42) true

title: Accumulating list results
text:
Append follows its left list
The preceding case used an unfold to carry the state needed to produce the next element. It did not retain a result derived from elements that had already been produced. Reversing a finite list creates that need: after seeing an element, the algorithm can either leave its placement to later traversals or carry the reversed processed prefix forward.
Both choices below produce the same list. Their difference is the source work that connects each element to that result. Append-based reverse completes the recursively reversed rest and then traverses that result again. Accumulator reverse remembers the work already done and passes it into the next recursive call.
Only the familiar finite List<A> representation is needed. The shared module also contains the two reverse functions and counted versions used later in the chapter.
The equations for append are controlled by its left operand. At Empty, the function returns right unchanged. At More(first, rest), it follows rest and constructs a new More containing first after the recursive result is available. The source therefore inspects the left spine and constructs one new More for each left-hand More; it does not traverse the right list. This describes these equations and does not infer a physical pointer-sharing strategy.
The static pattern and equation rules check the Empty and More cases, while the global-definition rules make a definition available in its own body. Those Ash rules support the recursive definitions; the traversal account comes from the particular equations shown here.
In reverse_through_append, the nonempty equation first binds reversed_rest. A binding evaluates its initializer before the rest of its block, according to the pinned dynamic binding rules. The recursive reverse of rest is therefore a value before append begins to traverse that already-built result. Append places the singleton containing first on its right.
The first entry runs both reverse definitions on the same four-element input.
Before running the entry, predict its first field by expanding the outermost append-based step. The reversed rest is [4, 3, 2]; append then follows that left operand and places the singleton [1] on its right:
Predict the same [4, 3, 2, 1] target for the accumulator field. Counting the source work separates the two mechanisms.
Run it from content/cases:
Both fields are More(4, More(3, More(2, More(1, Empty)))). The complete line follows the pinned tool’s successful-output contract: one observed value, its checked type, and a newline.

title: Accumulating list results
text:
Counting the revisited left operands
The next entry uses the counted variants. append_revisits adds one only when it encounters a More in the left operand; its Empty equation returns zero. reverse_revisits adds the counts from all the append calls. fold_left_visits separately counts one visit to each input More handled by the accumulator traversal. The pinned dynamic constructor and match rules govern constructor values and equational-clause selection. The counters remain instrumentation defined by this module, not language operations.
import lists as Lists

main : Unit -> ((Lists.List<Int>, Int), (Lists.List<Int>, Int))
main () = {
    let numbers = Lists.More(1, Lists.More(2, Lists.More(3, Lists.More(4, Lists.Empty))))
    (
        Lists.reverse_through_append_with_revisits numbers,
        Lists.reverse_with_accumulator_and_visits numbers
    )
}
Run the counted comparison:
ash accumulating-list-results/src/02-counted-work.ash
((More(4, More(3, More(2, More(1, Empty)))), 6), (More(4, More(3, More(2, More(1, Empty)))), 4)) : ((List<Int>, Int), (List<Int>, Int))
The append calls receive reversed left operands of lengths zero through three. The extra revisits are therefore:
0 + 1 + 2 + 3 = 6
This first counter excludes the four visits to the original input More values made by reverse_revisits. Under the named More-inspection metric, the append version has ten inspections in this example: four original-input visits plus six append revisits. The accumulator counter reports the four original input More visits. The displayed 6 and 4 are counters for different named parts of the source; they are not a comparison of total operations.
For a finite input of length n, the append left operands have lengths from zero through n - 1. Their extra revisit count is:
0 + 1 + ... + (n - 1) = n * (n - 1) / 2
Append-based reverse also evaluates n singleton More applications, one for each original element, and one copied More application per append revisit. Its result and intermediate More applications therefore total:
n + n * (n - 1) / 2
These append revisit and constructor-application counts grow quadratically with n. Accumulator reverse visits each input More once and constructs one More per visit, so those two named source metrics grow linearly. Neither description is a measurement or promise of elapsed time.

title: Accumulating list results
text:
Carrying the reversed prefix
fold_left is the left fold matching the preceding case’s right fold: it carries its result into the next recursive call instead of combining after the recursive result returns. The extra parameter carrying that result is called an accumulator. In the signature, List<A> supplies elements of type A, while B is the type of the accumulated result. The combine function accepts the current B, then the current A, and returns the next B:
(B -> A -> B) -> B -> List<A> -> B
At Empty, fold_left returns the accumulated B. At More(first, rest), the strict next_accumulated binding completes combine accumulated first before recursion continues with rest. The pinned static function and application rules connect each supplied argument to the corresponding function domain.
For reverse, B is List<A>. prepend constructs More(first, accumulated), so each element moves in front of the result retained from earlier elements. reverse_with_accumulator specializes the fold by choosing prepend and an initial Empty.

title: Accumulating list results
text:
What the accumulator means
The shape of fold_left does not explain which accumulated value is correct. For the call fold_left prepend accumulated remaining, use this invariant:
original = processed followed by remaining
accumulated = reverse(processed)
At initialization, processed and accumulated are both Empty, while remaining is the original list. Both relationships hold:
processed = []
accumulated = []
remaining = original
For preservation, suppose remaining is More(first, rest). The next processed prefix is the old prefix followed by first. prepend makes the next accumulator More(first, accumulated), which is the reverse of that longer prefix when accumulated is the reverse of the old prefix. The next remaining list is rest, so the processed and remaining parts still form the original list.
When remaining is Empty, the processed prefix is the whole original list. The Empty equation returns accumulated, and the invariant says that value is the reverse of the original.
The next entry exposes one midpoint. Its processed prefix is [1, 2], its derived accumulator is [2, 1], and its remaining suffix is [3, 4].
import lists as Lists

main : Unit -> (Lists.List<Int>, Lists.List<Int>, Lists.List<Int>)
main () = {
    let processed = Lists.More(1, Lists.More(2, Lists.Empty))
    let remaining = Lists.More(3, Lists.More(4, Lists.Empty))
    let accumulated = Lists.fold_left Lists.prepend Lists.Empty processed
    let complete = Lists.fold_left Lists.prepend accumulated remaining
    (processed, accumulated, complete)
}
Run the checkpoint:
ash accumulating-list-results/src/03-accumulator-invariant.ash
(More(1, More(2, Empty)), More(2, More(1, Empty)), More(4, More(3, More(2, More(1, Empty))))) : (List<Int>, List<Int>, List<Int>)
Continuing from the derived [2, 1] accumulator and processing [3, 4] produces [4, 3, 2, 1]. This executable checkpoint supports one midpoint. The initialization, preservation, and ending derivation from the source equations is the general argument; it is not a formal proof supplied by the language.

title: Representing a dictionary as a list
text:
Put the newest entry first
The preceding case placed new list elements at the front of an accumulated result. A dictionary can use the same front construction for key-value entries. Insertion then needs no search: it places the new entry before the previous dictionary. Lookup supplies the choice. It can return at the first matching entry, or it can follow the rest after a mismatch.
This newest-to-oldest order gives duplicate keys a meaning. If we insert key 1 with value 10, then later insert key 1 with value 11, lookup reaches 11 first. The older entry remains behind it. The new value shadows the old one; insertion does not delete the old entry.
The shared module gives each key and value one Entry<K, V>. A Dictionary<K, V> is either Empty or a More containing an entry and the rest of the dictionary. Option<A> separates an absent result, None, from a present result, Some(A).
The pinned syntax grammar provides these parameterized nominal declarations and constructor forms. The type and constructor scope makes Dictionary visible in its own More payload and binds each constructor to its nominal type. Under the static tuple and constructor rules, applying a payload constructor such as Entry, More, or Some produces a value of its declared nominal type.
Each shared function uses the pinned equational global presentation: a signature followed by its contiguous clauses. Module-wide global scope makes recursive functions such as lookup and fold_entries available in their own bodies. The static global and module rules check each clause against its declared function scheme.
Start from Empty and apply the three insertions used throughout this chapter. Expanding only the insert equation predicts the complete order:
This newest-to-oldest lookup order is a property of these equations, not a general property of Ash data.
Each insert evaluates one Entry(key, value) constructor application and one front More(entry, dictionary) constructor application. The complete previous dictionary is the new More tail. The pinned dynamic application rules and constructor rules govern those evaluations. The construction account names source operations; it does not yet make a claim about physical storage.
This way of deriving a recursive function from the forms of its input is inspired by HtDP’s design with self-referential data definitions.

title: Representing a dictionary as a list
section: Stop at the first matching key
text:
Stop at the first matching key
lookup receives equality as an explicit function because K can be any type. The pinned static function and application rules check same_key query key against that supplied function type. At Empty, there is no entry to return. At More, lookup applies equality exactly once. The static pattern, match, and coverage rules require the Empty and More equations to cover the dictionary and the true and false arms to cover the equality result. The true arm returns Some(value) and has no recursive call. Only the false arm follows rest. Ash’s dynamic match rules evaluate the scrutinee once and enter only the selected arm.
The first complete entry defines integer equality and asks for the newest key 1 and the absent key 3.
import dictionaries as Dictionaries

int_equal : Int -> Int -> Bool
int_equal left right = left == right

main : Unit -> (Dictionaries.Option<Int>, Dictionaries.Option<Int>)
main () = {
    let empty_dictionary = Dictionaries.empty ()
    let first_dictionary = Dictionaries.insert 1 10 empty_dictionary
    let second_dictionary = Dictionaries.insert 2 20 first_dictionary
    let dictionary = Dictionaries.insert 1 11 second_dictionary
    (
        Dictionaries.lookup int_equal 1 dictionary,
        Dictionaries.lookup int_equal 3 dictionary
    )
}
Before running it, predict the two branches. Query 1 matches the first entry, so its result should be Some(11). Query 3 should cross all three false arms and reach Empty, so its result should be None.

The definition of int_equal uses Ash’s primitive integer equality. The pinned static primitive operation rule requires two Int operands and produces Bool; the dynamic integer equality rules produce true exactly when those integer values are equal.

title: Representing a dictionary as a list
section: Count the comparisons that lookup enters
text:
Count the comparisons that lookup enters
lookup_counted preserves the same branches while returning the number of equality applications it entered. Empty contributes zero. A current match contributes one. After a mismatch, the recursive result supplies the later count, and the current comparison adds one.
import dictionaries as Dictionaries

int_equal : Int -> Int -> Bool
int_equal left right = left == right

main : Unit -> ((Dictionaries.Option<Int>, Int), (Dictionaries.Option<Int>, Int))
main () = {
    let empty_dictionary = Dictionaries.empty ()
    let first_dictionary = Dictionaries.insert 1 10 empty_dictionary
    let second_dictionary = Dictionaries.insert 2 20 first_dictionary
    let dictionary = Dictionaries.insert 1 11 second_dictionary
    (
        Dictionaries.lookup_counted int_equal 1 dictionary,
        Dictionaries.lookup_counted int_equal 3 dictionary
    )
}
Predict one comparison for query 1, because it matches at the front. Predict three comparisons and None for query 3, because every key differs.
Run the counted entry:
ash dictionary-as-list/src/02-counted-lookup.ash
((Some(11), 1), (None, 3)) : ((Option<Int>, Int), (Option<Int>, Int))
The counters confirm the selective control flow: a front hit enters one equality application, while a complete miss enters three. The result None after count 3 is the chapter’s negative semantic observation. Each field’s (Option<Int>, Int) type pairs an optional value with this source counter.
For a fixed query q, let m be the first matching position in front-to-back order, or the dictionary length when no key matches. Direct lookup visits exactly m More forms and performs exactly m equality applications. In the worst case, both named counts grow linearly with the number n of entries.
The counter does not reveal the work inside an arbitrary supplied equality function. Let E_q(k_i) name the source work performed by the complete application same_key q k_i at visited entry i. For a finite dictionary, assuming each required equality application returns, equality sub-work is:
E_q(k_1) + E_q(k_2) + ... + E_q(k_m)
Including constant inspection and branching work for each visited entry gives:
O(m + sum E_q(k_i))
Only under a uniform bound E_q(k_i) <= Emax may we abbreviate this as:
O(m * (1 + Emax))
worst case: O(n * (1 + Emax))

Separate node count from dependency depth
Two trees can have the same number of nodes but different shapes. Let n be the number of Node encounters in a finite structural expansion. Let h be the greatest number of Node forms on a path from the root to Empty, with height 0 for Empty.

Search before folding or after it
A direct search can place its predicate before either recursive call. Here find_counted uses current-left-right pre-order control. It tests the current value first. A current hit avoids both branches. After a current mismatch, it searches left; a left hit avoids right, and only left absence enters the right recursive call. Folded search separates evaluation order from result priority. choose_counted prefers a current match, then a found left result, then the right result. That is the same current-left-right result priority as the direct search. But fold_tree has already completed the left fold and then the right fold before choose_counted applies the current predicate. Changing the combiner’s choice cannot make those earlier branch traversals selective.

title: Searching an ordered tree
text:
Compare at one node
The previous chapter’s direct search could stop after a match, but a mismatch gave it no reason to rule out either branch. An ordered tree supplies that reason through an invariant. At Node(left, key, value, right), one comparison chooses the left branch, the current value, or the right branch. That choice finds every stored key only when the comparison behaves consistently and every descendant occupies the branch promised by its comparison with the node key.
This chapter develops that promise as a property of the program and its data. Ash checks and evaluates the functions, but the nominal tree type alone does not prove the ordering invariant. Keeping those boundaries separate will let us explain both the branch that lookup skips and a malformed tree that hides a key in that skipped branch.
The derivation follows ideas recorded from HtDP about designing from self-referential data and counting named source operations. That source provides inspiration only. The prose, programs, tree shapes, calculations, and exercises here are original; they do not translate HtDP’s examples, sequence, or teaching-language behavior into Ash.
The shared module uses four transparent data types. Tree<K, V> stores keys and values at its nodes. Ordering names the three outcomes needed to choose a branch. Option<A> distinguishes a found value from absence, and Natural provides the visible unary keys and heights in the observations. The pinned syntax grammar provides parameterized declarations, constructor patterns, curried functions, blocks, and matches. The type and constructor scope makes each type visible in its own recursive constructor payload and associates each constructor with its nominal type.
The four compare_natural equations follow the two forms of Natural. Two Zero values are equal. Zero precedes every Next value, and every Next value follows Zero. Comparing two Next values removes their outside forms and compares the two payloads. The pinned global function presentation makes the four equations one curried function, while the static patterns, matches, and coverage rules check that the equations cover both constructors.
The type Natural -> Natural -> Ordering does not make every function of that type a coherent order. Fix one comparator before stating the invariant. We assume every comparison required by an argument returns and that its results form one coherent total order:
For that comparator, Empty is valid. A finite Node(left, key, value, right) is valid when both branches are valid, every key anywhere in left compares with key as Less, and every key anywhere in right compares with key as Greater. A tree valid under this condition is called a binary search tree. The word anywhere matters. Checking only the two immediate child keys would not constrain a misplaced grandchild.
Now derive lookup from the invariant. Empty contains no key, so it returns None. At a node, Ash completes the curried application compare query key before choosing an Ordering arm under the dynamic application rules and constructor-match rules. Only the selected arm body evaluates. Under the invariant, Less rules out the current key and the whole right subtree; Greater rules out the current key and the whole left subtree. Equal returns the current value.
The function globals in this module enter its simultaneous global scope. The nominal types and constructors use the type and constructor scope described above. The global and module rules check the function signatures and bodies. title: Searching an ordered tree
text:
pub type Tree<K, V> =
    Empty
    | Node(Tree<K, V>, K, V, Tree<K, V>)

pub type Ordering =
    Less
    | Equal
    | Greater

pub type Option<A> =
    None
    | Some(A)

pub type Natural =
    Zero
    | Next(Natural)

pub compare_natural : Natural -> Natural -> Ordering
compare_natural Zero Zero = Equal
compare_natural Zero Next(right) = Less
compare_natural Next(left) Zero = Greater
compare_natural Next(left) Next(right) = compare_natural left right

pub lookup : (K -> K -> Ordering) -> K -> Tree<K, V> -> Option<V>
lookup compare query Empty = None
lookup compare query Node(left, key, value, right) = match compare query key {
    Less => lookup compare query left
    Equal => Some(value)
    Greater => lookup compare query right
}

pub insert : (K -> K -> Ordering) -> K -> V -> Tree<K, V> -> Tree<K, V>
insert compare key value Empty = Node(Empty, key, value, Empty)
insert compare key value Node(left, current_key, current_value, right) = match compare key current_key {
    Less => Node(insert compare key value left, current_key, current_value, right)
    Equal => Node(left, current_key, value, right)
    Greater => Node(left, current_key, current_value, insert compare key value right)
}

pub lookup_counted : (K -> K -> Ordering) -> K -> Tree<K, V> -> (Option<V>, Int)
lookup_counted compare query Empty = (None, 0)
lookup_counted compare query Node(left, key, value, right) = match compare query key {
    Less => {
        let (found, later_comparisons) = lookup_counted compare query left
        (found, later_comparisons + 1)
    }
    Equal => (Some(value), 1)
    Greater => {
        let (found, later_comparisons) = lookup_counted compare query right
        (found, later_comparisons + 1)
    }
}

maximum : Natural -> Natural -> Natural
maximum Zero right = right
maximum left Zero = left
maximum Next(left) Next(right) = Next(maximum left right)

pub height : Tree<K, V> -> Natural
height Empty = Zero
height Node(left, ignored_key, ignored_value, right) = Next(maximum (height left) (height right))



Equal names the chosen equivalence between keys;
reversing a Less comparison gives Greater, and conversely;
strict comparison is transitive; and
equivalent keys have the same ordering relationship to every other key.

C(q, k) = min(|q|, |k|) + 1
For these finite unary keys, the successful path performs C(three, two) + C(three, three) = 3 + 4 = 7 internal Natural comparison applications. The missing path performs C(Zero, two) + C(Zero, one) = 1 + 1 = 2. insert also follows one comparison arm. At Empty, it constructs one node. On Less or Greater, it recursively inserts into the selected branch and rebuilds the current node with the other branch unchanged. On Equal, it retains current_key, left, and right, replacing only the value. The next entry retains each earlier tree in a separate sequential binding. The pinned static block rules check the bindings and result, while the dynamic binding rules complete each initializer before extending the following scope.
import ordered_trees as Trees

main : Unit -> (Trees.Option<Int>, Trees.Option<Int>, Trees.Option<Int>)

    let replaced = Trees.insert Trees.compare_natural one 99 original
    let malformed = Trees.Node(

An Ash interface can move that requirement out of the source argument list. The operation declares where Order<K>, and checking must find evidence for that obligation at each use. What changes is the boundary: comparison arrives through evidence selected during checking instead of through a value argument written by the caller.
The shared module begins with the same transparent tree, ordering, option, and unary-natural representations as the preceding case. It then declares the one-method interface Order<A> and an implementation for Natural.
This module has no entry contract of its own. Each of the four entry commands below imports it, so every run loads and checks this complete source before it checks the entry.

Its parameter occurs in compare : A -> A -> Ordering, and the method’s outer type constructor is a function arrow, as required by the static interface rules. An interface is not an ordinary value type. It names a checking requirement whose evidence supplies the method when a constrained occurrence is used.
The four implementation equations preserve the previous Natural comparison: Zero precedes every Next value, every Next value follows Zero, and two Next values compare their payloads. The implementation must be pub because only public facts can be selected by a dependent. Under the pinned public declaration rules, a private implementation remains available only in its defining module, while pub impl publishes a body-free fact in this module’s summary. There is no implementation name or value for an importer to call.
Each tree signature states its requirement after the complete value type:
The where clause is not another function argument and is not part of the result type. While checking one of these constrained globals, its declared requirement is available as abstract evidence. The final Natural implementation equation is recursive for a different reason. While checking compare Next(left) Next(right), its compare left right occurrence uses exact current-implementation evidence for Order<Natural>. It does not start a new search for a concrete implementation. That current-evidence rule belongs to implementation-method checking and the same ordered evidence selection.

import ordered_trees as Trees

    let two = Trees.Next(one)

    let replaced = Trees.insert one 99 original

        10,
        Trees.Empty

        Trees.lookup one replaced,
        Trees.lookup two malformed

}

Retain the algorithm’s premises
Moving comparison into selected evidence does not make its laws part of Order<A>. Fix one implementation whose comparisons required by an argument return and whose results satisfy these premises:

Equal is the chosen equivalence between keys;
reversing a strict comparison reverses Less and Greater;
strict comparison is transitive; and
equivalent keys have the same ordering relationship to every other key.

sum from i = 1 to m of C(query, k_i)

title: Protecting the dictionary invariant
text:
Put construction behind the module
The preceding case made key order reusable, but its tree remained transparent. A client could still construct a Node whose keys occupied the wrong branches. Lookup trusted the ordering invariant, followed one branch, and missed a key that was structurally present.
A dictionary module can close that construction route. It can export the dictionary’s type identity and operations while withholding its constructors. Clients can name and pass dictionary values, but only the defining module can construct or inspect their representation directly.
That boundary controls source access. It does not prove that the module’s operations preserve the invariant, that an Order implementation obeys ordering laws, or that the representation is secret.
The dictionary module retains the preceding Order, Natural, Option, lookup, and insertion behavior. Its recursive representation now begins with pub opaque type.
Under Ash’s public, private, and opaque declaration rules, Dictionary<K, V> is nameable in an importing module, but Empty and Node are not available there as values or patterns. Both constructors remain available throughout this defining module.
The public API is:
Of these operations, empty, insert, and build are the exported routes that return Dictionary values. lookup and invariant_holds observe those values without exposing their representation constructors.
The where Order<K> requirements still declare the needed comparison evidence under the pinned interface and constrained-scheme rules. Opacity changes who can name the representation constructors; it does not select implementation evidence, change lookup’s branch selection, or change insertion’s equations.
The module also contains a private main. When dictionaries.ash is selected directly as the entry source, that main runs. When another source imports the module, its private main is not exported or evaluated as module initialization. Ash modules are passive dependencies, and only the selected entry module supplies the executed main, as described by the specification overview.

title: Protecting the dictionary invariant
text:
Construct through the public operations
Begin with empty, then insert three, one, two, and four.
import dictionaries as Dictionaries
import dictionaries (impl Order)

main : Unit -> (Bool, Dictionaries.Option<Int>, Dictionaries.Option<Int>, Dictionaries.Option<Int>, Dictionaries.Option<Int>, Dictionaries.Option<Int>)
main () = {

    let one = Dictionaries.Next(Dictionaries.Zero)
    let two = Dictionaries.Next(one)
    let three = Dictionaries.Next(two)
    let four = Dictionaries.Next(three)
    let with_three = Dictionaries.insert three 30 empty
    let with_one = Dictionaries.insert one 10 with_three
    let with_two = Dictionaries.insert two 20 with_one
    let dictionary = Dictionaries.insert four 40 with_two
    (
        Dictionaries.invariant_holds dictionary,
        Dictionaries.lookup one dictionary,
        Dictionaries.lookup two dictionary,
        Dictionaries.lookup three dictionary,
        Dictionaries.lookup four dictionary,
        Dictionaries.lookup Dictionaries.Zero dictionary
    )
}
The two imports perform independent static work. The complete import binds public names beneath Dictionaries, but selects no implementation facts. The impl Order item binds no name; it selects the dependency’s public Order facts for evidence selection in this entry. The pinned import rules define that separation. Selecting evidence neither reveals Empty or Node nor weakens their opaque access boundary. This private selector does not re-export the facts, make them transitively available to another client, or create a runtime implementation lookup.

Equal is the chosen key equivalence;
reversing a strict comparison reverses Less and Greater;
strict comparison is transitive; and
equivalent keys have the same ordering relationship to every other key.

A finite dictionary is valid when both subtrees are valid, every key in the left subtree compares Less than the current key, and every key in the right subtree compares Greater. A condition of this kind, which every value of the representation must satisfy, is called a representation invariant.
Under those premises, empty is valid. For a finite valid input whose entered-path comparisons return, completed insert preserves validity. import dictionaries (impl Order)

        Dictionaries.More(

            Dictionaries.More((two, 99), Dictionaries.End)

        Dictionaries.lookup two dictionary,
        Dictionaries.lookup one dictionary

Let insertion j enter m_j existing Node forms. Let C_j(i) count all completed selected comparison-method applications caused by comparing against its ith visited key. The comparison sub-work is:
sum over j of (sum from i = 1 to m_j of C_j(i))

O(n + sum over j of m_j)

title: Protecting the dictionary invariant
section: Check descendant bounds, not only children
text:
Check descendant bounds, not only children
invariant_holds begins with no lower or upper bound. At each Node, valid_between checks the current key against every bound inherited through that path:

the left recursion keeps the old lower bound and installs the current key as its upper bound;
the right recursion installs the current key as its lower bound and keeps the old upper bound.

An immediate-child check is insufficient. In the module’s private example, one is left of two, and three is right of one. Those local relationships hold. But three remains inside the complete left subtree of two, so it must also be less than the older upper bound two.
Run the defining module directly:
ash protecting-dictionary-invariant/src/dictionaries.ash
false : Bool
The defining module can construct this malformed value because its own constructors remain accessible. The value never crosses the public API.
The four bindings in valid_between evaluate the two bound checks and both recursive validations before the nested both applications combine them. Bindings evaluate their initializers before continuing under the pinned binding rules, and function arguments evaluate strictly under the pinned application rules. A completed validation therefore enters both branches even when an earlier Boolean is already false.
For a finite dictionary with n structural Node occurrences whose required bound comparisons return, completed invariant_holds visits exactly those n occurrences. Let B be the number of validator-initiated compare calls. It equals the number of present lower bounds plus the number of present upper bounds:

B = 0 for an empty or one-node dictionary; and
n - 1 <= B <= 2n - 2 when n > 1.

For validator call r, let C_r count every completed method application performed by the selected comparison for that pair, including recursive applications and the terminal Natural equation. Exact comparison sub-work is:
sum over the B calls of C_r
Only when every C_r <= Cmax, with Cmax >= 1, may this be summarized as O(B * Cmax) and therefore O(n * Cmax). The traversal’s surrounding named source work is O(n). These counts describe source operations, not elapsed time or machine instructions.

Keep the guarantees attached to their premises
For finite valid dictionaries and the fixed ordering premises, completed insert preserves the invariant. Starting from empty, completed build preserves it across a finite input list by applying insert in list order. The exact module gives clients no constructor route around those operations.

A cyclic value payload does not add a dictionary Node, and a completed lookup can return Some(cyclic_value) without inspecting that payload. If the entry main returns that option, final structural observation traverses the option and its payload and renders an active-path revisit as <cycle>. A reachable dictionary-spine cycle can prevent the whole-tree validator from returning because it enters both branches. Lookup and insertion follow only their selected path, so a cycle in an unentered branch need not affect that call. A cyclic input list can prevent build from reaching End.

Practice and continue

Suppose build receives three entries for the same key with values 20, 99, and 7, in that order. Predict the retained value and explain which fold and insertion equations determine it.
At valid_between lower upper Node(left, key, value, right), state the two bounds passed to the left recursive call and the two passed to the right recursive call.
Describe a three-node dictionary in which each child has the correct relationship to its parent but one deeper descendant violates an older ancestor bound. Explain why an immediate-child-only check accepts it.

The opaque boundary keeps clients from constructing malformed dictionary nodes, but insertion can still produce a chain whose height equals its number of keys. How can the hidden representation itself prevent that degeneration while preserving the public dictionary operations?

title: Guaranteeing logarithmic retrieval
text:
Describe the colored data
The dictionary from the preceding case hides its constructors, but insertion can still build a long chain. Insert the associations (3, 30), (2, 20), and (1, 10) into an empty dictionary. Ordered insertion puts 2 below the left branch of 3, then 1 below the left branch of 2. Looking up 1 visits all three nodes. Repeating that pattern gives height h = n: one ordered branch can contain every key.
We want insertion to keep lookup paths short while retaining the same associations. For these three keys, 2 can be the root, with 1 and 3 as its children. Lookup still uses the key comparison from the preceding case. The change belongs in how insertion constructs the tree.
A hidden color on each nonempty node will tell insertion when a local path needs repair. We will develop that data, state the operations it needs, then calculate their bodies using the three-association example. Insertion is persistent: it returns a new dictionary, leaving the earlier value available. A data structure is called persistent when every update returns a new version while earlier versions remain usable. The structure this case develops — a sorted tree whose nonempty nodes hide a color, kept short by local rearrangements after insertion — is the literature’s red-black tree.
The keys and values retain their meanings. A Dictionary<K, V> associates keys of type K with values of type V. Its recursive alternatives tell us whether there is an association at the current position. The following non-executable declaration excerpt adds a color to the representation:
Empty has no association. Node contains a color, the left dictionary, a key, its associated value, and the right dictionary, in that order. K and V describe every association in that tree. We reuse Natural, Option, Ordering, and the Order<K> comparison from the preceding case. The new Color has exactly two alternatives, Red and Black.
A color is useful only with rules for interpreting it. Empty counts as black. A black node adds one to the count on every path below it; a red node adds none. We call the common count, including the terminal Empty, the subtree’s black-height. It measures the black forms on a path, rather than all its nonempty nodes.
A subtree is recursively consistent when three conditions hold:
A recursively consistent subtree may have a red root. A completed public dictionary adds one more condition: its root is black, unless the dictionary is Empty. Separating that final condition lets red subtrees participate in insertion. In the three-key result, a black 2 with black children 1 and 3 meets all four conditions: every path counts the root, one black child, and its terminal Empty, giving black-height three. A black 3 with only a red left child 2 also has equal counts. The shorter right path counts 3 and Empty; each longer left path counts the same two black forms. Equal black-height therefore allows some difference in total path length. The rule against adjacent red nodes limits how much longer a path can become.
The opaque declaration controls source access. Importers can name Dictionary<K, V>, but cannot name its constructors under Ash’s public and opaque declaration rules. The defining module can construct any of its forms, including invalid ones. Neither the nominal type nor Order<K> proves the representation laws. We must design the operations to preserve them.

title: Guaranteeing logarithmic retrieval
text:
type Color =
    Red
    | Black

pub opaque type Dictionary<K, V> =
    Empty
    | Node(Color, Dictionary<K, V>, K, V, Dictionary<K, V>)




It has the global ordering invariant from the preceding case. Every left descendant is Less than the current key, and every right descendant is Greater.
A red node has no red child.
Every path from the subtree root to Empty contains the same number of black forms.

title: Guaranteeing logarithmic retrieval
text:
Repair one colored path
We have the function types and the conditions each operation must maintain. Now fill the public operation, follow its call into recursive insertion, and develop the smaller repair it needs. The three-association example will let us check each choice with a concrete tree.
The following calculations are schematic source calculations, not runnable programs or tool output. Numerals stand for the corresponding Natural keys; values such as 10 remain integers.
Begin with the public goal. The type calculation already tells us how the two operations connect: obtain the internal insertion result, then pass that whole dictionary to blacken_root. Assuming those operations do their stated jobs, this expression gives public insertion the required result:
pub insert : K -> V -> Dictionary<K, V> -> Dictionary<K, V> where Order<K>
insert key value dictionary = blacken_root (insert_colored key value dictionary)
The body names the two remaining jobs. We can develop each one from its promised input and result, starting with the insertion that produces the dictionary for blacken_root.

Insert into the recursive data
insert_colored must give public insertion a dictionary with the new or replaced association. Its input is either Empty or Node, so those two alternatives supply its first cases. At Empty, a new association needs two empty children. The replaced Empty contributes one black form. A red node above two Empty children also contributes one on each path, leaving the count unchanged. A black node would make that count two on only the entered branch. This determines the new node’s red color and gives the first expected result:
insert_colored 1 10 Empty
=> Node(Red, Empty, 1, 10, Empty)
At a Node, comparison gives three cases. In the compact node pattern below, a and b name the left and right dictionaries, while k and v name the stored key and value. The separate key and value name the association being inserted. For Less, recur on a. Its type is D, and insert_colored key value a returns D. Assume this smaller call inserts the association and preserves ordering and black-height, allowing a red-red edge directly below a red root.
The returned dictionary belongs with the parent’s association in RArg(insert_colored key value a, k, v). Pass that group to restore after color, then supply b as the right dictionary. At a black parent, restore can repair the returned child’s edge; at a red parent, it reconstructs the subtree for the enclosing ancestor. This calculates the combining expression in the Less arm. Greater keeps RArg(a, k, v) and supplies the recursively returned right dictionary. Each recursive input is a smaller child, so descent through a finite dictionary reaches Empty or an equal key, provided the comparisons return.
On Equal, inserting (2, 99) over (2, 20) retains the stored key, children, and color, changing only the value. This supplies the middle arm without recursion or repair. The completed excerpt is:


insert_colored : K -> V -> Dictionary<K, V> -> Dictionary<K, V> where Order<K>
insert_colored key value Empty = Node(Red, Empty, key, value, Empty)
insert_colored key value Node(color, a, k, v, b) = match compare key k {
    Less => restore color (RArg(insert_colored key value a, k, v)) b
    Equal => Node(color, a, k, value, b)
    Greater => restore color (RArg(a, k, v)) (insert_colored key value b)
}



Repair the returned child
Insertion asks restore to rebuild a parent with one child replaced by the recursive result. A black parent may receive a red child with a red child of its own. The two red nodes can follow left-left, left-right, right-left, or right-right branches. These are the function’s four repair cases. We will follow each equation separately, then add a fallback for candidates that need no local repair.
Every case must retain the same three associations and four intervening subtrees. Short names let us compare the input pattern with the reconstruction: a, b, c, d are the subtrees from left to right; k means key and v means value. (k1, v1), (k2, v2), (k3, v3) are the associations in increasing key order. The indices indicate that order, rather than literal key values or insertion order:
a, (k1, v1), b, (k2, v2), c, (k3, v3), d
Each case collects the first three subtree-and-association groups into RArg values and leaves d separate. The shared helper will place the middle association above black first and last nodes. For now, its promised result lets us calculate the calls that each case needs.
The optional sketches show each candidate above its repaired result. The upper half of a circle records red or black. The lower colors track the ordered associations: yellow is (k1, v1), blue is (k2, v2), and violet is (k3, v3). A white lower half marks Empty, which has no association.
The triangles track whole dictionaries: green is a, orange is b, pink is c, and cyan is d. Each subtree stays unchanged while its attachment changes. After repair, a and b belong below the yellow association; c and d belong below violet. The same colors appear before and after, so you can trace the rewiring without reading names inside the diagram.

Left-left.1 Inserting 3, 2, 1 gives our running candidate: black 3 above red 2 above red 1, following left branches. The black parent supplies the last association, (k3, v3); its red child supplies the middle, (k2, v2); and the red grandchild supplies the first, (k1, v1). The remaining fields name a, b, c, and d in their ordered positions:
1 





Figure 51.1: Rewire the same pieces - left-left.



restore Black RArg(
    Node(Red, Node(Red, a, k1, v1, b), k2, v2, c),
    k3,
    v3
) d = (restore_three
        (RArg(a, k1, v1))
        (RArg(b, k2, v2))
        (RArg(c, k3, v3))
        d
    )
The repeated groups on the right show what survives the pattern. In this example, all four subtrees are Empty. The bindings supply this schematic call to the helper:
restore_three
    (RArg(Empty, 1, 10))
    (RArg(Empty, 2, 20))
    (RArg(Empty, 3, 30))
    Empty
=> red 2 above black 1 and black 3, with the same values
Left-right.2 Inserting 3, 1, 2 still puts the last association at the black parent. Its red left child now supplies the first association. The child’s red right branch supplies the middle. The second pattern selects that changed position, then sends the same ordered groups to the helper:
2 





Figure 51.2: Rewire the same pieces - left-right.



restore Black RArg(
    Node(Red, a, k1, v1, Node(Red, b, k2, v2, c)),
    k3,
    v3
) d = (restore_three
        (RArg(a, k1, v1))
        (RArg(b, k2, v2))
        (RArg(c, k3, v3))
        d
    )
The destination remains red middle above black first and last. Only the fields from which we obtain the groups have changed.

Right-left.3 Inserting 1, 3, 2 puts the first association at the black parent and the last at its red right child. The child’s red left branch supplies the middle. The parent’s group already contains a, k1, and v1; the nested right pattern supplies the remaining pieces:
3 





Figure 51.3: Rewire the same pieces - right-left.



restore Black RArg(a, k1, v1) Node(
    Red,
    Node(Red, b, k2, v2, c),
    k3,
    v3,
    d
) = (restore_three
        (RArg(a, k1, v1))
        (RArg(b, k2, v2))
        (RArg(c, k3, v3))
        d
    )
Here b and c come from the middle node’s children. Their names retain the same ordered positions as in the preceding cases, so the reconstruction call is unchanged.
Right-right.4 Inserting 1, 2, 3 puts the first association at the black parent, the middle at its red right child, and the last at that child’s red right branch. This is the final orientation:
4 





Figure 51.4: Rewire the same pieces - right-right.



restore Black RArg(a, k1, v1) Node(
    Red,
    b,
    k2,
    v2,
    Node(Red, c, k3, v3, d)
) = (restore_three
        (RArg(a, k1, v1))
        (RArg(b, k2, v2))
        (RArg(c, k3, v3))
        d
    )
The four equations differ in where they find the first, middle, and last associations. Each requests the same reconstruction after collecting them.
When no repair case matches. Inserting 2 below black 3 creates only one red child, so there is no red-red edge to repair. Reconstruct the node from the supplied fields. The same fallback also reconstructs a red parent; if its child is red, an enclosing black ancestor will handle that edge:
restore color RArg(a, k, v) b = Node(color, a, k, v, b)
Ash tries these patterns in source order and selects the first matching equation once the arguments have arrived. The final equation handles every remaining color and subtree shape. The pattern and coverage rules check that the equations cover the input type. The evaluation rules for matches and equations explain which body executes. Neither check establishes the ordering or black-height premises used in the repair calculation.


Construct the shared repair result
restore_three receives three RArg values and the final subtree d. Unpack the groups to name a, b, c, their keys, and their values. The middle association separates the first two subtrees from the last two. Place the first association above a and b, and the last above c and d. Those two constructed dictionaries become the middle node’s children.
Give the first and last nodes black colors to remove the red-red edge and allow red-rooted surrounding subtrees. Keep the middle root red to retain the black-height. For the running example, the four subtrees are Empty and the associations are (1, 10), (2, 20), and (3, 30). The expected local result makes the construction concrete:
Node(
    Red,
    Node(Black, Empty, 1, 10, Empty),
    2,
    20,
    Node(Black, Empty, 3, 30, Empty)
)
This is the result of the local repair, before public insertion blackens its root. Each value stays with its key. The larger drawing shows the general arrangement. It uses the same shapes and colors as the case sketches, with the program’s names beside them:







Figure 51.5: Rewire the same pieces - left-left, with the program’s names.





The ordering tells us where each subtree belongs. a and b are the first node’s children; c and d are the last node’s children. The middle key separates the two constructed dictionaries. Each subtree must retain its inherited key bounds: a below k1, b between k1 and k2, c between k2 and k3, and d above k3. Their roots may be red; making the first and last nodes black also prevents a new red-red edge where those subtrees attach.
In the following definition, the three repeated let patterns unpack the input groups; the final expression rebuilds their components in the arrangement we just calculated. The local names retain the legend: ordered subtrees a, b, c, d and associations (k1, v1), (k2, v2), (k3, v3):
restore_three : (
    RArg<K, V> -> RArg<K, V> -> RArg<K, V> ->
    Dictionary<K, V> -> Dictionary<K, V>
)
restore_three first second third d = {
    let RArg(a, k1, v1) = first
    let RArg(b, k2, v2) = second
    let RArg(c, k3, v3) = third
    Node(
        Red,
        Node(Black, a, k1, v1, b),
        k2,
        v2,
        Node(Black, c, k3, v3, d)
    )
}
This definition is a non-executable excerpt from the complete companion module. Its three local patterns each bind their own input group under Ash’s block and pattern rules. It constructs three dictionary nodes and passes the four subtree values unchanged into them. It needs no comparison: its caller must supply the associations and subtrees in the required order.
For the insertion candidates we will produce, the four surrounding subtrees are recursively consistent and have one common black-height. The candidate may contain the one red-red edge being repaired. If the common height is q, the former black grandparent contributes one, giving q + 1 on every path. The result’s black children each contribute one and its red root contributes none, so every path still has q + 1. This calculation explains why the colors in the body preserve the count.


Restore the public root condition
Internal insertion has kept the associations ordered and the path counts equal, but our calculated root is red. blacken_root has three meaningful inputs: Empty, a black node, or a red node. The first two already meet the public root condition and should be returned unchanged. For a red node, retain its association and both children and change only its color:
blacken_root : Dictionary<K, V> -> Dictionary<K, V>
blacken_root dictionary = match dictionary {
    Empty => Empty
    Node(Black, ignored_left, ignored_key, ignored_value, ignored_right) => dictionary
    Node(Red, left, key, value, right) => Node(Black, left, key, value, right)
}
For our local result, that final case returns black 2 with black 1 and 3 beneath it. Every path gains the same one black form. Recoloring the root changes neither ordering nor key-value associations.


Assemble and run the example
Starting with Empty, inserting (3, 30) creates red 3, then blackens it. Inserting (2, 20) leaves black 3 with a red left child because no repair pattern fits. Inserting (1, 10) now selects Less at both nodes. At Empty, the first equation returns red 1. The pending reconstruction at 2 receives that result:
restore Red (RArg(Node(Red, Empty, 1, 10, Empty), 2, 20)) Empty
=> Node(Red, Node(Red, Empty, 1, 10, Empty), 2, 20, Empty)
Its parent color is red, so none of the four repair equations fits; the fallback produces the temporary red-red edge. The next pending reconstruction, at black 3, receives the candidate derived for the left-left repair. Its first pattern selects restore_three, which returns red 2 with black 1 and 3 as children.
The nested recursive expression is evaluated before restore receives that child value, under Ash’s strict application rules. The calculation therefore descends through comparisons, then reconstructs from the returned child toward the root. A repair can return a red root beneath a red ancestor; the next black grandparent handles that edge. Starting from a valid black-rooted dictionary ensures that any such edge has a black grandparent before the internal result reaches the top.
The final blacken_root call changes the returned red 2 to black. Predict that black root with black children 1 and 3, and the original values 10, 20, and 30 still paired with their keys.
The complete client below names the three Natural keys explicitly and uses only public operations. The impl Order import item supplies the public ordering implementation, as in the preceding case.
import dictionaries (Dictionary, Natural, Zero, Next, empty, insert, impl Order)

main : Unit -> Dictionary<Natural, Int>
main () = {
    let one = Next(Zero)
    let two = Next(one)
    let three = Next(two)
    let after_three = insert three 30 (empty ())
    let after_two = insert two 20 after_three
    insert one 10 after_two
}
Run it from content/cases:
ash guaranteeing-logarithmic-retrieval/src/03-repair.ash
Node(Black, Node(Black, Empty, Next(Zero), 10, Empty), Next(Next(Zero)), 20, Node(Black, Empty, Next(Next(Next(Zero))), 30, Empty)) : Dictionary<Natural, Int>
The printed tree makes each predicted association and color visible. Opacity prevents the client from constructing or matching these nodes; the tool can still display the returned value. The result checks this particular calculation. It does not establish preservation for every dictionary.
The complete dictionary module also contains the ordering and balance checks used later in the chapter. valid_between checks inherited key bounds. A separate pass obtains each child’s black-height, rejects red-red edges and unequal counts, and a final check examines the root. Both passes bind both recursive child results before combining them. Ash’s strict binding rules mean that a completed validation enters both branches.
The defining module’s private main constructs five trees to distinguish these checks. Predict one true followed by four false values:

a valid one-node black tree;
a deeper key beyond an inherited ordering bound;
a red root whose recursive properties otherwise hold;
a red parent with red children whose ordering and black-height hold; and
two root paths with different black counts.

Run the complete companion directly from content/cases:
ash guaranteeing-logarithmic-retrieval/src/dictionaries.ash
(true, false, false, false, false) : (Bool, Bool, Bool, Bool, Bool)
This observation distinguishes the selected malformed values from the valid one. The finite examples supplement the ordering and black-height calculations; they do not replace the argument about what repair preserves.
This functional insertion strategy takes conceptual inspiration from the tradition evaluated in the persistent red-black insertion record. The Ash program, diagram, derivation, examples, and exercises here are original.

title: Guaranteeing logarithmic retrieval
text:
Check every selected insertion prefix
The repair calculation ended with a valid dictionary containing (3, 30), (2, 20), and (1, 10). Could a final successful lookup hide a problem after an earlier insertion? Starting from the empty dictionary, we want observations after 3, after 3, 2, and after 3, 2, 1. Each is an insertion prefix: an initial part of the same input sequence.
After inserting (1, 10), finding that association is only one part of the answer. The dictionary must also retain earlier associations, keep its ordering and color conditions, and return no value for a key we never inserted. We will calculate a client that records selected facts after each step, then checks every association in the final dictionary.

Describe the input and observations
The input is a List<(Natural, Int)>: each element pairs a key with its expected value. For our three-step example, those pairs are (3, 30), (2, 20), and (1, 10), in that order. We also choose (3, 30) as the first association to retain, and 0 as an absent key. These numbers stand for the Natural values whose constructor forms we used in the repair client.
The report needs three new data types. PrefixCheck groups four Boolean observations about one dictionary, in this order:

Its ordering, root color, red-child colors, and black-height satisfy the invariant.
Lookup of the key just inserted returns its expected value.
Lookup of the first inserted key still returns its expected value.
Lookup of the selected absent key returns None.

Scenario groups the empty dictionary’s invariant check, the list of those prefix checks, and a final list of association checks followed by the absence check. Keeping these observations separate lets us locate a failure in the run. A true invariant alone cannot tell us whether a value stayed with its key.
PrefixRun serves a different purpose inside the client. It returns the prefix checks together with the final dictionary, so another operation can examine that dictionary. The type keeps these two results together without exposing the dictionary’s hidden constructors.
The client uses the familiar complete import for qualified public names and selects Order implementations separately:
import dictionaries as Dictionaries
import dictionaries (impl Order)

The three report declarations are non-executable excerpts from the complete client:
type PrefixCheck =
    PrefixCheck(Bool, Bool, Bool, Bool)

type Scenario =
    Scenario(Bool, Dictionaries.List<PrefixCheck>, Dictionaries.List<Bool>)

type PrefixRun =
    PrefixRun(
        Dictionaries.List<PrefixCheck>,
        Dictionaries.Dictionary<Dictionaries.Natural, Int>
    )
List still has its ending form End and its More form containing one element and the rest. Option still distinguishes None from Some. What is new here is the purpose and order of the report fields, rather than another form of list or optional value. The Boolean types describe the shape of an observation; they do not establish that it will be true.
For the selected runs, keys are distinct, the retained pair is the first input pair, and the absent key does not occur in the input. Those choices make the expected report meaningful. If a later entry replaced a value for the same key, checking the earlier value in the final dictionary would correctly return false. Replacement belongs to the next example.


Choose the operation types
Start with the result we want. scenario consumes the entry list, the retained key and its expected value, and the absent key. It returns a Scenario:


scenario : Dictionaries.List<(Dictionaries.Natural, Int)> -> Dictionaries.Natural -> Int -> Dictionaries.Natural -> Scenario

Its body must begin with an empty dictionary and somehow obtain both the intermediate observations and the final dictionary. Give that task to prefix_run. Its inputs are the same four pieces of scenario information, followed by the dictionary to continue from. Its result must be PrefixRun, not just a list of checks, because the caller still needs the final dictionary:


prefix_run : Dictionaries.List<(Dictionaries.Natural, Int)> -> Dictionaries.Natural -> Int -> Dictionaries.Natural -> Dictionaries.Dictionary<Dictionaries.Natural, Int> -> PrefixRun

Supplying the entries, retained pair, and absent key leaves a function from Dictionary<Natural, Int> to PrefixRun. In the recursive case we can supply the smaller remainder of the entries and the updated dictionary to that same operation. The type tells us what can connect; the calculation must determine what each check means and which dictionary to pass.
Lookup returns an optional value. We need two short operations to turn that answer into a Boolean observation. has_value receives an expected Int and an Option<Int>; it must report whether the value was found and agrees:
has_value : Int -> Dictionaries.Option<Int> -> Bool
is_none receives an optional value and reports whether it is absent. It does not inspect the payload, so its signature can retain the type parameter A:
is_none : Dictionaries.Option<A> -> Bool
Finally, lookup_checks consumes the complete entry list, the absent key, and one final dictionary. It returns a list of Boolean observations:


lookup_checks : Dictionaries.List<(Dictionaries.Natural, Int)> -> Dictionaries.Natural -> Dictionaries.Dictionary<Dictionaries.Natural, Int> -> Dictionaries.List<Bool>

We have now described every operation needed by scenario. Fill their bodies from the overall result toward the smaller tasks.



Assemble a scenario
Create the empty dictionary with the concrete key and value types. Passing it to prefix_run produces a PrefixRun. Matching that result supplies checks and final_dictionary with the types required by the report. The empty invariant check is a Bool, checks is a List<PrefixCheck>, and applying lookup_checks to the original entries and final dictionary supplies the List<Bool>. Those are precisely Scenario’s three fields:


scenario : Dictionaries.List<(Dictionaries.Natural, Int)> -> Dictionaries.Natural -> Int -> Dictionaries.Natural -> Scenario
scenario entries retained_key retained_value absent_key = {
    let empty : Dictionaries.Dictionary<Dictionaries.Natural, Int> = Dictionaries.empty()
    let run = prefix_run entries retained_key retained_value absent_key empty
    match run {
        PrefixRun(checks, final_dictionary) => Scenario(
            Dictionaries.invariant_holds empty,
            checks,
            lookup_checks entries absent_key final_dictionary
        )
    }
}

The entry list has two uses. prefix_run consumes it to construct successive dictionaries. lookup_checks uses it as the associations to expect in the finished value. The final pass can therefore check all earlier associations, not just the first and the latest ones.


Record the next prefix and continue
prefix_run follows the entry list’s two forms. With End, there is no next insertion and no new prefix check. The required result is PrefixRun(End, dictionary): retain the supplied dictionary and return an empty check list.
With More(entry, rest), split the entry into key and value. Inserting that pair into dictionary returns next_dictionary of the same dictionary type. All four observations must examine this returned value. Checking the old dictionary would answer questions about the preceding prefix.
The four stated positions of PrefixCheck now determine the meanings of its Boolean expressions: validate next_dictionary, look up the new key and value, look up the retained key and value, then look up the absent key. The two small adapters already have the types needed to interpret those lookups.

The remaining work has the same form as the original task, with the smaller list rest. Assume that calling prefix_run on that remainder and next_dictionary returns its checks in insertion order and the dictionary after all remaining entries. Match that result, place current_check before later_checks, and return the same final_dictionary. This determines the complete equations:


prefix_run : Dictionaries.List<(Dictionaries.Natural, Int)> -> Dictionaries.Natural -> Int -> Dictionaries.Natural -> Dictionaries.Dictionary<Dictionaries.Natural, Int> -> PrefixRun
prefix_run Dictionaries.End retained_key retained_value absent_key dictionary = PrefixRun(
    Dictionaries.End,
    dictionary
)
prefix_run Dictionaries.More(entry, rest) retained_key retained_value absent_key dictionary = match entry {
    (key, value) => {
        let next_dictionary = Dictionaries.insert key value dictionary
        let current_check = PrefixCheck(
            Dictionaries.invariant_holds next_dictionary,
            has_value value (Dictionaries.lookup key next_dictionary),
            has_value retained_value (Dictionaries.lookup retained_key next_dictionary),
            is_none (Dictionaries.lookup absent_key next_dictionary)
        )
        let later_run = prefix_run rest retained_key retained_value absent_key next_dictionary
        match later_run {
            PrefixRun(later_checks, final_dictionary) => PrefixRun(
                Dictionaries.More(current_check, later_checks),
                final_dictionary
            )
        }
    }
}

The base case supplies the promise for an empty remainder. The recursive case adds one observation to the front of the returned list, so the list order remains the insertion order. For a finite entry list, each call removes one More; the recursion reaches End, provided insertion and the checks return. The function records every Boolean result and continues even if one is false.
Each invariant check visits the whole current dictionary. This observation client therefore does more work than its insertions alone. The logarithmic bound later in the chapter concerns the search path; validation has its own cost.
The global scope rules allow these bodies to call helpers defined later in the complete source. The function and application rules check that the argument and result types fit. The list-order promise comes from the equations we just calculated.


Interpret the optional lookup results
For has_value, None cannot be the expected association. Some(actual) contains an Int, so compare it with expected:
has_value : Int -> Dictionaries.Option<Int> -> Bool
has_value expected Dictionaries.None = false
has_value expected Dictionaries.Some(actual) = expected == actual
For example, has_value 30 (Some(30)) is true, while both has_value 30 None and has_value 30 (Some(31)) are false. These are calculations from the two equations, rather than additional CLI observations.
For is_none, the None case is the successful absence observation; any present payload makes it false:
is_none : Dictionaries.Option<A> -> Bool
is_none Dictionaries.None = true
is_none Dictionaries.Some(ignored_value) = false
The payload’s value and type do not affect that answer. These two small functions let the caller distinguish an absent association, a present wrong value, and the expected value.


Recheck every final association
The four prefix flags inspect the new association, one retained association, and an absent key. After inserting 1, they do not separately inspect 2. A final pass must therefore compare every input association against the final dictionary.
lookup_checks also follows the list’s two forms. With More(entry, rest), look up this entry’s key in the same final dictionary, compare its value, and place that Boolean before the checks for rest. With End, all associations have been examined; return a one-element list containing the absent-key check. The result has one flag per entry followed by that final absence flag:


lookup_checks : Dictionaries.List<(Dictionaries.Natural, Int)> -> Dictionaries.Natural -> Dictionaries.Dictionary<Dictionaries.Natural, Int> -> Dictionaries.List<Bool>
lookup_checks Dictionaries.End absent_key dictionary = Dictionaries.More(
    is_none (Dictionaries.lookup absent_key dictionary),
    Dictionaries.End
)
lookup_checks Dictionaries.More(entry, rest) absent_key dictionary = match entry {
    (key, value) => Dictionaries.More(
        has_value value (Dictionaries.lookup key dictionary),
        lookup_checks rest absent_key dictionary
    )
}

It distinguishes what the final pass asks from what the four local flags ask.

title: Guaranteeing logarithmic retrieval
section: Retain build, replacement, and older values
text:
Retain build, replacement, and older values
Balancing changes the hidden shape, not the public dictionary operations. The next client first inserts two and one, retains that older dictionary, replaces two with 99, and extends only the newer dictionary with three. It also builds the extended value independently from the input order (two, 20), (one, 10), (two, 99), (three, 30).
Predict four valid dictionaries. Lookup of two should return 20 in the old value and 99 in both later constructions. Lookup of three should return None in the old value and Some(30) in the extended and built values. The structural part should show a black root with red children where those children are present.
import dictionaries as Dictionaries
import dictionaries (impl Order)

main : Unit -> (
    (
        Dictionaries.Dictionary<Dictionaries.Natural, Int>,
        Dictionaries.Dictionary<Dictionaries.Natural, Int>,
        Dictionaries.Dictionary<Dictionaries.Natural, Int>,
        Dictionaries.Dictionary<Dictionaries.Natural, Int>
    ),
    (Bool, Bool, Bool, Bool),
    (
        Dictionaries.Option<Int>,
        Dictionaries.Option<Int>,
        Dictionaries.Option<Int>,
        Dictionaries.Option<Int>,
        Dictionaries.Option<Int>,
        Dictionaries.Option<Int>
    )
)
main () = {
    let one = Dictionaries.Next(Dictionaries.Zero)
    let two = Dictionaries.Next(one)
    let three = Dictionaries.Next(two)
    let empty : Dictionaries.Dictionary<Dictionaries.Natural, Int> = Dictionaries.empty()
    let with_two = Dictionaries.insert two 20 empty
    let older = Dictionaries.insert one 10 with_two
    let replaced = Dictionaries.insert two 99 older
    let extended = Dictionaries.insert three 30 replaced
    let entries = Dictionaries.More(
        (two, 20),
        Dictionaries.More(
            (one, 10),
            Dictionaries.More(
                (two, 99),
                Dictionaries.More((three, 30), Dictionaries.End)
            )
        )
    )
    let built = Dictionaries.build entries
    (
        (older, replaced, extended, built),
        (
            Dictionaries.invariant_holds older,
            Dictionaries.invariant_holds replaced,
            Dictionaries.invariant_holds extended,
            Dictionaries.invariant_holds built
        ),
        (
            Dictionaries.lookup two older,
            Dictionaries.lookup two replaced,
            Dictionaries.lookup two built,
            Dictionaries.lookup three older,
            Dictionaries.lookup three extended,
            Dictionaries.lookup three built
        )
    )
}

((Node(Black, Node(Red, Empty, Next(Zero), 10, Empty), Next(Next(Zero)), 20, Empty), Node(Black, Node(Red, Empty, Next(Zero), 10, Empty), Next(Next(Zero)), 99, Empty), Node(Black, Node(Red, Empty, Next(Zero), 10, Empty), Next(Next(Zero)), 99, Node(Red, Empty, Next(Next(Next(Zero))), 30, Empty)), Node(Black, Node(Red, Empty, Next(Zero), 10, Empty), Next(Next(Zero)), 99, Node(Red, Empty, Next(Next(Next(Zero))), 30, Empty))), (true, true, true, true), (Some(20), Some(99), Some(99), None, Some(30), Some(30))) : ((Dictionary<Natural, Int>, Dictionary<Natural, Int>, Dictionary<Natural, Int>, Dictionary<Natural, Int>), (Bool, Bool, Bool, Bool), (Option<Int>, Option<Int>, Option<Int>, Option<Int>, Option<Int>, Option<Int>))
The first two rendered dictionaries differ only at the value paired with two. The old one remains separately observable. The extended and built dictionaries have the same structure and associations because the finite build applies public insertion in input order.
Red, Black, Node, and Empty appear because Ash’s observation rules render nominal data structurally. That output does not export the private color type or either opaque dictionary constructor. It gives client source no new name to construct or match.

title: Guaranteeing logarithmic retrieval
text:
Derive the logarithmic bound
Let n count nonempty Node forms. Let h be the largest number of Node forms on a path from the root to Empty. Let q be the equal number of black forms on such a path, including the terminal Empty.


Counting cue. Count terminal Empty in q, but only Node forms in n and h.
For a nonempty valid dictionary, each path contains q - 1 black Node forms. The root is black, and two red nodes cannot be adjacent. At most one red node can therefore accompany each black node on a path:
h <= 2 * (q - 1)
Now let N(q) be the least number of nodes in any recursively consistent subtree whose paths contain q black forms. N(1) = 0 because Empty has one black form and no Node. For q > 1, a black root contributes one node, and both children have black-height q - 1:
N(q) >= 1 + 2 * N(q - 1)
A red root contributes no black form, so each of its nonempty black children still has black-height q. Each black child contributes one node above two subtrees of black-height q - 1. The red-rooted case therefore contains at least 1 + 2 * (1 + 2 * N(q - 1)) nodes, which is larger than the black-rooted case. Induction gives at least:
2^(q - 1) - 1
nonempty nodes. Rearranging the two bounds gives:
q - 1 <= log2(n + 1)
h <= 2 * log2(n + 1)
The empty dictionary has n = h = 0 and is handled separately. These formulas are mathematical consequences of the representation conditions, not Ash numeric operations or timing measurements.
If lookup or insertion enters m existing nodes, it initiates exactly one top-level key comparison at each node, so m <= h. If comparison i causes C(query, key_i) selected method applications, exact comparison sub-work is:
sum from i = 1 to m of C(query, key_i)
Only when every term is at most Cmax, with Cmax >= 1, may the combined comparison account be summarized as O(log(n + 1) * Cmax). Lookup constructs no dictionary Node forms.
For an absent insertion, let r be the number of entered levels whose restore call selects the three-node repair, and let b be 1 exactly when root blackening constructs a replacement root. The evaluated source Node applications are:
m + 1 + 2r + b
Each entered level returns either one fallback Node or a repaired result with three Node forms. Counting one result form per level as the baseline gives two extra constructions for every repaired level, followed by one red leaf and at most one final root construction. Because 0 <= r <= m and 0 <= b <= 1, there are at most 3m + 2 applications. Insertion therefore constructs O(log(n + 1)) source-level representation nodes.
Equal replacement after entering m existing nodes constructs exactly m Node forms: one replacement at the equal key and one fallback reconstruction for each ancestor. It creates no red leaf, selects no repair, and returns the already-black root unchanged.
invariant_holds is separate work. For a finite n-node dictionary, its ordering pass visits every node once, and its balance pass visits every node once. The ordering pass initiates B = 0 bound comparisons when n <= 1; for n > 1, n - 1 <= B <= 2n - 2. Its exact comparison-method work is sum C_r, or O(n * Cmax) only under the same explicit bound on every term. The balance pass performs a bounded number of named source operations per node, with at most one child-height equality and one Int increment. The separate root check is constant named source work. Thus validation uses linear named source work outside comparison-method sub-work, and its two full traversals are not part of the logarithmic lookup or insertion account. This account excludes the arbitrary-precision bit cost of the private Int equality and addition.
